### CHAPTER IV.

->Concerning false wisdom, spurious philosophy, and the philosopher; with<-
->their marks or characteristics.<-

Now that I have sufficiently expressed and revealed to you the nature and essence of true wisdom—and consequently of essential philosophy and the true philosopher—it is most appropriate and necessary that I describe for you the false wisdom of this world, along with the fragile philosophy grounded upon it. Furthermore, I will outline the characteristics and marks not only of this kind of wisdom but also of the philosopher who is hatched and nourished from this false brood or misbegotten offspring.

<margin>James 3:17.</margin>
The Apostle St. James says *that as the true wisdom which is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, willing to yield <note>original: "swasible"</note>, full of mercy and good fruit, not judging, and without envy <note>original: "emulation"</note> or hypocrisy:*

<margin>James 3:14–15.</margin>
So, on the contrary, *that wisdom which is not from above is earthly, animalistic or sensual, diabolical, and contradicts the truth*, and consequently is litigious, immodest, stubborn <note>original: "unswasible"</note>, void of fruit, and full of envy and dispute. Now, as the foundation of the first is Jesus Christ (inasmuch as he is the true wisdom), so the foundation of the other is the traditions and inventions of man, animated and introduced by the devil. This led the divine philosopher <note>referring to St. Paul</note> to say, in distinguishing between these two opposites, "In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" <note>original Latin: "In Christo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ & scientiæ absconditi"</note>.

<margin>Colossians 2:3, 8.</margin>
"I say this so that no one may deceive you with subtle or persuasive words... See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ, because in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells in bodily form" <note>original Latin: "Hoc dico, ut nemo vos decipiat in subtilitate seu suasiabilitate sermonum... Videte ne quis vos decipiat per Philosophiam & inanem fallaciam secundum traditionem hominum secundum elementa mundi, & non secundum Christum, quia in ipso habitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis corporaliter"</note>. All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ. This I say to you, so that no man might deceive you by philosophy and vain sophistication <note>In this period, "sophistication" often meant "adulteration" or "falsification."</note> or fallacy, following the traditions of men according to the elements of this world and not according to Christ; for in him dwells the fullness of the Divinity in bodily form. In this speech, he seems to confirm that all wisdom and knowledge—and consequently true philosophy and all the sciences comprehended under it—reside and are to be sought for in Christ, that eternal wisdom and only cornerstone which fills, informs, and animates all things. They are in no way to be found in false philosophy, which is full of falsification and bears scarcely a semblance of truth. This is because it is masked with worldly human inventions, framed according to the rules and orders of this obscure and erroneous world, rather than the precepts of Christ, the eternal wisdom, who (as the Scriptures tell us) is the worker of all marvelous conclusions, both natural and supernatural. For this reason, the Apostle condemns philosophy in general terms. It is not that the love of true wisdom is anything but good—and consequently the lover of it should be honored and esteemed—but he means that the love of worldly and human wisdom is vain. He terms it so because the pagan <term>Ethnick</term> <note>original: "Ethnick" — referring to non-Christian or pagan cultures.</note> philosophers added "love" <note>original Greek: "$\phi\acute{\iota}\lambda os$" (philos)</note> to their false "wisdom" <note>original Greek: "$\sigma o\phi\acute{\iota}\alpha$" (sophia)</note>. Thus, the word "philosophy" being a term from pagan invention is, in regard to its erroneous and jarring rules, to be rejected. It is only framed and made after pagan traditions; it leads even Christians themselves (and much more the Gentiles) toward errors and seduces them from the knowledge of God rather than directing them toward the true path of finding him. For that reason, it became the occasion for widespread idolatry in this world, in that it persuaded the ignorant worldling to worship the creatures instead of the Creator. For this cause, therefore, it was forbidden for Christians to embrace it, and the Apostle admonishes us to beware of "philosophy and vain fallacy," etc. Of such philosophers who do not build upon the truth, he speaks elsewhere:

<margin>Romans 1:18.</margin>
"The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of those men who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what may be known of God is manifest in them; for God has revealed it to them. For since the creation of the world his invisible attributes are understood and seen through the things that are made—even his eternal power and divinity—so that they are without excuse. Because although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like corruptible man, and birds, and four-footed animals, and serpents, etc." <note>original Latin: "Revelatur ira Dei de cælo super omnem impietatem & iniustitiam hominum eorum qui veritatem Dei in injustitia detinent, quia quod notum est Dei manifestum est in illis; Deus enim illis revelavit. Invisibilia enim ipsius à creatura mundi per ea quæ facta sunt, intellecta, conspiciuntur. Sempiterna quoque ejus virtus & divinitas, ita ut sint inexcusabiles. Quia cum cognovissent Deum, non sicut Deum glorificaverunt aut gratias egerunt, sed evanuerunt in cogitationibus suis, & obscuratum est insipiens cor eorum: dicentes enim se esse sapientes, stulti facti sunt; & mutaverunt gloriam incorruptibilis Dei, in similitudinem corruptibilis hominis, & volucrum, & quadrupedum, & serpentum, &c."</note>. <header>Section 1. Mosaical Philosophy.</header>

*God is revealed from heaven upon all the impiety and injustice of those men who keep the truth of God in unrighteousness, because that which is known of God is made manifest to them, for God has revealed it to them. For the invisible things of him, and also his everlasting power <note>original: "vertue"</note> and divinity, being understood by such creatures as were made since the world's creation, are seen or made manifest. So that they are inexcusable, because when they knew God, they did not glorify him or give him thanks, but faded away or vanished in their own imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened. And therefore, in saying that they were wise, they became fools, and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed beasts, and of serpents, etc.*

<margin>Wisdom 13:1.</margin>
*Again, Solomon speaks to the very same sense in these words: All men are vain by nature, in whom there is ignorance of God, and who, from those good things which are seen, could not understand him who truly is, nor by considering the works acknowledge the craftsman <note>original Latin: "Vani sunt homines omnes naturâ, in quibus inest ignorantia Dei, & qui ex iis, quae spectantur, bonis, eum, qui est, intelligere non potuerunt, neque ex operibus consideratis, ipsum opificem agnoverunt"</note>. All men are vain by nature, who are ignorant of God, and cannot understand him who truly is by the good creatures of his which they behold, nor yet can acknowledge the workman by the consideration of his works. It is very necessary, therefore, for each Christian to be wary in his reading of ethnic <note>original: "Ethnick," meaning pagan or non-Christian</note> philosophy, and to consider seriously—before he wades too far in it or gives too much credit to it—the sayings of the two aforementioned sacred philosophers <note>St. Paul and Solomon</note>, who followed the rules of true wisdom. And again, let him call to mind the precepts which the first of them (I mean St. Paul) gave to the worldly philosophers of Athens, when he saw that they adored and worshipped strange and unknown gods, and how he taught them a new philosophy and new wisdom, namely Jesus Christ, which was a strange doctrine to them. And therefore they said, "Let us hear what this babbler will say, who brings in this strange doctrine of Christ." By this it appears that true wisdom never sounded in their ears or dived into their hearts. Let him (I say) observe that it was at this kind of bastard philosophers, with their philosophy, that the Apostle points when he says in the place cited above: "Let no man deceive you with subtlety and persuasiveness of speech: Beware of philosophy and vain fallacy, which follow the traditions of men, and are according to the elements or rudiments of this world, and not after Christ," etc. In these words he distinguishes false philosophy or wisdom from true sapience <note>wisdom</note>, and he seems to suggest that false philosophy is but vain fallacy, framed after the manner of men of this world—specifically as it was taught at Athens; that is to say, with vain fallacy, subtleties, and appearing to be more in appearance and probability than it was in reality. And for that reason, it filled men fuller of doubts by inquiries made through misty and foggy passages, than if they had gone the plain and simple way of teaching—namely, after the true image of the real and essential philosophy, or rather Sophia or Wisdom, which as the Wise Man <note>Solomon</note> tells us, is: A holy spirit of understanding, unique, simple, modest, eloquent, sweet, clear, loving what is good, humane, kind, stable, certain, having all power, making friends of God, and moving into holy souls <note>original Latin: "Spiritus intelligentiae Sanctus, unicus, simplex, modestus, disertus, suavis, perspicuus, amans bonum, humanus, benignus, stabilis, certus, omnem habens virtutem, amicos Dei constituens, & in animas sanctas se transferens"</note>:*

<margin>Wisdom 7:22.</margin>
*The holy spirit of wisdom is unique and simple in its essence, modest, eloquent, sweet, plain, and open without ambiguity: Loving that which is good, humane, kind <note>original: "benigne"</note>, stable, sure, comprehending in itself all virtue, and an introducer of man to the friendship of God, by transferring itself into the souls of pious and godly men. Look here, we see that in its condition, this description of the good and true wisdom exactly agrees with that wisdom whose character is described by St. James, as was said before: For he calls it modest, kind, peaceful, persuasive <note>original: "suasible"</note>, without envy or competition.*

<margin>James 3.</margin>
*Again, (as St. James says,) it is from above, namely, from the Father of Light.*

<margin>Wisdom 7:25.</margin>
*So also does Solomon express her pedigree thus: Wisdom (he says) is a breath <note>original: "vapor"</note> of the power of God, and a certain emanation or flow of the pure brightness of the Almighty God, and the radiance or splendor of eternal light, and a spotless mirror of the majesty of God, and the image of his goodness <note>original Latin: "Sapientia est vapor virtutis Dei & emanatio quaedam seu fluxus claritatis omnipotentis Dei sinceri, & candor seu splendor lucis aeterne, & speculum sine macula Majestatis Dei, & imago bonitatis illius"</note>. By this definition it is evidently discerned: First, that it is that wisdom which is from above; next, that it is not the vain wisdom of this world, which is nothing but a plain fiction or empty shadow compared to this which alone is truth; lastly, this wisdom brings good fruit with it, for it imparts to men essential virtue and power to act both naturally and miraculously. And therefore the Apostle says, "The signs of my apostleship were performed among you in all power, in signs..."*

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of "pagan" philosophy, specifically contrasting the miraculous power of divine wisdom with the empty arguments of Aristotelian logic. It picks up mid-sentence from a Latin quotation of 2 Corinthians 12:12.</meta>

<page-num>28</page-num>
<header>Mosaical Philosophy. Book 1</header>

<margin>2 Corinthians 12:12.</margin>
...with signs, wonders <note>original: "prodigies"</note>, and powers <note>original: "virtutibus"</note>: *The signs of my apostleship were performed among you with all patience, in signs, wonders, and powers.* And again, <margin>Galatians 3:5.</margin> *He who gives <note>original: "tribuit"</note> you the Spirit and works powers <note>original: "virtutes"</note> or miracles among you.* <note>original Latin: "Qui tribuit vobis Spiritum & operatur virtutes, seu miracula, in vobis"</note> Look here, our Christian philosophers may see how this Wisdom brings forth power and virtue, which St. James, in the place cited before, calls "good fruits." For he says that the Wisdom which is from above is full of good fruits. 

But Paul seems to call the "Ethnic" <note>term: Ethnic philosophy refers to the pagan or non-Christian systems of thought, such as those of the ancient Greeks.</note> philosophy a vain fancy. Therefore, if it is vain, then it is void of good fruit. Consequently, there is no true, fruitful philosophy, nor truly "fruitful" philosopher, except for that which is grounded on that true and eternal Wisdom, Jesus. 

Besides all this, true Wisdom is peaceable, not ambiguous, nor apt to be quibbled with or contentiously disputed. Neither does it need an infinity of distinct "quiddities" <note>term: "quiddities" refers to the subtle, hair-splitting definitions used by medieval Scholastic philosophers.</note> framed out of a man's brain, which leads the disciple into ignorance through their complexity rather than clarifying the brightness of the naked truth. 

But false philosophy is so full of distinctions, subtle and sophisticated evasions, and so subject to quibbles and disputations—so contentiously composed and, in the end, so difficult and effectively fruitless—that instead of true and essential grain, we find only chaff. Instead of truth, we gather only words; instead of essential reality, we collect scarcely a type or shadow of Verity; and in place of sincerity, we find only vanity. In conclusion, it is more a matter of appearance, masked for the most part with a seeming probability, than something that can be truly discerned. For this cause, the Apostle says, <margin>1 Corinthians 2:4.</margin> *My preaching was not with the persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration <note>original: "ostensione"</note> of the Spirit and of power.* <note>original Latin: "Prædicatio mea non in persuasivis humanæ sapientiæ verbis, sed in oſtenſione ſpiritus & virtutis"</note>

For this reason, therefore, we find in one of these two kinds of wisdom the fruits of power, virtue, and miracles—such as the true and divine philosophers produced by the Omnipotent "Cornerstone" (I mean the true Wisdom) in times past, making them manifest to the world. Whereas the other kind can do nothing, indeed, but produce quibbling, disputes, contentions, and fallacies. Their fruits, in the end, are nothing but vanity. It is not I, but the Spirit of Truth that assures you of this much. 

And yet now, even in this later age of the world in which Satan—the prince of this world which is darkness—has the upper hand, this earthly <note>original: "terrene"</note> wisdom or vain philosophy (which is plastered over with dark ignorance) has the dominion. By that means, Christ, who is the true Wisdom, is daily crucified among some Christian philosophers and buried in darkness through the misty and ambiguous clouds of that wrangling <note>original: "brabling"</note>, heathenish philosophy. They so adore and follow this, along with their master Aristotle, as if he were another Jesus rained down from heaven to open the treasures of true wisdom to mankind.

This is contrary to the character of the pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> doctrine, which claims there is an infinity of essential agents in this world—such as demons, stars, elements, meteors, fire, water, cold, heat, humans, beasts, plants, minerals, and the like. They consider these to be secondary <note>original: "subalternate"</note> agents that act and operate on their own. They do not understand that there is but one universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> and indivisible Agent in many dwellings <note>original: "mansions"</note>, who operates by and in an infinity of organic vehicles, in all things and over all things. And this doctrine of theirs has so infected our Christian philosophers who follow their sect that they make distinctions about God's being. They say that He is present "virtually" <note>original: *virtualiter*, meaning through His power or influence</note> and not "substantially" <note>original: *substantialiter*</note> or "essentially" <note>original: *essentialiter*</note>. In this way, they imagine that certain qualities <note>original: "accidents"</note> exist in God that are distinct from His essence. How can this be if He is only the first efficient cause, and not the general cause of all action in this world through His blessed Spirit? He sent that Spirit into the world to do the will of Him who sent it, as well in heaven as on earth. And although things appear in outward show to act or work by themselves in this world, our true philosopher Paul teaches us through his philosophy (the basis or ground of which is the true wisdom, Jesus Christ) that he can discern no other agent but one primary one, from whom are all things, and another secondary one, through whom are all things. He acknowledges both to be but one in essence; for because the one is an emanation out of the other, he alone and by himself operates in all things. This is the perfect tenet <note>original: "tenent"</note> of essential philosophy. Therefore, we should not in any case believe whatever worldly <note>original: "mundan"</note> and pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophy tells us, or persuasively suggests through subtle insinuation, if it is clearly contrary to the true philosophy. And to this, the aforementioned divine philosopher seems to consent in these words:

<margin>Galatians 1:8.</margin>
> *Though an angel from heaven preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed. If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed.*

Therefore, seeing that Aristotelian learning contradicts the positions of essential wisdom or philosophy in several main points, a true Christian ought not to believe its core arguments. As Saint James says, its grounds and tenor are opposite to the Holy Bible, which is the only cabinet of truth; therefore, it is declared by him to be earthly <note>original: "terrene"</note>, animalistic, and demonic. On this subject, Saint Paul writes to his scholar Timothy in this style:

<margin>1 Timothy 6:20.</margin>
> *Timothy, keep that which is committed to your trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called: which some professing have erred concerning the faith.*

In these words, he seems to forewarn his disciples not to be entangled with the sophistical allurements of worldly philosophy, which contradicts the truth and is not peaceful, but troublesome and full of vain disputes and opposition. He pronounces such kinds of philosophy—as well as all the sciences that depend on it—to be not truly but falsely called "science." Moreover, he suggests to his disciples that those Christians who profess it with excessive devotion and confidence have been subtly led into errors concerning the faith. This faith is grounded upon the "anchor-hold" of this invisible wisdom, which is the spiritual Jesus Christ. Again, in this sense, he gives this previously specified caveat to his Colossian disciples:

<margin>Colossians 2:8.</margin>
> *Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments <note>original: "Elements"</note> of the world, and not after Christ, etc.*

By this, he admonishes us Christians to avoid the false philosophy of the pagans <note>original: "Ethniks"</note> and to stick firmly to the rules and doctrine of true wisdom. Therefore, he says in the same text, "Walk firmly rooted and built up in Christ" <note>original: *In Christo ambulate radicale et ædificati in ipso &c.*</note>. By this, he intends to show that Christ is the only cornerstone and groundwork of true philosophy, as all creatures—and indeed the whole world—are founded upon him. Consequently, the foundation of pagan philosophy is sandy and of no validity, regarding which this Apostle says:

<margin>1 Corinthians 3:11.</margin>
> *For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ <note>original: *Fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere præter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Jesus*</note>.*

Now, that this is completely contrary to the false grounds of the pagans, the said Apostle seems to suggest in these words:

<margin>Ephesians 4:17–18.</margin>
> *This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that ye henceforth walk not as other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart <note>original: *Hoc dico ut non ambuletis sicut et gentes ambulant in vanitate sensus sui, tenebris obscuratum habentes intellectum, alienati in vita Dei per ignorantiam quæ est in illis propter cæcitatem cordis eorum &c.*</note>.*

I must now come to specify the erroneous and false doctrines of the Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: A follower of Aristotle's philosophy.</term> or Aristotelian philosophy, so that I may better reveal them to the world by comparing their vanity with the goodness and perfection of the divine and sacred Sophia <term>Sophia: The Greek word for "Wisdom," often used in mystical texts to refer to the divine wisdom of God.</term>.

# Section 1. Mosaical Philosophy.

Why should not the foundation of philosophy be the true wisdom which came from God?

But before I come to answering this objection, I beseech you (gentle Reader) to give me liberty first to apologize a little for myself. Therefore, please understand from my just and upright spirit that I acknowledge and confess this Prince of the Peripatetic <term>The school of philosophy founded by Aristotle.</term> Philosophy to be a person of profound speculation, and that he had as deep an insight into the light of nature as any of the common rank of philosophers in his time. Indeed, he had such a sharp intellect <note>original: "ingeny"</note> and such a subtle and refined spirit that he not only allured the pagan Greeks by his worldly craft and human invention (whereupon he was called by them *Cacodæmon* <note>original: "Cacodæmon"; a Greek term for a deceitful or evil spirit</note>, or a seducing spirit), but even Christians themselves of every sect, even to this present day. They are so wedded to his worldly wisdom that they admire every new student in the Universities who maintains Aristotle’s ideas and does not deviate from his doctrine. 

As for myself, though I may be ranked in that number, I have now collected my thoughts and have, by God’s grace, attained that light of the Holy Scriptures which enables me to distinguish and discern their essential truths from the deceptive <note>original: "præstigious"; in this period, it meant "full of tricks" or "illusory" rather than "honored."</note> ones of the Pagans. I must say with Cicero that *certain promises must be kept, namely those that are lawful* <note>original: "Quædam promissa sunt servanda nimirum licita"</note> and, on the other side, *certain promises must not be kept, specifically those that are unlawful.* <note>original: "Quædam promissa non sunt servanda, nempe quæ sunt illicita"</note> Now God forbid that good Christians should imagine that any oath made to diminish the truth of the Holy Bible should be perpetually upheld, for that would be to rebel against the truth. Therefore, my essential motto in my old age (notwithstanding any allegiance which I vowed to Aristotle in a ceremonial rite during my youth) shall be: *Though Plato and Aristotle are my friends, truth is a greater friend, and therefore ought most to prevail with me.* <note>original: "Amicus Plato, amicus Aristoteles, sed magis amica veritas"</note>

And now to answer the previously mentioned objection directly, we must compare the two wisdoms proposed by the Apostles. 

<margin>1 Corinthians 1:20</margin> 

First, St. Paul says *that God has made the wisdom of this world foolishness.* And again, *The wisdom of this world is foolishness before God, for God knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are foolish.* <note>original: "Sapientia hujus mundi stultitia est apud Deum, Deus enim novit cogitationes sapientum quod stultæ sunt."</note>

<margin>1 Corinthians 3:19</margin> 

And for this cause, the same Apostle says in another place: *We have not received the spirit of this world, but the spirit which is from God, and we speak those things which are given to us by God, not in the learned words of human wisdom but in the doctrine of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things: For the physical man does not perceive the things which are of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them.* <note>original: "Nos non spiritum hujus mundi accepimus, sed spiritum qui ex Deo est, & quæ à Deo donata sunt nobis loquimur, non in doctis humanæ sapientiæ verbis sed in doctrinâ Spiritus, spiritualia spiritualibus comparantes: Animalis enim homo non percipit ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei, stultitia enim est illi & non potest intelligere."</note>

<margin>1 Corinthians 2:12</margin> 

By these words, we ought first to examine whether Aristotle was a "physical man" <term>original: "Animalis homo"; referring to a person living only by their natural soul or senses, without spiritual illumination.</term> or not. If so, then what should we expect from him but mundane wisdom and philosophy, which St. James terms "natural" <note>original: "animal"</note> and "earthly" <note>original: "terrene"</note>? Indeed, this is nothing in itself but mere foolishness, as St. Paul tells us, because the natural man does not perceive the things of God, esteeming them as foolishness. The same Apostle bids us to beware of this kind of philosophy and wisdom, since, as he says, *it is grounded upon the traditions of men and the elements of the world, and not upon Christ.* 

<margin>Colossians 2:8, 9</margin> 

But he points at this Greek-style wisdom more directly in these words, in which he distinguishes both it and Jewish wisdom from the wisdom of God, whose foundation is Jesus Christ: *The Greeks seek wisdom, the Jews seek signs, but we preach Christ crucified.* <note>original: "Sapientiam Græci quærunt, Judæi signa, nos Christum crucifixum prædicamus"</note>

<margin>1 Corinthians 1:22</margin> 

He argues by these words that the Greeks search after the wisdom of the world, which consists chiefly in speculation or contemplation, just as the wisdom of the Jews is more concerned with signs and visual demonstrations, for without them, they will not believe. Lastly, the third wisdom—which is that true wisdom that both the Greeks and Jews rejected and scoffed at—was Jesus Christ, in whom the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily. This is the real and essential wisdom which Christians ought to search after, and upon which they ought to ground their philosophy, which is divine and not human. 

<margin>Colossians 2:9</margin> 

But if they reply that perhaps Aristotle had an insight into Christian doctrine, or apprehended Christ in some manner, or at least had an eye toward the wisdom of Moses...

### Mosaical Philosophy. Book [I].

And the Prophets. First, I answer that just as Aristotle lived before the incarnation of the Word, it is also evident that he knew little of the Mosaical learning, which consists of the Creation, brought about by the spagerick <term>An alchemical term referring to the divine process of separation and purification.</term> act of the divine Word. Otherwise, he would not have claimed the world to be eternal. I confess that his master, Plato, was essentially grounded in true wisdom. However, Aristotle, being puffed up with conceit and seeking to disparage the Stoic doctrine of his master, arrogated wisdom to himself by framing or fashioning a new worldly wisdom of philosophy, which was afterward termed *Peripatetic* <term>The school of philosophy founded by Aristotle, known for teaching while walking.</term>. Out of vainglory, he added many of his own inventions to certain truths, making a jumble <note>original: "Galli-maufry"</note> of good and bad, true and false, and wisdom and folly together. This is far from the nature of perfect Christian wisdom, which must be nothing but the truth itself, because it is described by the Spirit of God, in whom there is nothing but truth.

Again, if the Peripatetic, Stoic, or Epicurean doctrines had been perfect and according to the true wisdom of Jesus Christ, why should the Athenian philosophers have so persecuted the right and exact philosopher Paul for teaching the true wisdom of Jesus Christ? In him alone is the fullness of divinity, as the same Apostle teaches in various places. By this, therefore, we may perceive more plainly what kind of wisdom it is on which Aristotle built his philosophy. I will come a little nearer to the point, or the main mark, and compare the divine wisdom expressed by St. James—another true Christian philosopher and Apostle of Christ.

<margin>James 3:15.</margin>
He tells us in the place mentioned above that *the wisdom which contradicts the truth is not from above—that is to say, from the Father of Light—neither is it peaceful and modest, but earthly, sensual <note>original: "animal"; referring to the lower soul or biological nature rather than the spirit.</note>, and diabolical.* Now, it appears that this philosophy or wisdom of the Peripatetics is exactly like that. First, it is litigious and full of disputes, fallacies, petty quarrels <note>original: "brables"</note>, and controversies, which are contrary to the rules of true Wisdom. Therefore, the Apostle Paul advises Timothy to separate himself from those who teach any doctrine other than that of true Wisdom, saying:

<margin>1 Timothy 6:4.</margin>
*They who do so are puffed up and know nothing, but dote on questions and strife over words—that is to say, over verbal distinctions, twisting every passage into a multiplicity of senses. From this comes envy, strife, railings, and evil suspicions, arising from the disputations of men of corrupt minds who are destitute of the truth.*

<margin>2 Timothy 2:23.</margin>
And again, he says, "Avoid foolish and unlearned questions, knowing that they breed strife" <note>original Latin: "Stultas & sine disciplina quaestiones devita; sciens quia gerant lites"</note>. Such is the philosophy of our Christian Aristotelians. For their method and fashion is to be constantly occupied with questions and cavilling <note>making petty or unnecessary objections</note> disputations in their schools. This is the cause of equivocation and the infinity of distinctions, which allow for the maintenance of falsehood as well as truth. This is the foundation of so many opposing sects as we find in common philosophy and religion alike. From this arise disputations, strife, contention, and malice—not only in the schools between contrary factions, but also among the common people who belong to various religions. 

Whereas, if their philosophy or wisdom were founded on the true *Sophia* <note>original Greek: "Sophia"; meaning Wisdom</note>, which is Christ Jesus (who, as he is all in all, is but one simple essence), they would agree in the unity of him who is one and the same in us all. For in him and by him, we are all made brothers and co-heirs with him of eternity. 

<margin>Acts 17.</margin>
And again, seeing that *in him we live, move, and have our being* (as Paul says), we should, as a consequence—and without any question, dispute, or brawling quarrels—know and understand within ourselves that *highest good* <note>original Latin: "summum bonum"</note> which truly wise men seek after and, with a hunger like that of Tantalus <note>A figure in Greek mythology cursed with eternal hunger and thirst for things just out of reach.</note>, so fervently desire. Does not the philosophy of Christ teach us that *the Kingdom of God is within us* <note>original Latin: "Regnum Dei sit intra nos"</note>?

<margin>
Luke 17:21.
1 Corinthians 6:19.
2 Corinthians 6:15.

Or why should our mature senses be battered to pieces by foolish distinctions, which are the inventions of human or diabolical wisdom, designed on purpose to submerge and drown us deeper in the abyss of complexity or the depth of ignorance? The only endeavor of truth is to conduct us through those clouds of errors (in which the foolish wisdom of this world has involved our understandings) toward the fountain of Unity and Concord, which is the eternal Wisdom, the spiritual Christ Jesus. # Section 1. Mosaical Philosophy. 33

<margin>James 3</margin>
Greek philosophy is contentious, litigious, and full of disputes, quarrels <note>original: "brables"</note>, and rivalries. For this reason, it is pronounced by St. James to be *earthly <note>original: "terrene"</note>, natural <note>original: "animall" (referring to the lower, unspiritual nature)</note>, devilish, and not from above*. In contrast, that philosophy which is grounded in true wisdom—which is from above—*must be first pure, then peaceable, gentle, easy to be entreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without judging, envy, or hypocrisy.* For this reason, our Christian philosopher Paul 
<margin>1 Timothy 6:20</margin>
admonishes his student Timothy to *avoid all profane and empty babbling, and the contradictions of knowledge <term>original: "Sciences" (here meaning knowledge or systems of thought)</term> falsely so called, which some have professed and thereby strayed concerning the Faith.* All Christians who have their anchor-hold too firmly fastened to Aristotle’s philosophy should seriously consider this: our eminent Master, St. Paul, seems to warn them with such fervor that the observation of this pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophy—which consists of contentions, questions, vain babblings, and the opposition of "sciences" (which seem like knowledge but are not, being falsely named)—is the reason well-intending Christians have been deceived and have erred concerning the Faith in the true Wisdom and only truth, Jesus Christ. Again, the Apostle James says, *The wisdom which contradicts the Truth is not from above, but is earthly, natural, and devilish.*

<margin>James 3</margin>
Now, I am certain that all good Christians will maintain that the fountain of Truth and Verity is the Holy Bible. What will our Christian followers of Aristotle say if I prove evidently that Aristotle's doctrine strays from the main grounds of Holy Writ (which is the treasure of Truth) and consequently from that wisdom which is the Father of Light? It is a common phrase among our pretentious scholars <note>original: "lip-learned Sophisters"</note> to say, when any contradiction is found between some axioms of Greek philosophy and sacred assertion: "Oh, this is true in Philosophy, but in Scripture it is found otherwise." To these people, I say that if any contradiction is found between the points of one and the other, there is a foul error, falsehood, or contradiction in one of them. Therefore, one of the two must necessarily issue from an earthly and devilish, or worldly and human, wisdom. Now, let every good Christian judge whether we should rather stick to God's Word, which is the only Truth, or the affirmation of Aristotle, who derives his wisdom from the father of lies—I mean worldly wisdom, which for that reason is termed "devilish" by the Apostle.

Others say that men are so deeply involved in the secrets of nature, or natural philosophy, that they have become atheists and will acknowledge no God. They must surely be referring to pagan philosophy and not to that of Jesus Christ. For Christ's philosophy leads and directs the understanding spirit of man even to the Throne and Majesty of the true God; it persuades him to forsake the crowd of this wicked world to betake and return <note>original: "contract it self"</note> to that blessed union from which his bright Spirit was originally derived.

A third sort of men seem to grumble and storm that any man should presume to mingle natural philosophy with divinity, or should dare to attempt to draw any axioms or authorities from Scripture to prove or maintain the principles or causes of philosophy. They aver boldly but erroneously that the Bible only teaches man what belongs to Salvation—that is to say, how we should fear God and behave toward our neighbors—as if to say that the Holy Scriptures had recorded anything in vain. And yet it is plainly found in them *that 
<margin>Colossians 2</margin>

However, if these people would rightly understand that *Philosophy*, in its original sense, means *wisdom* <note>original: "sophia"</note>, they would acknowledge and confess that true and essential philosophy—or wisdom—is nothing else but the sacred wisdom, or the holy spirit of discipline. This is the foundation not only of what worldly men <note>original: "animal men," referring to those focused on the physical rather than the spiritual</note> call "Natural Philosophy," but also of the entire subject of Theology. 

So, if we consider the matter correctly, we will plainly see that sacred Philosophy is nothing other than the groundwork of Divinity. It is an expression of God and his actions within his creatures—or, if you prefer, in things both supernatural and natural. No one can find a single instance where God is mentioned or specified in the Scriptures except in relation to this world he framed and its creatures. Thus, he is *said to be clothed with light as with a garment. To be a consuming fire. To fill the heavens and to make the earth his footstool. To set his tabernacle in the sun. To make the dark clouds his dwelling or tabernacle. To speak in thunder from heaven. To speak with Job out of the whirlwind. To blow out of the north and south. To be everywhere.* 

Also, his Spirit is said *to descend from heaven like a dove, and in the form of cloven tongues of fire, and to fill the earth, and to make man his temple, and to be in all things.* To conclude, all Scriptures are full of nothing else but his essential operation in all created things through his infinite instruments <note>original: "organs"</note>. 

Therefore, I may justly say that true Philosophy (since its foundation is the Spirit of wisdom, which descends from the Father of Light) is effectively the same as Theology. We may make a distinction for the sake of clarity: essential Philosophy seeks after the *highest good* <note>original: "summum bonum"</note> by moving from the creature’s outer circumference toward its internal center. It does this to find or describe that eternal essence who is the only good and the sole actor in all things. In this way, it proceeds by *reasoning from effect to cause* <note>original: "demonstratione a posteriori"</note>—that is, *from the visible creature to the invisible Creator*—according to St. Paul's rules and Solomon's precepts in the passages cited above. 

The Theologian or Divine, however, seems to move in the opposite direction: from the radical center, or the invisibility of God. He proceeds *as if reasoning from cause to effect* <note>original: "quasi demonstratione a priori"</note>—that is, moving from the divine internal act or center toward the visible circumference or external creature. In the end, we can see that both sciences reach the same point: the one and self-same thing, or the highest goodness in effect. 

And yet, it happens that many a scholar <note>original: "Academist"</note> in this world is so distracted beyond the limits of the creature in their research that they seek God out beyond the moon—even beyond the edges of the vaulted world—and so divide him absolutely from his creatures. In doing so, they only attempt or presume to climb a ladder that has no steps or rungs. They wish to soar to the highest pitch without considering the lower degrees; they attempt to find God without any respect for his creatures, even though the Scriptures guarantee us *that he is not far off from any of us.* Therefore, it is unnecessary to seek or expect him beyond the sphere of fire or above the starry heavens, when he is nearer to us than we realize.

# Section I. Mosaical Philosophy.

These Aristotelian "sophistications" <note>logical fallacies or overly complex arguments</note> attempt to disgrace the truth of him who says in plain terms, "God works all in all" <note>original: "Deus operatur omnia in omnibus"</note>. For if we look correctly into the matter, we shall find that just as God fills everything by his essential Spirit of wisdom, so that Spirit works all in every thing which it fills, and it does so without any help. For how can a created instrument <note>original: "organ"</note>, by any act of its own, help the Creator who fills it to operate? Whatever it possesses, it receives from that eternal Action which bestows it. "I," says Jehovah, "am the Lord who makes and does all things alone, and no one is with me" <note>original: "Ego... sum Dominus faciens omnia solus, & nullus mecum"</note>. And again, "The incorruptible Spirit of <margin>Colossians 1:16.</margin> God is in all things." And again, the Apostle says (as mentioned before): "In Christ all things are founded; by Christ and in Christ all things are created; all things consist in him, and he is in all things, holding the preeminence" <note>original: "In Christo omnia sunt condita, per Christum & in Christo omnia sunt creata, omnia in ipso constant, ipse est in omnibus primatum tenens"</note>. Since this is so, it follows that the distinction must be false which claims that God acts indirectly <note>original: "mediate"</note> and not directly <note>original: "immediate"</note>. Consequently, it is false to say that a creature can act by itself without the direct action of God <note>original: "per se sine actu immediato Dei"</note>. It is as if one were to say that the divine essence or virtue is divisible, or that God's essence must be partitioned or separated simply because it exists in many different instruments.

I may therefore boldly conclude and say that if Christian scholars would spend those seven years—which they currently employ in their Aristotelian studies—in true, essential, and sacred Philosophy, they would not err in the manner of the Pagans <note>original: "Gentiles"</note>. Instead, they would embrace the precepts of true wisdom without any rebellion or contradiction. They would hold these so firmly that, at the end of those seven years, they would be complete in that essential doctrine. They would be made fit members to proceed in the straight way of inquiring into and acquiring the mystical wisdom which God has ordained to be revealed to his Elect. Thus, following the example of the Apostles, they might become as powerful in virtue and power as they now appear only powerful in words. Currently, they are hindered from the good fruit that accompanies true wisdom by the erroneous doctrine of their seducing Master [Aristotle]. I know that this good persuasion of mine will make the followers of worldly wisdom storm and say of me, as the Stoic and Epicurean philosophers did to Paul in Athens: "What will this <term>babbler</term> <note>referring to Acts 17:18; "babbler" (spermologos) originally meant a "seed-picker," implying someone who picks up scraps of knowledge without understanding</note> have, or what does he tell us of a new way of learning?" I answer: It is not I, but the Word they follow that teaches them—if they would only be pleased to mark it well and, in the meantime, separate themselves from the rules or teachings of their Heathen <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> Master.

<margin>James 3.</margin>
But I will come to my more immediate proofs, by which I will most evidently show that the doctrine of Aristotle is a manifest enemy, opposite and contradictory to the truth. Because this is so, it is condemned by the Apostle James as a branch of that wisdom or philosophy which is earthly, unspiritual <note>original: "animal," referring to the lower soul rather than the spirit</note>, and devilish.

It appears (and shall hereafter be proved from the Book of Truth) that the power by which God manifestly operates in this world is expressed either by attraction (from the circumference toward the center) or expulsion (from the center toward the circumference)—namely, Contraction or Dilatation. For in this manner, Condensation and Rarefaction <note>the process of matter becoming more or less dense</note> are produced, by which the heavens, the earth, and the elements—along with compound creatures, whether atmospheric phenomena <note>original: "Meteorologicall"</note> or imperfectly mixed, as well as those complete in their composition—were created and made. Furthermore, through this, God operates in this world either sympathetically (that is, by a desire-driven attraction) or antipathetically (that is, by a hateful expulsion). Since all things in this world are effected by attraction or expulsion, let us see Aristotle's opinion regarding the cause of attraction, and then examine whether it accords with the tenor of truth.

The Peripatetics <note>the followers of Aristotle</note>, being persuaded by their Master Aristotle, agree in this: that the winds, thunder, comets, clouds, and other such atmospheric phenomena are made and caused by the attractive heat of the Sun and other stars, which draw up vapors and exhalations out of the water and earth and elevate them into the regions of the air. And therefore, as Velcury <note>Johannes Velcurio (1490–1559), a commentator on Aristotle's physics</note> says <margin>Velcurio's Commentary on Physics, Book 3, chapter 5.</margin> (according to the mind of Aristotle): "In proportion as the vapors are more or less hot, they are elevated higher or lower by the heat of the Sun and other stars, just as we see the Sun drinking and drawing up water" <note>original: "Prout... magis minusve calidi sunt vapores, ita altius, aut humilius elevantur sursum à solis calore aliorumque astrorum : sicut videmus in sole bibente & attrahente aquam"</note>. As vapors are more or less hot, so are they elevated higher or lower by the heat of the Sun and other stars, as we see that the Sun drinks up...

...and attract water unto it. Hence, a clear error has been introduced into this world: namely, the idea that fire and heat suck and draw vapors and fumes toward them. However, it can be made perfectly obvious even to the simplest person—provided they have their human senses about them—that the heat of the Sun and fire actually disperses <note>original: "discusse"</note> and expels things through expansion <note>original: "dilatation"</note>, rather than alluring them through attraction. 

For example, if fire drew vapors toward itself, it would not allow any smoke to leave it. Yet the contrary is seen: fire disperses through dissolution, and through rarefaction <term>the process of making a substance less dense</term> it expels and separates the subtle from the gross. It does not do this with a desire to draw the vapors toward itself; rather, it expels and disjoints them from the whole heavy body it is working upon. This is why we see fumes and smoke fly away; they are forced to avoid the action of the fire, without the fire showing any inclination to retain them. Similarly, if we hold a wet handkerchief to the fire, we will see the watery substance in it thinned by the heat into a steaming vapor. But the fire is so far from attracting it that the steaming smoke will be seen rising up in the house at random, without any evident attraction from the fire. 

The same thing happens with the Sun’s operative faculty. It thins or rarefies water and humid substances through its heat, and consequently, it draws nothing at all toward itself; rather, it breaks down what was thick into thinner portions. Now, the reason that water or heavy humid substances ascend upward once they are rarefied is not due to any attractive power in the Sun or stars, but a natural inclination in the thing itself. For it is a common axiom that *all light and subtle things* <note>original: "omne leve et subtile"</note> tend, by a natural sympathy or appetite, *to move upward* <note>original: "tendere sursum"</note>. Therefore, once it is so thinned, it soars upward by its own inclination toward its natural and destined region or place, as we see in fumes, smoke, and the like. Conversely, *everything heavy* <note>original: "omne grave"</note> likewise *tends downward* <note>original: "tendere deorsum"</note>; everything that is ponderous descends by a natural desire toward the *center*. 

But so that I may more exactly and reliably expose this error of the Peripatetic <note>Peripatetic refers to the followers of Aristotle, who famously taught while walking</note> theory of the attraction of exhalations and vapors by the Sun, stars, and fire, I ask you to observe our *weather-glass* <note>an early form of thermometer or thermoscope</note>, or experimental *machine*. We shall find there through practice that all attraction from the circumference toward the center is caused by cold, not by heat. By cold, the water is drawn or attracted up into the neck of the *glass*, and that is achieved by the thickening <note>original: "inspissation"</note> of the air and its reduction into a smaller space. Conversely, we note that if the Sun heats the head or bowl of the *matrass* <term>a long-necked glass flask used in chemistry</term>, or if the warmth of a hand even touches it, the trapped air expands <note>original: "dilateth"</note> itself and immediately flies away from the heat. It is so far from being attracted by the heat that it actually drives and pushes the water downward. 

Since this is the case—as visual experience, the "mother of fools," has taught us—let our *Christian Peripatetics* <note>Christian scholars who attempted to reconcile Aristotelian philosophy with theology</note> duly observe the "subtle wisdom" of their *Master* <note>Aristotle</note> whom they have followed until now. Let them see and consider how grossly he has erred in the main argument, pillar, or prop of his *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle’s treatise on natural philosophy and atmospheric phenomena</note>. This being so, what else can be expected but that the whole fabric of his system should fall before the eyes of every wise observer? 

To be brief, these and similar errors of his have forced several of his most discreet disciples and naturalists to dissent and turn away from his doctrine—both regarding his opinion on the winds and thunder, as well as the origin of fountains. They were persuaded and drawn to this abandonment by a truer spirit. For *Johannes Fregius*, a very learned *naturalist* and a man who has taken great pains in searching out the truth

### CHAPTER VI.

->*Here, the one great God JEHOVAH seems to call the false wisdom, or wise*<-
->*men and philosophers of this world, to an account for their erroneous*<-
->*doctrine concerning the causes and manner of the creation of the*<-
->*world and the generation of atmospheric phenomena.*<-

I have explained to you in the previous chapter that the great master of the <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> doctrine is not without reason called a *Cacodæmon* <note>original: "Cacodæmon," a Greek term for an evil spirit or demon</note> by the Greeks themselves. This is because he has deceived the world with his inventions, led it away from the right path of wisdom, and directed it toward that way which leads to certain error and ignorance. He does this through the painted mask of <term>sophisticated</term> <note>In this context, deceptive or fallacious</note> reasons, smeared over with a false and outward show of mere probability, pretending that those things are accidental and caused by chance which in truth come from above—that is to say, they are essentially produced by the power of the Holy Spirit, which works in all things. For according to his doctrine, the Earth, the Stars, and the Elements were eternal and not created; he hides this false claim with natural-looking inventions framed out of his own brain, saying, <note>original: "ex Nihilo, nihil fit"</note> *nothing is made out of nothing.* He also gives a human explanation for life and motion, sets limits or borders for the seas, and invents causes according to his fancy for how things are born and how they decay. He speaks of "first matter" and "form" in his own way, though he does not truly know what they are. He tells us—unreasonably—the reasons for snow, frost, ice, hail, rain, and clouds...

## The Third Book of the First Section, Concerning the Essential Principles of Mosaic Philosophy.

### The Argument of this Third Book.

*In this present Book, the Author teaches in general terms the true and essential principles of divine Philosophy. Specifically, he expresses how various and differing the Pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"; referring to non-Christian, particularly Greek and Roman, philosophers.</note> philosophers have been in their opinions concerning the origins of all things. Here he proves that the wisest among those Pagan naturalists stole and derived their main foundations or principles from the true and sacred philosopher, Moses, whose philosophy was originally outlined by the finger of God; its fiery characters were stamped or engraved in the dark <term>Hyle</term> <note>original: "Hyle"; a Greek term used in philosophy to describe the primal, formless matter of the universe.</note> by the Eternal Wisdom, or Divine Word. He shows that although the aforementioned Pagan philosophers claimed the Mosaic principles as their own and assigned new titles to them to better hide their theft, they were not able to dive into the core understanding of them, nor rightly conceive or apprehend the mystery of the everlasting Word. Consequently, they erected upon their principles only a vain and worldly wisdom—fashioned not from the essential rock of truth, nor relying on Christ, the only cornerstone, but framed according to human invention and shaped according to the elements of this world. It is much like a castle made of straw or stubble: though it may be built on a rock, it is still subject to change and easily shaken and toppled by every gust of wind. In conclusion, our Author sets down what the true Mosaic principles are: namely, Darkness, Water, and Light. He then shows that all fullness and emptiness in the world consists in the presence or absence of the formal principle, which is Light. Finally, he shows how the two apparent active properties—namely, Cold and Heat—issue from the two aforementioned fountains of Darkness and Light, just as the two passive natures, Moisture and Dryness, claim their origin from those active properties.*

# Section 1. Mosaic Philosophy.

### CHAPTER I.

->Wherein is set down the uncertainty of the ancient Greek and Arabian philosophers in their opinions regarding the principles or beginnings of all things.<-

It is an evident argument that the Gentile <note>original: "Ethnick," meaning non-Christian or pagan</note> philosophers were not well-settled upon the grounds of their philosophy, but instead wavered in their imaginations regarding the true principles of nature. Among each of their sects, there was maintained and upheld a variety—and sometimes a plain contradiction—of opinions concerning them. For example, **Thales of Miletus**, who was enrolled among the number of the wise men of Greece, held the opinion that **Water** was the beginning of all things. But **Anaximenes** and his disciples affirmed that an **infinite air** was the first cause or origin of every existence. For this reason also, **Anaximander** esteemed this universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> air to be God. 

Again, on the other side, **Zoroaster** argued that all things take their beginning from **Fire and light**; just as the **Pythagoreans** say that there is one universal Fire in and over all things in this world. And truly, if each of these opinions is duly considered, they will be found to approach and have a near relation to the Mosaic truth. For a divine fire or light, issuing forth from darkness (or the dark abyss), suddenly revealed and made manifest by its bright presence the hidden and invisible waters, the subtler part of which is the vast spirit of the air. For this reason, both Thales and Anaximenes seem in some way to agree on one subject. And yet, if we penetrate more profoundly into the matter, we shall perceive that these two insisted only upon the material or passive principle, since from it the substance of heaven and earth, and everything within them, has its existence or material being. 

On the other side, Zoroaster did not without reason choose fire for the primary beginning of all things, in that it proceeded and appeared in action before the waters or moist nature were made manifest—no differently than action goes before passion, or the cause precedes the effect. And yet, nevertheless, he erred in this assertion because the active principle can in no way rightly be considered except in its relation to a passive origin. **Zeno the Stoic**, therefore, being more cautious than the rest, established his opinion concerning the first Principle by a firmer tie, saying that the substance of the fire, being converted into water by the air, is the beginning of all things. But **Empedocles** wanted to be sure to lay his grounds more securely (as he vainly imagined) than Zeno; for that cause, he ordained the **four Elements** to be the radical principles of all things, of which two are agents <note>active forces</note> and two are patients <note>passive recipients</note>.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 1:4.</margin>
Now, the main error of these philosophers in their judgments concerning the principles was that they did not mark or consider that the divine power <note>original: "puissance"</note> or sacred Word was more ancient, and of a greater antiquity, than any of their aforementioned principles. If they had understood this through a riper contemplation, they would have confessed—being instructed and directed by reasons produced from the eternal unity, or the essential point and beginning of all things—that the divine light or sacred emanation (which the Scriptures entitle by the name of the Holy Spirit of Wisdom) was the actual beginning of all things. Yet, even before that, there was another property in one and the same sacred essence, which was termed the **divine power** <note>original: "potentia divina"</note>, which preceded its act or emanation, no differently than the Father is justly said to exist before the Son in time, order, and being, or the Creator before the creature. Thereupon, the wise man says: **"Wisdom was created before all things."** <note>original Latin: "Omnium prior creata est sapientia"</note> 

And yet it is most apparent that some of the Greek and Egyptian philosophers—namely **Plato**, **Pythagoras**, **Socrates**, **Hermes**, etc.—did so instruct their understandings (partly by observing the doctrine of their predecessors, and partly through the experience they gathered in their long travels among the Ethiopians, Egyptians, Hebrews, Armenians, Arabians, Babylonians, and Indians) that they undoubtedly discerned the true light from afar, and as if through a cloud. (Historians worthy of credit have related that Plato, Pythagoras, Hippocrates, and others traveled through most of these countries to increase their knowledge.)

### CHAP. II.

-> What the Mosaical Principles or beginnings were in general: how they were produced and extracted out of "Nothing." Then, what is meant by that word "Nothing." And lastly, the first Principle, which is the dark Abyss or Chaos without form, is particularly described. <-

<margin>Gen. 1.</margin>
The Mosaical Principles are very plain and evident to all who wisely contemplate and observe the words of the most excellent philosopher *Moses* in his first chapter of *Genesis*. Before there is any mention made of that Spagyrical <term>Spagyrical: an alchemical term referring to the process of separating and then recombining the constituent parts of a substance to purify it.</term> separation which was effected by the Word of God or the divine Spirit (*Elohim*) in the six days' work of the Creation mentioned there, it is said that "darkness was upon the face of the Abyss" and that "the Earth was without shape and form" <note>original: "Terra erat inanis & vacua"</note>. Here it appears that the heavens and the earth were not as yet enacted or formed but were one deformed, rude, and undigested mass. Consequently, all things were implicitly comprehended in one dark Abyss, but explicitly they were as yet nothing. 

For example, we see that a great tree—with its body, branches, bark, leaves, and fruit—is implicitly comprehended in a grain or kernel; but explicitly it is no such thing, being only something in the imagination <note>original: "in imaginatione"</note>. *St. Augustine* compares this "Nothing" to speech: while it is in the mind of the speaker, it is as nothing to the person it is spoken to—that is to say, it is something in potential <note>original: "puissance"</note> and nothing in essence. But when it is uttered or spoken, then that which was before implicit in the mind of the speaker <note>original: "in animo loquentis"</note> is now explicitly understood by the hearer. *Plato* compares it in this state of "nullity" to a vision in a dream which, when a man awakes, proves to be nothing except a mere imagination. But because this statement (that God created all things out of nothing) has puzzled the minds of many understanding persons—since it could not be clearly perceived what was intended by this word "Nothing" (*Nihil*)—I purpose in a few words to discuss it and express my opinion on what is meant by it.

The Prince of the Peripatetics <note>This refers to Aristotle, whose followers were called Peripatetics because he taught while walking around.</note> says: "From nothing, nothing is made" <note>original: "Ex Nihilo nihil fit"</note>. This is a learned sentence and an infallible axiom from such a learned personage, if the sense of the word were always to be interpreted the same way. But I say, being founded on good grounds, that if there are any who—either by presumption or through ignorance—are of the opinion that in these words ("God created all things out of nothing"), the word "nothing" (*Nihilum*) ought not to be taken or interpreted as a negative nothing <note>original: "Nihilum negativum"</note> (or such a negative nothing that falls outside the capacity of human reason or intellect). Such a kind of "Nothing" was never meant to be the first matter of Creation. 

It appears both by the infallible sense of Holy Scripture and the sacred light of nature that the first essence and matter of all things was from all eternity in God and with God, being one and the same thing. We prove this out of Scripture in this manner: <margin>Gen. 1. 1.</margin> *Moses* says: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" <note>original: "In Principio creavit Deus cælum & terram"</note>. In this statement, the word "Beginning" (*Principium*) is not to be taken for a negative nothing. <margin>Rom. 11. 36.</margin> For the Scripture tells us in plain terms that "of him, and through him, and in him are all things" <note>original: "ex ipso, & per ipsum, & in ipso sunt omnia"</note>. And therefore, if all things proceed from God the Creator, who is the highest of Entities, it follows that they do not proceed from a negative nothing. <margin>Wisd. 11. 18.</margin> And again, the Scriptures say (as *St. Jerome* translates it), "Almighty Lord, your hand created the world" <note>original: "Omnipotens Domine, manus tua creavit orbem terrarum"</note>—or "the universe" <note>original: "mundum"</note>, according to *Tremellius*—"out of matter" <note>original: "ex materia"</note>...

Invisible matter <note>original: "materia invisia"</note>, as Saint Jerome interpreted it—though Tremellius has it as "From unformed matter" <note>original: "Ex materia informi"</note>—"Almighty Lord, your hand has created the earth or world out of an invisible or unformed matter." Nor could it rightly be attributed to him; that is to say, if all things were not essentially from him, nor took their beginning from him, then it must follow that all things were not made by him, but would have their existence from "Nothing." ...[the things] which are, he might destroy <note>original: *quae sunt destrueret*; a reference to 1 Corinthians 1:28</note>. God chooses the things which are not, to destroy the things which currently exist. For this reason also, Reuchlin <note>Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a German humanist and scholar of Greek and Hebrew</note> speaks of the beginning through the mouths of the mystical and learned Rabbis in these words: It is written in the book of *Bahir* <note>The *Sefer Ha-Bahir*, an early and influential work of the Kabbalah</note>, <margin>Reuchlin, Book 3 of *The Art of the Kabbalah*.</margin> *Nothing is the beginning except wisdom; and this is the infinity itself of the three highest numerations of the Kabbalistic tree, which you are accustomed to call the three persons in the divinity. This is the most absolute essence which, while it is retracted and immanent in the abyss of darkness, and at rest, or, as they say, having respect to nothing, is therefore called Ayin <note>Hebrew: אין; original: *Ain*</note>, that is, Nothing, or non-being, and without end; because we, being penalized by such a thin poverty of mind toward divine things, judge those things which do not appear just as we do those things which do not exist. But when it has shown itself so that it is something and truly exists, then the dark Aleph <note>Aleph (א) is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet; here it represents the transition from potential to manifest being</note> is converted into a bright Aleph: for it is written, "As his darkness is, so also is his light"* <note>original: *Nihil est principium nisi sapientia; & haec est infinitudo ipsa trium summarum cabalisticae arboris numerationum...*</note>.

Nothing is the beginning but wisdom or sapience, and it is the infinity of the three highest numerations of the Kabbalistic tree, which you are accustomed to call the three persons in divinity. This is an absolute essence which—while it is pulled back into the abyss of darkness and remains still and quiet, or, as they say, having respect for nothing—is for that cause termed by the Hebrews *Ayin* <note>original: *Ain*</note>, that is to say, *Nihil*, or nothing, or no entity. This is because we, being affected with extreme shallowness or poverty of wit and capacity in the understanding of divine things, judge those things which do not appear in the same way we judge those things that do not exist at all. But when it has shown itself to be something indeed, and that it does really (in human understanding) exist as something, then is the dark *Aleph* converted into a light *Aleph*: for it is written, <margin>Psalm 139:12.</margin> *As his darkness is, so is his light*, or as the express words of the Prophet are, *Darkness is to him as Light* <note>original: *Tenebrae sunt ei sicut ipsa lux*</note>.

By this it is evident that although darkness or invisibility appears to our senses to be nothing compared to that which is made manifest in light, in truth all things are real and essential before God. Therefore, that "nothing" or deformity—relative to our weak capacity—out of which the waters (the material principle of all things) were originally extracted, seems to him (in whose divine power they remain) a material existence. For as much as nothing exists in God except what is essential reality, or something in being, <margin>Romans 11:32.</margin> but *of him, by him, and in him are all things*, as we are taught by holy Scripture. Therefore, both the dark matrix or womb of the waters, and the watery infant or moist nature which sprang out of the belly of the gloomy abyss or *Chaos*, were really in God before they appeared to sight. That is to say, they remained in the Almighty’s power or will, to be disposed of by him as he pleased, no differently than how the blueprint of a building first exists in the mind of the builder.

That this is so—namely, that the world was framed and made of a matter which was called "without form" because it was invisible—we find proved and maintained by the authority of Scripture mentioned before, <margin>Wisdom 11:18.</margin> which Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius, a 16th-century Jewish convert and leading Hebraist who translated the Bible into Latin</note> interprets this way: *O Omnipotent, your hand has created the world out of unformed matter* <note>original: *Omnipotens, manus tua creavit mundum ex informi materia*</note>. Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> translates this as *out of invisible matter* <note>original: *ex invisa materia*</note>.

Now, the text of Moses seems to confirm evidently that this general matter was waters, which the presence of the all-informing Spirit of the Lord invigorated and enacted as a whole, calling them by the name *Shamaim* <note>Hebrew: שמים; meaning "Heavens" or "waters-there"</note>. These waters were the first material principle of which the world was made, just as a great palace is fashioned or framed out of a rough mass of clay. First, the text mentions the waters upon which the Spirit of the Lord was carried, and it does this immediately after naming the confused *Chaos* under the title of the dark abyss, and the *empty and void earth* <note>original: *Terra inanis & vacua*</note>, and immediately before the separation of the first day. This plainly argues that waters were the material principle, being created or enacted by the Spirit of the Lord, or *Elohim Ruach* <note>Hebrew: רוח אלהים; the Spirit of God</note>, since they were mentioned before the first day’s work.

Secondly, it was that same eternal Wisdom, or the Spirit *Elohim*, who, acting as if playing the part of a midwife, delivered and brought forth this birth, giving it action and form. Again, we may learn from the same chapter of Moses that the waters were the subject of that separation which was effected by the spagyric <term>spagyric: an alchemical term referring to the process of separating and recombining elements through divine or natural heat</term> or fiery power of the said Spirit, or divine Word. Thirdly, the heavens above were made of the purer, brighter, and more worthy waters, and the elementary world beneath was made of the grosser, darker, and viler sort of waters. There was also a middle kind of water <margin>Genesis 1.</margin> which, participating in both extremes, was called the firmament; its main office was to divide and separate the water from the waters. Then, out of the lower waters, by the same Word or Spirit, the Elements were proportioned and placed, their

This is also most plainly verified by the text of the Apostle Peter: *“The heavens were first and the earth, of waters, and by waters existing in and by the word of God”* <note>original Latin: *Cœli erant prius et terra, de aqua, et per aquam existens verbo Dei*</note>. I come now to my description of that universal principle which gives life and being to all the waters and everything fashioned from the waters, and consequently to the whole world.

## CHAP. IV.

### *How the universal formal principle—by which the waters in general, and consequently the heavens, elements, and everything else in particular, were fashioned, informed, and brought into a specific act or essential being, and are preserved in that state—did proceed and was immediately derived from God.*

<margin>Ephesians 4:6</margin>
<margin>Romans 11:36</margin>
<margin>Asclepius 7</margin>
I told you that, according to the opinion of the Rabbis or Kabbalistic doctors, the eternal Wisdom <note>original: "Sapience"</note> is the radical beginning or unity of all things. When it remained, as it were, quiet and at rest, being retracted in the dark abyss, it was considered by our weak capacities as *Ayin* <note>Hebrew: אין; original: *Ain*</note>, that is to say, "nothing," or non-being and without end <note>original Latin: *non ens & non finis*</note>. And yet, out of this "nothing," infinity was revealed to us, because the emanation which issued from it is "all in all and yet outside of all" <note>original Latin: *omnia in omnibus, & extra omnia*</note>. It is that fountain out of which the universal waters are drawn, which is the existence of all things (as I said before). That universal and bright-shining, or fiery and formal virtue, is sent out to impart an essence to everything. In conclusion, both the external (passive) and internal (active) parts of all creatures in the world issue out of this eternal principle, which is "nothing" in regard to us, but "all in all and outside of all" in respect to itself. In its eyes, darkness and light, invisibility and visibility, and therefore all potential "nothing" (first matter) and actual "something" are one and the same thing in essence, without any difference. 

For this cause, this eternal infinitude—this all in all and outside of all—is rightly described, first by the Apostle and then by the divine philosopher Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various mystical and philosophical texts are attributed</note>, in this manner: *“One God is the Father of all, who is above all, and over all, and in all”* <note>original Latin: *Unus Deus Pater omnium... qui super omnes & per omnia, & in omnibus*; Ephesians 4:6</note>. *“Of him, by him, and in him are all things”* <note>original Latin: *Ex ipso, per ipsum, & in ipso, sunt omnia*; Romans 11:36</note>. And Hermes says: *“God is an intellectual circle, whose center is everything that exists, and whose circumference is outside of and beyond all things”* <note>original Latin: *Deus est circulus intellectualis, cujus centrum est omne illud quod est, circumferentia verò extra omnia*</note>. 

Because of this, in another place, he calls God *“the place in which the world is contained”* <note>original Latin: *Locum in quo mundus continetur*</note>, inferring thereby—according to the Scriptures—that He fills all the world and yet remains in Himself outside of it all, in the very same nature of a unity as He was. For as He seemed in the eyes of man’s weak and fragile capacity to be *Ayin* or "nothing" before He would create anything, yet He was both unity and infinity unto Himself. Therefore, all things were enfolded <note>original: "complicite"</note> within Him—namely, as He appears to our blinded imagination as the *dark Aleph* <note>original: *Aleph tenebrosum*; referring to the Hebrew letter א in its unmanifested state</note>, or dark and deformed Aleph. Also, although He shined forth out of darkness, and by the revelation...

These philosophers were necessary tools for the Prince of this world <note>Satan</note>, because their worldly discipline distracts even Christians from Truth and Unity by using a confusing variety of distinctions. Instead, we should realize that the only act and Universal agent in all things comes immediately from God, is essentially one with God, and exists essentially in all things.

## CHAPTER V.

### Of Fullness and Vacancy, and what true fullness and voidness or emptiness is.

Now that we have in a few lines discussed and set down the nature of both the two constituting or composing Principles, and also of the privative <note>The "privative" refers to the absence of light or form, which allows for decomposition or chaos.</note> and decomposing nature, it is necessary for us to know the property and sense of Fullness <term>Plenitude</term> and Vacancy <term>Vacuity</term>, according to true Wisdom or Christian Philosophy. And first, I will speak a word or two of that Vacancy or Emptiness, which is so detestable and hateful in the works which the Creator has made. Just as the fathers of the Philosophers, as well as those who have been expert in Theology, have termed it by the name of "Nothing" <note>original: "Nihil"</note>. *Moses* calls it a deformed darkness, or a dark abyss. *Hermes* <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure associated with ancient Egyptian-Greek wisdom.</note> calls it a fearful or horrible shadow, void of shape or form. The Kabbalists <note>original: "Caballists"; Jewish mystical scholars who interpreted the hidden meanings of the Bible.</note> call it a potential being, which is as yet nothing in action. *Plato* makes it a thing scarcely credible, and therefore hardly to be imagined, and likens it to a mere dream, which when a man is awake, proves to be nothing. *St. Augustine* says, "When I conceive of anything formless, I first understand 'nothing' before I understood anything, just as by seeing nothing, darkness is seen, and by hearing nothing, silence is heard" <note>original: "Cum aliquid informe concipio, prius nihil intelligo quam intelligebam, quemadmodum nihil videndo videntur tenebræ, nihil audiendo auditur silentium"</note>. By this it appears that he compares this "Nothing" to darkness and silence. *Job* therefore says: <margin>Job 26:7.</margin> "God stretched out the North over emptiness and vacancy, and he hung the earth upon nothing" <note>original: "Aquilonem Deus extendit super inane & vacuum, & suspendit terram super Nihilum"</note>. And again, elsewhere, <margin>Job 12:22.</margin> "He reveals the foundations out of darkness and brings the shadow of death into light" <note>original: "Revelat fundamenta è tenebris, & educit in lucem umbram Lethalem"</note>. By all this, he argues that Vacancy, Emptiness, Nothing, and Darkness are one and the same thing: namely, Vanity, Emptiness, or Voidness, because all fullness and abundance <term>plenitude</term> is from God in his actual property. But God did not yet shine forth into the world, and therefore as the first deformed matter of the world was void and destitute of all activating grace and formal goodness, it was said to be *Vain, Empty, and Darkness*: For this reason...
