Therefore, the Earth—which before the revelation of God’s Spirit was empty and void—has now become full of divine Light and multiplying Grace. Consequently, it was no longer void and empty (that is to say, lacking essential being), but became fertile and fruitful, being now replenished with divine fire and the incorruptible Spirit of God. This aligns with the words of Solomon: "The holy spirit of discipline fills the world" <note>original: "Spiritus Disciplinæ sanctus implet orbem terrarum"</note>. And again: "The incorruptible Spirit of God is in every thing" <note>original: "Incorruptibilis Spiritus inest omni rei"</note>. By this light, says Saint John, "the world was made" <note>original: "Per hanc lucem mundus est factus"</note>. And the Apostle says, "Christ fills all things" <note>original: "Christus implet omnia"</note>. 

From this, we may perceive that all fullness <term>plenitude</term> comes from the divine Act. Conversely, "emptiness" <term>vacuity</term> occurs when the life-giving form is absent from the waters. This is the reason that a "vacuum" or "emptiness" <term>inane</term> is considered such a horrific thing in Nature. The total absence of the eternal emanation of God is intolerable to any creature, because everything has a natural appetite and desire to be shaped and given form <term>informed</term>. Therefore, it is offensive to every natural thing to be utterly deprived of being. 

For this reason, it follows that unless God had filled all things in this world with his Spirit, emptiness and deformed vacancy would have possessed the world. But because he, by his presence, created all things from nothing through the illumination and presence of his emanating Spirit—and by this spiritual Word he maintains and sustains them all—it follows that there is nothing in this world which is "inane" (in vain), or void and empty. This is supported by the assertion of 

<margin>
Wisdom 11:18.
</margin>
the Wise Man mentioned before: "The hand of the Almighty," he says, "created the world out of formless matter" <note>original: "Manus Omnipotens mundum ex informi materia creavit"</note>. This means it was created from an empty and void matter, and consequently from "Nothing" or *Nihil*. Since it had no name <note>it lacked distinct identity</note>, it is the "form" that provides both the name and the essence. 

This shows how empty the concept of a "vacuum" is as held by the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle</note>, compared to what the true Wise Man considers "empty" and "void." They imagine their "vacuum" to be a mere imaginary space in the air that is not filled by any physical body, not even by air itself—even though they admit it is capable of receiving some watery existence, such as air, water, or earth. Thus, they dream of an imaginary chimera <note>an impossible or foolish fancy</note>, which in reality is absolute nothingness. It is impossible for any place to be formed in the Universe that could be void in that way; therefore, it is not worth dreaming about. 

But our "empty" and "void" <term>Vacuum and Inane</term> refers to "potential matter"—the earth or the deep <term>abyss</term> without form. That is, it exists only in "potential toward action" <note>original: "in potentia ad actum"</note>, waiting to be brought into actual existence by the presence of Divine Light. It is no wonder Aristotle did not consider this kind of emptiness and fullness. In one place he says, "From nothing, nothing is made" <note>original: "Ex nihilo nihil fit"</note>, and in another, he claims Light is merely an "accident" <note>a non-essential property</note>. To his senses, it did not seem that such an "accident" could remove emptiness or fill all things essentially by its presence.

But I will fight our Christian Peripatetics with their own weapons, for they hold it as a maxim that "the existence of an accident is to be within something else" <note>original: "accidentis esse est inesse"</note>. I will challenge them with this logical argument <term>syllogism</term>: 
*   If Light is an "accident," then its existence depends on adhering to or being within some subject. 
*   But the existence of true Light is to exist without any dependency on matter or a subject. 
*   Therefore, Light is not an "accident." 

The first premise <term>major</term> is proven by Aristotle’s own rule: "The existence of an accident is to be in, or to adhere to, some material subject" <note>original: "Accidentis esse est inesse, aut adhærere subjecto alicui"</note>; otherwise, it cannot exist. The second premise <term>minor</term> is supported by the words of Moses: Light was created on the first day, before any other creature. Therefore, there was no pre-existing actual matter or "subject" for it to be inside or to adhere to. Furthermore, it is beyond imagination that God would create non-essential properties <term>accidents</term> before creating any essential or substantial creature.

### CHAPTER VI.

->*How the two essential but opposite active properties first emerged, and afterward how many passive natures issued from the aforementioned principles; by the power of which all mutations and alterations were, and are, effected in this sublunary world.*<-

In this place, I will relate to you the births and beginnings, first, of the two opposite active natures or essential virtues which proceed from the two radical or main principles mentioned before. Then, I will describe the conditions of the two passive natures, which are derived from the effects of those two mutual actions. 

You must know, therefore, that just as the potential or dark principle is contrary and opposite in its essential property to the actual emanation of light, so also have each of them manifested or brought forth into this world two offsprings, or essential properties. These are opposing in condition and flat adversaries in their nature to one another; these two active virtues are **Cold** and **Heat**. I purpose to speak of the manner of their production and the several conditions of each in this present Chapter, starting first with **Cold**.

It is evident by what has already been said, and shall be more amply expressed in the first book of my *Sympathetic History*, that darkness is the immediate effect of the divine **Nolunty** <note>original: "Nolunty," a term Fludd uses for God’s "non-willing" or the retracted, passive state of the divine will</note>, or hidden Divinity, and consequently of God's restrictive property or divine power <note>original: "puissance"</note>. By consequence, darkness is the mother of lack, death, emptiness, vanity, formlessness, and so forth. 

The property of the dark "Nothing," or the deformed abyss, is naturally to rest and not to act or operate. The reason for this is that all its desire is to be centered in and around the core—beyond which there is no motion or action—and not to expand itself toward the outer circumference, as the Spirit of light (or God in His **Volunty** <note>The "willing" or active, outgoing state of God’s will</note>, or revealed nature) is accustomed to do. For this reason, the dark principle claims for itself, by a natural instinct, rest and quietness. This property begets or produces one essential virtue of its own condition, namely **Cold**. 

Cold is chosen as a champion to resist the assaults of her opposite, **Heat**, whose companions are motion and action (for the restless antagonist and provoker of Cold is Heat). Unless it is roused or stirred up by the assaults of Heat, Cold does not move, but seems to wait upon its drowsy mother, **Darkness** and lack. Her children are solidification and rest, which sleep in and cleave fast to the center, and therefore are unwilling to look forth toward the circumference. 

In truth, Cold is an essential act proceeding from and attending on the divine power. In this property, the Divinity contracts its beams from the circumference back into itself, according to the words of the philosopher **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>: <margin>*In the Pimander.*</margin> *The Unity begets the unity and has reflected the heat into itself* <note>original: "Monas generat monadem & in se reflexit ardorem"</note>. That is to say, it would not shine forth but retained its activity centrally within itself, and so seemed to rest in itself. This is the same concept described by the **Cabalist Bahir**: *When Wisdom was withdrawn into the abyss of darkness, remaining within itself, inactive, and regarding nothing* <margin>Reuchlin, book 3, *On the Art of the Kabbalah*.</margin> *it is called Nothing* <note>original: "Ayin" or "Nihil"</note>; *in which state it is called dark Aleph* <note>original: "Aleph tenebrosum," referring to the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet in its hidden or unmanifested state</note>. 

In this contracted—or rather, sequestered or private—state of the divine Unity, it operates according to this negative property or condition through its essential agent, **Cold**. This proves that Cold is not an "accident," as the empty doctrine of the Peripatetics would persuade us; for it is apparent to every wise man that no accidental qualities are in, or can come from, God. This is because the divine Nature is merely a simple, essential, and formal purity, existing in Himself and of Himself,

It manifests the divine will in that state through its effects—namely, by drawing things from the circumference toward the center. In the opposite divine property—namely, in this spirit’s manifest, revealed, and positive nature, or as it is termed, "Light *Aleph*" <note>referring to the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, often used by Fludd to symbolize the beginning or divine light</note>—where it moves or sends out its...

And therefore, just as the Light principle, with all its branches, is said to be the father of position, action, form <note>original: "information"</note>, fullness <note>original: "plenitude"</note>, motion, life, health, and heat, so also does heat operate according to the nature of its restless and ever-working father, which is Light, to destroy the effects of darkness and cold. We see this in the nature of the hot winds, specifically those of the South and the East. For as the Northern cold wind gathers, contracts, hardens, thickens, makes heavy, fixes, and makes the air unmoving and opaque—changing it through thickening <note>original: "inspissation"</note> into the nature of heavier elements—so, conversely, the hot winds or spirits dissipate, expand, soften, rarify, and make thin, light, volatile, movable, and transparent what the cold winds had changed.

Light of itself, as it was considered without any action upon the passive mass, was of a fiery condition; that is to say, only heat and dryness <note>original: "drouth"</note> appeared in it. It follows, therefore, that just as cold in effect is nothing else but the act of the divine power <note>original: "puissance"</note> made potent and evident by the absence of Heat, so also is dryness nothing else but an apparent passive nature, always accompanying the two aforementioned active powers in their absolute purpose, where moisture is totally absent. 

Now moisture is, as it were, a hybrid <note>original: "mongrell"</note>, begotten between the two opposite active forces, which is proved this way: The North wind, by its dominion, turns the Air into snow, hail, ice, or frost—that is, into a cold and dry substance. So, moisture is nothing else but a mixture of heat and cold in one solid substance, which is potentially fluid <note>original: "fluxible in potentia"</note>; then, little by little, the cold and dryness depart and become faint, according to whether the power of the wind is more or less vigorous in heat. For we must observe this: just as cold makes things immobile and fixed, it is an evident sign that the Southern or Eastern Heat has taken possession of the mass when, by their action, it begins to moisten, to revive, and to move again. Indeed, nothing performs that function except Heat. 

In the very same manner, the increased and all-creating Spirit of Light, moving upon the face of the dark abyss, operated within it and caused the congealed mass to thaw <note>original: "relent"</note>. It was then called "waters" by Moses, and the "humid nature" <note>original: "humida natura"</note> by Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure linked to alchemy and philosophy</note>. And so they continue to this day, being altered from one nature into another according to the will of God, which he accomplishes through his ministers, the angelic winds, causing the spiritual waters to change and wheel about from one nature into another. We must observe in these changes that even the visible waters were first made and derived from the invisible waters, according to St. Paul's doctrine mentioned before. For Heaven existed before the Sea and Earth, which were, as it were, the sediment <note>original: "feces"</note>, dregs, or grosser part of the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> sublunary element.

### ->A visual demonstration, confirming the Divine properties or virtues mentioned above.<-

Before we proceed to our visual <note>original: "ocular"</note> demonstration, which shall be made by our experimental instrument <note>likely a thermoscope or "weather-glass," used by Fludd to show how air expands and contracts with heat and cold</note>, we must first consider that the universal air or sublunary heaven is the subtler and more spiritual portion of those waters which are under the Firmament (of which division Moses makes mention). Therefore, every particular part of it corresponds to the whole. Consequently, the air included in the glass of the instrument is of the same nature as the whole universal air; and therefore, by reason of their continuity, as the external whole fares, so also does the internal part. 

Again, just as the Spirit which walked upon the waters did animate, vivify, inform, and dilate them, giving them motion, so also by its absence—or by hiding its act or contracting its emanating beams into itself—the waters are also contracted, condensed, and darkened. This is apparent in the property of the Northern wind, which proceeds from the restrictive <note>original: "privative"</note> or contractive action of this Spirit. 

But as the waters, by their existence, fill the vaulted cavity of the world, so also does the all-informing Spirit fill every corner of them. Inasmuch as it operates "all in all," but in a diversity of properties (and therefore it is termed "manifold wisdom" <note>original: "multiformis Sapientia"</note>), so sometimes it operates in its restrictive property in these lower waters, as is already told you—namely, when it blows from the North and West—and sometimes in its positive nature, as when it breathes from the South or East. In the first case, by its cold action, it contracts from the circumference toward the center; in the latter, namely by its hot property, it expands <note>original: "dilates"</note> from the center to the circumference. 

Seeing then that water is the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> passive element out of which the shape of the whole world and everything therein was carved out and fashioned (as St. Peter tells us), and that the eternal creating and all-enacting Spirit of the Lord is the universal actor which moves all in all in the waters (as Moses suggests to us), and that it does so in and by an infinity of organs—such as Angels, Sun, Moon, Stars, Winds...

Therefore, just as the Sun, the hot winds, the fire, or the natural heat of a human body have their power to expand from His emanating and acting virtue, and by it alter the cold air, the winds, and water from His restrictive disposition: so it follows that both the expansion and the contraction of the air in the Glass are the immediate acts of this Spirit’s positive or restrictive property. For when this Spirit blows from the North or West, the air is contracted more or less into a smaller space within the Glass. This is proved because the water is drawn up higher into the neck of the Glass, lest a physical vacuum <note>original: "corporall vacuity"</note> should be allowed in nature. And again, it is most apparent that the air in the Glass is contracted more whenever the Northern cold dominates the outward air, because the air is gathered into a narrower <note>original: "strait"</note> place or passage than it was before the water was raised up. On the other side, if the hot winds or the summer Sun inflame the external air, then the air trapped inside will also expand itself, and in its expansion require a larger space. That the air is so expanded by heat is plainly demonstrated by the fact that the water is pushed down many degrees lower than it was before. Again, if one puts their hand on the top of the ball of the Glass, the water will sink, for the air will immediately be expanded. Now, the Scriptures confirm in many places (both above and hereafter mentioned) that the spirit of life, which gives this heat to Man or Beast, is from this eternal Spirit, which—as the Apostle says—*gives life to <note>original: "vivifie"</note> all things*. Again, the Prophet calls this one *Spirit from the four winds*,
<margin>Ezekiel 37:9.</margin>
> *to breathe into the dead carcasses so that they might live again.*
Thus you see it evidently confirmed by a visual demonstration that cold contracts, thickens <note>original: "inspissate"</note>, and makes the trapped air heavy, which is shown by the drawing up of the water and the narrowing of the air. And again, you see that heat expands and disperses air, shown by the enlargement of the air in hot weather, or by placing a hand on the bolt-head <note>The bulbous top of the glass flask</note>, which is made evident by the pushing down of the water.

Note (I beg you), you who will not be overly biased on behalf of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle</note>, the two notable errors of the Aristotelians: the first of which is revealed in their claim of a maxim that *heat gathers together things of one nature* <note>original: "calidum doth congregare homogenea"</note>. Now you see it demonstrated visually here that heat operates in the exact opposite way; for it dissipates and disperses the air, which is made of uniform parts <note>original: "homogeneall"</note>, and therefore heat does not gather it together. Rather, it is cold that gathers, compacts, and brings uniform things together, as well as different things. For you see in our instrument that cold contracts and gathers together the air, and even the water, into a narrower and smaller place. Therefore, their assertion is also unsound when they say that *cold only gathers together things of different natures* <note>original: "frigidum doth onely congregare heterogenea"</note>.

The second of their obvious errors is also described by this visual experiment. For while they say that the Sun, stars, and fire—indeed, all heat whatsoever—attracts and draws toward itself the vapors and moisture of the earth and waters, we find the contrary by our experimental Glass. For by only laying a warm hand upon the Glass, the air expands itself immediately; it is so far from being attracted by the heat that, on the contrary, it flies away from the hand. That this is so appears by the pushing down or forcing down of the water, as has been said. Thus we have sufficiently mentioned in this present Book the state of the first and second Principles of all things, though only in brief terms; because it is my purpose to discuss them with a more large and detailed style in the first Book of my *History of Sympathy and Antipathy*.

I will now proceed to the next Book, wherein I purpose to handle the mystery of Rarefaction <note>the thinning of matter</note> and Condensation <note>the thickening of matter</note>, along with the nature of the variety in the heavenly structure <note>original: "Fabrick"</note>, and the rotation of the one universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> element below the moon into a four-fold nature or existence. And in the last place, I will conclude with the fundamental efficient cause of Creation, Generation, Decay <note>original: "Corruption"</note>, and Resurrection.

# The Fourth Book

## The Argument of this Book

In this book is expressed the universal mystery of Rarefaction <term>thinning or expansion</term> and Condensation <term>thickening or contraction</term>. It is also proved that by these processes the world was made, the Heavens were established in their proper order, and the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> Element was altered and changed in a fourfold manner and condition.

### Chapter 1

In this chapter, the common or universal subject of Condensation and Rarefaction is once again recited and repeated. It is also proved that the two essential opposite properties or virtues—which are derived from the eternal Principle in its negative <note>original: "privative"</note> and positive nature—are the immediate causes of both those alterations in the general Element of Waters.

I have made it (as I imagine) most plain and evident to your understanding—both by the testimony of ancient philosophy and the infallible wisdom of Holy Writ, as well as by visual demonstration—that the common or universal matter and subject of all things was the Waters. These Waters were enacted and created by the bright Spirit of the Lord before all other things. Because this is so, and because all Condensation and Rarefaction require a subject or material substance in which they must be performed, it follows that the only matter which undergoes <note>original: "suffers"</note> the act of either of them must be water, or a humid and moist nature. This is because it is the only substantial material which fills the vast cavity of the world; consequently, it is the material existence from which both Heaven and Earth, and all things within them, are framed and were originally shaped.

This is, therefore, the main subject of Condensation and Rarefaction. Through these means, all things in this world are made to differ from one another and are disposed and ordered by God according to weight, number, and measure in their proper ranks and places. That is, they are placed in a higher or lower region according to the dignity which the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> or eternal Actor has bestowed upon them in their creation. 

The common matter of thickening <term>incrassation</term> and thinning <term>subtiliation</term> being thus made manifest, we are now to find the universal actor or operator in this work. I indicated to you before that it was the sacred emanation of that divine splendor which operated from the beginning, operates at this present time, and shall hereafter work everything that shall be effected in the heavens above and the earth beneath. This assertion of mine accords well with this axiom of the Apostle, which I have often repeated for good reason: *God works all in all* <note>original: "Deus operatur omnia in omnibus"</note>.

The virtue issuing from the Sun and its beams is, in the same way, inseparable in essence from the other two—even as we find that the Holy Spirit, which is emitted from the Father and Son, is one in essence with them both. For this reason, the divine Philosopher Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with ancient wisdom and alchemy</note> says: <margin>Pim. 12.</margin> *The mind is by no means divided from the essence of God, but rather connected to him in the same way that light is connected to the body of the sun.* <note>original: *Mens ab essentia Dei nequaquam divisa, sed illi potius co modo connexa, quo solis corpori lumen*</note> *The intellectual beam is not at all divided from the essence of God, but rather joined and knit unto him after the same manner that the light is continued unto the Sun.* 

From this, it is evident that the virtue of heat is essential to light, just as the act of motion is never absent from the emanating brightness. I conclude, therefore, that **Rarefaction** <term>thinning or expansion</term> is nothing other than the dilating of water by heat, which was first contracted by cold. **Condensation**, on the other side, is a contraction—a sucking and drawing together—of those watery parts which were dilated or dispersed by heat. So the subject of both these actions is water, and the fountain of both the negative and positive agent is the **Nolunty** or **Volunty** <term>the "No-will" (withdrawing) or "Will" (emanating) of God</term>. That is to say, it is the negative or affirmative will of that one eternal Unity, who is that all-shaping and operating Spirit, who acts and accomplishes his pleasure in all and over all through his various instruments <note>original: "organs"</note>, both angelic and celestial as well as elementary. According to their different dispositions, these instruments are moved by this internal act to operate in this world the will of the Creator, both positively and negatively, as shall be told you in the chapter following.

Then, by the mixing of various windy forms in that one element, they produce meteorological compositions of diverse natures, depending on the diversity of the windy forms that alter it.

# Section 1. Mosaic Philosophy.

...and altered from the original copy, and therefore interprets the Hebrew thus: *He made for the Sun a tabernacle in the heavens.* <note>original Latin: *In caelis posuit Soli tabernaculum*</note> And Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius (1510–1580) was a Jewish-Italian convert and leading Hebraist of the Reformation.</note> explains it: *He made the heavens a pavilion for the Sun.* <note>original Latin: *Soli disposuit tentorium in iis*</note>

Truly, if we consider all things rightly, we must imagine that either the text must be altered and corrupted from that original copy which Saint Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was the scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> had, or else the reverend Jerome's worth must of necessity be called into question for such a gross mistake. Regarding his character: surely the whole Christian Church in his days would not have chosen a man of low skill in the Hebrew language to undergo a task of such importance—it being for the primary good of the whole Christian Church—as was the translation of the Bible out of Hebrew into Latin. It would not, I say, have relied upon a man of little skill, either in the Hebrew language or the mysteries of divinity, to judge the likelihood or coherence of the Scripture's harmony. Therefore, the ability of the person to whose charge so great a business was committed, and consequently the fruits of his labors, could in no way be undervalued when compared to either Pagnini <note>Sante Pagnini (1470–1541), a Dominican Hebraist who produced a literal translation of the Bible.</note> or Tremellius. 

Again, that he was held as a person of holy conduct, the title of "Saint" attributed to him confirms and proves. Besides all this, he had a much deeper insight into the mystery of the Bible and a more profound grasp of the nature of divine wisdom than any interpreter of the Bible who ever lived, and much more than those of later days. Johann Reuchlin, in his third book of the *Cabalistic Art*, <margin>Reuchlin, book 3 of the *Cabalistic Art*</margin> seems to verify this in these words: "When Jerome had often turned over the Book of Yetzirah, or of the Creation, <note>The *Sefer Yetzirah* is one of the oldest and most influential books of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</note> with a hand busy both day and night, it is reported that the 'daughter of the voice' <note>original Latin: *filia vocis*. For he had known the arrangement of the combination from the Book of Creation before. From this, the alphabetic Kabbalah—that is, the reception—passed down to posterity, through which the greatest secrets of divine things are disclosed."

If Reuchlin meant this regarding Saint Jerome, as many of the learned imagine, you cannot deny that he was deeply learned in the profound and secret meaning of the Scriptures; therefore, he was a man who should not easily be so deceived or deluded in his interpretation. Again, no one can deny that the Pope and the entire Christian clergy assisted him in this business with all the ancient manuscripts which might direct him to the true way or sense of interpretation. Thus, he did not lack the support of ancient authority, but could discern between the true and corrupt text in his interpretation. Therefore, so that we neither accuse the later interpreters for their exposition, nor detract from Saint Jerome's labors—which deserve an everlasting monument—we must instead attribute the error to the corruption or alteration of the Hebrew text. This is because the whole harmony of the Scriptures, and the main subject of the Psalm in which it is recited, tend and incline rather toward the interpretation of Saint Jerome, as I will particularly prove and express to you by these following arguments.

Next, from the mystical and Kabbalistic explanation of the Hebrew word for the Sun. Then, from the consensus of the ancient theologians along with other circumstances belonging to them. Fourthly, from an astronomical observation and the dignity and excellence of the sun as a creature. Fifthly, from an arithmetical consideration. Sixthly, from the point and circle in geometry. Seventhly, from the consonance of the greatest perfection in music or harmony. Eighthly, from a physical or natural regard. And lastly, by the declarations of the wisest and most divine philosophers, which accord exactly with the symphony of the Scriptures. Each of these will be addressed in their order.

As for the first argument, it is evident that the main subject of this Psalm <note>Psalm 19</note> concerns the revelation of Divinity or God in His heavenly creatures; and therefore it must also be intended in this Psalm that the Divine Spirit does plentifully, and essentially, inhabit this illustrious palace of the heavenly Sun, as there...

<margin>Psalm 19:1</margin>

Therefore, it follows logically that this Creator—who has filled the Sun of Heaven with his glory and the beautiful influence of essential virtue and light—has revealed himself strikingly and clearly to all the world from his sunny tabernacle. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 42:16</margin>
confirms this more plainly when he says: *The Sun shining forth looks over all, and its work is full of the glory of the Lord.* <note>original Latin: *Sol illuminans per omnia respexit; & gloria Domini plenum est opus ejus*</note> This means the Sun is full of essential Divinity—not that Divinity is trapped within it, but that it also exists outside and over everything. This is much like how the spirit in human blood is said to have its primary "tabernacle" in the heart, yet it is still present in every part of the spirit and body. Again, it appears from these words that the Eternal Spirit of Wisdom chose the celestial Sun as a pure vessel or subject in which to operate and act, for the purpose of giving life and animation to every 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 24:5</margin>
creature. Therefore, Wisdom says in her own person: *I came out of the mouth of the Most High, being the first-born; I caused a never-fading light to rise in the heavens.* <note>original Latin: *Ex ore Altissimi prodii primogenita; in cælis feci ut oriretur lumen indeficiens*</note> By this, this universal agent shows that the Sun moves in and by 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 43:5</margin>
it. *The great Lord (says the text in another place) made the Sun, and by his commandments he causes it to run hastily*, etc. This is as if he had said that the Sun moves by the Divine Word. But this will be better proved later.

Regarding the second point, which depends on the Cabalistic <term>Cabalistic</term><note>Referring to the Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism that looks for hidden meanings in the Hebrew language.</note> explanation of the Hebrew word for the Sun: while the Latin word is *Sol* and the English is *Sun*, in Hebrew it is written <term>שמש</term> (*Shemesh*). In this word, we find two of the letter <term>ש</term> (*Shin*), which Cabalists use as the symbolic character for fire and light. In the middle is the letter <term>מ</term> (*Mem*), which signifies a watery physical substance, as *Mem* is the symbolic expression of the waters. It is as if we should say that the moist nature of the heavens, being concentrated in its center, is illuminated with a double portion of the divine emanation streaming down from the *Sephiroth* <term>Sephiroth</term><note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note> (or Cabalistic numbering) called *Tiphereth* <term>Tiphereth</term><note>The sixth Sephirah, representing Compassion, Beauty, and Balance; often associated with the Sun.</note>, which means beauty. By this, it is argued that this heavenly mass is made into a tabernacle for the Spiritual Sun or the beautiful and divine Spirit of Light. This does not mean the Spirit is confined by it, but—as the Scriptures say—the Holy Spirit was abundantly within the physical Christ, and yet it still filled the earth and heavens.

<margin>Wisdom 1. Theological Resolutions, Tract 2, Part 2, Section 2.</margin>
Concerning the third point: Theologians affirm that the Light which was spread over all the heavens and operated in place of the Sun for the first three days of Creation was, on the fourth day, gathered into the body of the Sun. But this Light, which was so dispersed, was the immediate act of that Eternal Spirit which "moved upon the face of the waters." Therefore, the Light that is in the Sun participates in divinity, as shall be more clearly expressed in the eighth and final argument.

According to the fourth point—proved by the celestial or astronomical dignity that the Sun represents—it is most evident that the Sun’s mansion contains divinity. For the more perfection a thing possesses in itself, and the more it excels others in glory, the more closely it approaches divinity. Indeed, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed.</note> rightly tells us (agreeing with the doctrine of our Savior Christ) that "Only God is good and perfect." Now, the Sun's dignity and perfection in the Macrocosm <term>Macrocosm</term><note>The "great world" or the universe as a whole, as opposed to the "microcosm" of the human being.</note> are easily seen: this Royal Phoebus <note>A common classical name for the Sun god, Apollo.</note> sits in his chariot in the very center or middle of the heavens, glittering with his golden hair as the sole visible Emperor, holding the royal scepter and government of the world. Within him, all the virtues of the celestial bodies reside, as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD).</note> and many other learned people have confirmed. Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD).</note> also asserts that all the powers of the stars are gathered into one at the sight of the Sun, and these powers are afterward scattered by the Sun's fiery breath upon the Earth. Does not the Wise Man also compare the brightness of the uncreated Spirit (the fiery emanation of divinity) with the Sun, because of the Sun's excellence in 
<margin>Wisdom 7:24. Ecclesiasticus 42:16.</margin>
brightness? And again, has it not been proved before, by the Son of Sirach, that the structure of the Sun is full of the glory of the Lord? But I will say more on this point in the eighth and final argument.

# Section 1. Arithmetical, Geometrical, and Musical Arguments for the Sun's Divinity.

The fifth argument shows how, from an arithmetical perspective, Divinity must necessarily dwell in the Sun. Specifically, it is a single unity from which all the multitude of stars in heaven derive their essential nature, just as all numbers whatsoever are produced from arithmetical unity. For the number two is merely the form of the same unity conceived twice, and then adding one more unity makes three, and so on to infinity <note>original Latin: *in infinitum*</note>. In exactly the same way, just as one candle lights another and a third, and so proceeds to infinity <note>original Latin: *in infinitum*</note>, this one heavenly Candle provides light and beauty to all the starry candles in heaven; yet it still preserves its accustomed unity in perfection, power, and glory, without any loss.

By the sixth argument (which is geometrical), because the Sun is a most bright circular body, it must necessarily have a central point within its circumference where all its illuminating power resides. This is because the circumference is nothing more than the expansion of a point-like and essential virtue from the center out to the edge. This is the meaning of the philosophical axiom: *Virtue and truth consist in the middle* <note>original Latin: *In medio consistit virtus & veritas*</note>. Now, if that wonderful beauty and clear brightness within the Sun were not extended from the center, it would not proceed from an internal principle <note>original Latin: *a principio interno*</note>. In that case, it would require some other external physical light source, just as the Moon does. But that is proven not to be the case, as there is no body found in the world that is equal to the Sun in brightness. This is an argument that it has a central divinity or divine virtue within it which, like the soul in the center of a creature, gives life and acts from the center to its circumference. By making the surface of the body a fiery and bright colored form <note>original term: *coloratum*, referring to a surface that has been given the quality of light and color</note>, it causes its beamy radiation to extend to all the limits of the vast world, according to the infinity of its central agent. Hence it is said that God is "the center of all, whose circumference is nowhere"—that is to say, He is in and over all, and beyond or without all. Nor should it seem strange to anyone that I say the uncreated light is visible in the "tent" <note>original: "tabernacle"</note> which it occupies, since the Scriptures testify *that he is a consuming fire.* And again, that *the spirit of wisdom exceeds the sun and stars in brightness.* And again it is said, *He is clothed with light as with a garment.* To conclude, He is the source and father of light <note>original Latin: *fons & pater luminis*</note>, and therefore there can be no light, either visible or invisible, in this world which does not come from Him. Does not St. Paul seem to affirm *that all visible things were first from things that were not visible*? This argues that all visible light was first from the invisible light whose fountain is God; this invisible light continues in essence within its likeness in created beings, as shall be shown shortly.

The seventh argument is confirmed by an observation in music: namely, that the divine Spirit has chosen the Sun for His dwelling place because of its position in heaven. For if we consider that God—as He is said to exist in Himself—is described by Scripture as seated in *the heaven of heavens*, and in another place, *in the highest heavens, yet he respects and looks down upon the earth*; in that regard we may compare Him (if it is permitted to compare sacred things with worldly ones <note>original Latin: *si sacra cum mundanis componere fas sit*</note>) to a unison <note>term: *unison*, the fundamental pitch or a ratio of 1:1</note> in harmony. For if a string of a musical instrument is struck while open, it sounds a unity from the bridge of the instrument to the nut or head. So we imagine that a chord may be extended from the world's circumference (the highest heavens) to the center (the earth). Again, if we press the string exactly in the middle, then each half-string, when struck, will sound an octave <note>term: *diapason*, the interval of an octave, which represents a 2:1 ratio</note> relative to the whole. This will prove to be the center or perfection for each end of the chord, which will then point out the circumference.

Now the harmonious octave <note>term: *diapason*</note> is the most perfect accord of all others; therefore, it signifies that the middle point between the light (or heaven) and the earth is the seat of the greatest perfection. This corresponds to the unison as 1 does to 2, which is in a double proportion <note>original Latin: *in proportione dupla*</note>. It follows, therefore—and is visible in effect—that the Sun is placed in this central seat, which corresponds to the whole as 2 does to 1, because it is the consensus of all astronomers that the Sun is placed in the middle or center of the heavens. Now, I beseech you to observe how this perfect accord was mystically shaped out of the divine and radical unity, or unison, which said, "Let it be done" <note>original Latin: *Fiat*</note>, and it was done: Unity said, "Let it be done," and so this unison caused a divine radiation which made 2, and had the exact same relationship to unity as the octave <note>term: *diapason*</note> or perfection has to a unison. Now this bright radiation, by which all things were created and framed in true harmony, chose

# Mosaicall Philosophy. Book 4

...in this world the perfect seat of its royal regard for all creatures, at the point of the *diapason* <note>original: "diapason"; the octave in music, representing total harmony</note>, which is always in the middle of the unison, and therefore in the center of the heavens. But it is visible to our eyes that the Sun is ranked in the middle of the seven planets; furthermore, it appears by the divine glory shining from it that it is a seat of divine perfection. Therefore, the Platonists have imagined that the solar orb, or sphere, is the seat of their *soul of the world* <note>original: "anima mundi"</note>. 

Now, just as this royal and most harmonious *diapason* includes within its capacity the other two lower musical chords—namely, the *diapente* <note>original: "Diapente"; a musical interval of a fifth</note> and the *diatessaron* <note>original: "Diatessaron"; a musical interval of a fourth</note> (for the octave is composed of these two united)—it is likely that the entire harmony of the heavens, and consequently of the world, is put into practice in this created organ. The actor or player of this organ is the Eternal Spirit, who plays every minute from this, his glorious instrument, melodies of life, animation, multiplication, peace, or preservation for all creatures. For this is the office of the eternal Christ in this world—that is, the divine Word, in which, as the Evangelist John testifies, there is life. But more of this in the next section.

Eighth, this is proven by a physical or natural perspective: For we observe—and not only we, but the animals themselves; even the very herbs and plants of the earth feel and, in a way, confess—that the Sun is the primary storehouse of life and growth in this world. Consequently, it is apparent that when the Sun approaches us, the herbs and trees which seemed dead before now revive, put on their "green coats," and flourish with blossoms and flowers. But on the contrary, when the Sun departs to the other side of the equator <note>original: "Æquinoctiall"</note>, they cast off their flowers and green clothing and begin to mourn, as it were, for its departure. 

But St. Paul says, "God gives life to all things" <note>original Latin: *Deus vivificat omnia*</note>. Therefore, if the Sun brings the power of life to the world by its presence, it is obvious that it receives this gift from the Spirit of God, which is the Spirit of life. Being poured abundantly by God into this heavenly vessel, the Spirit carries out these life-giving acts in the world, in the same way that the same spirit, being richly poured into Christ, Moses, Elijah, and other saints on earth, performed wonders on the earth—healing, raising the dead, and so on. Does not the sacred text also state that <margin>Ecclesiastes 1</margin> "God has poured out his wisdom upon all his works according to his gift" <note>original Latin: *Sapientiam Deus effudit supra omnia opera sua secundum datum suum*</note>? This means God has poured out his spirit upon all his works, more or less. 

Why then should anyone hesitate or question whether the Spirit lives in the Sun in abundance? This, therefore, is the chief subject of this Psalm of David: to show that the glory of God appears clearly through the creatures of heaven. Indeed, the eternal Spirit shines or expresses his glory through every creature, more or less, and can be recognized in it according to the gift given to it. 

Regarding this, Job says, <margin>Job 26:13</margin> "God has adorned the heavens with his Spirit" <note>original Latin: *Cœlos ornavit Deus Spiritu suo*</note>. From these words, it is manifest that it is the essential Spirit of God which, by the abundance of its presence, gives luster and glory to the Sun. For that reason, the Platonists (who in this imitated the divine poet Orpheus) correctly called it the "Eye of the world" <note>original Latin: *Oculus mundi*</note>, because in it and by it—as if in a clear and smooth looking glass or mirror—all things are seen and discovered. 

And again, the philosopher Heraclitus says: "If you take the Sun out of the world, what is our little body if the soul is missing? No beating vein or pulse is felt there; no power of judgment is found within; there is neither breath nor respiration in it" <note>original Latin: *Si solem è mundo sustuleris, quid est nostrum Corpusculum, si desit anima? Nulla ibi contractatur vena pulsatilis, sentiendum nullum inest judicium, Nullus in eo vitalis halitus aut respiratio*</note>. For this reason, it is also called the "Heart of heaven" <note>original Latin: *Cor caeli*</note>, because just as the heart contains the lively fountain of blood that waters and moistens <note>original: "humect"</note> the other members of the body, it also appears in practice that the power, growth, and preservation of all things (both lower and higher) spring from the Sun. This is because the Sun imparts and breathes life and heat into lower things through its light, and grants formal light to the higher things. 

Now this light is a certain simple action that draws all things to itself through a life-giving or lively heat, which penetrates all things and ripens <note>original: "concocteth"; to mature or refine by heat</note> their qualities everywhere, while also scattering and driving away all darkness and obscurity. <margin>John 1:4; 1 Timothy 6:13; Acts 17:25; Judith 16:17; Wisdom 7:22; 1 Corinthians 12; Wisdom 7:24</margin> From this it is clear that if life in general is found in the Word, as St. John says; and if this universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> spirit of life gives life to all things, as St. Paul and Judith affirm; and if the spirit of wisdom is brighter than the sun, and is a simple and pure spirit more movable and active than all things—and therefore...

# Section 1: Mosaic Philosophy

...therefore he operates all in all; and if he penetrates all things by reason of his purity, as Solomon says, and all these properties are found in the solar power <note>original: "vertue"</note>; what should dissuade a man from thinking that the Hebrew text was not rightly understood by Jerome when he interpreted it as, *He placed his tabernacle in the sun*? <note>original Latin: "Posuit tabernaculum suum in sole." This refers to Psalm 19:4.</note> Truly, it was necessary for man to understand this, given that until this very hour, there are few who will acknowledge that the Spirit of God operates and works immediately in his organ, the Sun, and through the Sun. Instead, being seduced by secular learning <note>original: "Ethnick learning"; referring to pagan or non-Christian philosophies</note>, they admit many secondary agents or efficient causes *by themselves* <note>original: "per se"</note>—that is, acting on their own—as distinguished from the essential act of God. This is the cause of idolatry: the worshipping of the creature instead of the Creator, and the neglect or ignorance of the Creator within the creature. For

<margin>Wisdom 16:28</margin>
although it is said by Solomon, *That we ought to go before the sun to give God thanks* <note>original Latin: "Quod solem prævenire oportet ad benedictionem Dei"</note>, and again we read that when we pray, we should turn our faces toward the east or the rising sun; yet we should understand that he teaches this doctrine for the sake of the Creator, who dwells in that bright tabernacle, and not for the sake of the tabernacle or the creature itself. For it was into this error that the Egyptians fell, who, by adoring this illuminated creature instead of the Illuminator, built a temple and a city in honor of the Sun. For this reason, the

<margin>Isaiah 19:18</margin>
chariot and horses of the sun, which the ignorant Jews had set up before the gate of God’s temple, were justly pulled down, for they did not distinguish the Creator from the creature. This error, which to this hour clings to those of this world learned in Aristotelian philosophy, is described in its true character by that Evangelist who assured us that all life is in the Word.

<margin>John 1:4, 10</margin>
*This Word or light*, he says, *is in the world, and the world was made by it, and the world did not know him. But as many as did receive or acknowledge him* (namely, that he made all, and was all, and in all) *were numbered among the children of God.* Therefore, all true Christians ought to understand that he fills all, gives life to all, sustains all, and operates all in all; for without this understanding, they cannot be considered the legitimate children of God. They should not be so ignorant of the Creator within the creature, since his glory shines out of them and may be perceived by them more or less. They should not think that he is absent even from the most beautiful creature in the world, for he is present with all. For it is said that he fills all, and that not just "virtually" or "accidentally"—as some worldly wise men claim through their secular distinctions (distorting the truth of Scripture in the process)—but in essence. In plain terms, it is said in one place: *Christ is in all, and over all; in him are all things.*

<margin>Colossians 1:3; Wisdom 7:25, 12:1; Romans 11:36; 1 Corinthians 8:6</margin>
But Christ, who is the true wisdom, is the powerful <note>original: "vertuous"</note> or essential emanation from the Father, and therefore no "accident" <term>accident: In Aristotelian philosophy, a quality that is not essential to the nature of a thing.</term>. In another place it says: *The incorruptible Spirit of God is in all things.* But that Spirit, which has no corruption in it, and preserves from corruption, and truly gives life, is no accident, but a perfect essence. In another place: *Of him, by him, and in him are all things*; therefore this is meant essentially, and not accidentally. In another place: *God is all in all.* And again the Apostle says: *Of God the Father are all things by our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things.* All of this cannot be meant otherwise than as God’s essence, which is in and over all, because in himself he is only essential, and therefore no "accidents" can be attributed to him. Consequently, we may conclude that God’s Spirit is essentially in his creatures, and for that reason, we ought simply to consider him and acknowledge him in his works. For any person who professes to be a Christian and does not know this is but a Christian in name, and is consequently vain and miserable. This is partly confirmed by the words of St. Paul, and partly by those of Solomon mentioned before:

<margin>Romans 1:18</margin>
*The anger of God (says St. Paul) is revealed from heaven upon the impiety and injustice of those men who hold back the truth of God in unrighteousness; because what is known of God is made manifest to them, for God has revealed it to them. For his invisible attributes are discerned by the creatures of this world, through the things that are understood by creation, as are his everlasting power and divinity. So they are inexcusable because, when they knew God, they did not glorify him or give him thanks, but faded away or vanished in their own imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened; and therefore, while claiming to be wise, they became fools, and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of a corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed beasts, and serpents, etc.* By this he argues, first, that God ought to be contemplated and known in his creatures, and that we ought to acknowledge and ascribe all their glory and power to his Spirit or divinity within them, and not mistake the Creator for the creature. For his words imply that the invisible things of him—as well as his everlasting virtue and divinity—are discerned by the things that are created. And why not? Since in the Word there is and was from the beginning life, or that life-giving <note>original: "vivifying"</note> Spirit; and since life is in the creatures, it follows that the Word, and consequently the incorruptible Spirit, is also there. Solomon confirms the aforementioned point in this passage:

<margin>Wisdom 13:1</margin>
*All men are vain by nature who are ignorant of God, and cannot understand him who truly is by the good creatures of his which they behold, nor acknowledge the workman by the consideration of his works.* By this, he argues that divinity in the creature may be perceived in and through the appearance <note>original: "aspect"</note> of the creature. Therefore, it is evident that the Prophet spoke correctly when he affirmed that the heavens declared the glory and majesty of God by the beautiful appearance of that glorious Spirit which animated <note>original: "inact"</note> them and adorned their beautiful eye—I mean the Sun—with such divine life-giving and illuminating virtue, which possesses and inhabits it in abundance.

And therefore I conclude that the Prophet spoke correctly and instructively to an ignorant world: that the bright Spirit of God dwelt in the sun of heaven, as in a tabernacle, and from it imparted and distributed his gifts of form, life, growth <note>original: "vegetation"</note>, and multiplication to every creature. And yet, I will not acknowledge with Aristotle that *the Sun and man beget a man* <note>original Latin: "Sol & homo generant hominem"</note>; but rather that the life-giving Spirit—which is powerful in the sun and present in every specific creature—is the only one who gives life to all things. He sends his breath <note>original: "spiracle"</note> of natural heat and life through an ordinary course out of the sun to help and assist the creatures to live and multiply. Yet he is not contained solely within the sun, but also works "all in all," both within and without it, since he fills all things. 

This is good doctrine, which attributes all life-giving action—both direct and indirect—solely to him who completely acts and brings about all things, and consequently not to the created organ in which and through which he operates. For in doing the opposite, we would take away from the Creator to ascribe what does not truly belong to the creature. As for the later interpretation which says, *He made the sun a pavilion or tabernacle in the heavens* <note>original Latin: "Soli posuit tentorium in cœlis"</note>, what profit (I ask you) can that doctrine bring to man? 

The first interpretation teaches man that the Spirit of God is in this bright creature of heaven, and therefore teaches us to adore the Lord and not the palace. The ignorance of the divine Spirit's presence in beautiful creatures has been the cause of infinite errors in the world. Therefore, it is an interpretation of special importance and instruction. 

The second interpretation is a thing so trivial that it needed no such poetic expression to signify that the sun has its seat or place in heaven. Alas, what child does not know this by looking up <note>original: "ocular direction"</note>, without any such teaching from the Prophet? And how is this relevant to the preceding text, *The heavens declare the glory of God, etc.*? Why should he mention the sun immediately afterward? What? To tell us that the sun was in heaven? A thing known to every man? No, it was to tell us that the heaven’s beauty was derived from that glorious Spirit of God which primarily had his abiding or dwelling in the sunny Tabernacle. This was so that blind, worldly men might discern that it was God in that beautiful creature—and not the creature itself—who sent down those virtuous influences and lights so fluently from the vessel of the sun. Because of the misunderstanding of that knowledge, so many of God’s creatures (whom he framed in his own image) have been seduced into error and allured ignorantly to adore the sun and other stars as gods—which in truth are nothing of themselves. *By his spirit he has adorned the heavens* <note>original Latin: "Spiritu suo ornavit cœlos"</note>, says Job. 

<margin>Job 26:13</margin>
He does not say *by the sun*, but *by his spirit*, which made the sun its tabernacle.

And now to our last argument, where I will show you how that exposition by Jerome seems to be confirmed by the assertions of certain wise philosophers. One says (an opinion to which Saint Augustine <note>original: "Austin"</note> also adheres), *Everything claims as much of divinity for itself as it is capable of light* <note>original Latin: "Quælibet res tantum sibi Dei vindicat, quantum capax est luminis"</note>. But the sun is the brightest creature in the world; therefore, it possesses the Spirit of divinity abundantly. Many philosophers, therefore, agree in this, not straying from the tenets of Scripture: namely, that *In light is divinity, and in divinity is light* <note>original Latin: "In lumine numen, in numine lumen"</note>. And Plato says: *Do not speak of God without light* <note>original Latin: "Ne loquaris de Deo sine Lumine"</note>.

# Section I. Mosaic Philosophy.

Yes, truly, he is said to be a *consuming fire*. I conclude, therefore, that Jerome has translated that passage according to its true sense. Consequently, we may understand the reason for expansion <term>rarefaction</term> and contraction <term>condensation</term> from the presence or absence of the Sun. We can confess, after a proper examination of the case, that the only agent of these two operations in the waters or the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> element is the presence, action, and emanation of the Eternal Spirit—or his absence and rest. 

This is easily demonstrated by our experimental glass <note>A thermoscope or weather-glass, an early instrument used to show changes in temperature by the rising and falling of water in a tube.</note>: for the nearer the Sun is to us, and the deeper we are in Summer, the more the air in the glass will be thinned <term>dilated</term>. This is proven because, in summertime, the water is pushed down and forced to its lowest point. Conversely, the further the Sun is from us, and the deeper we are in winter, the more the air is thickened <term>condensed</term> in the glass; this is made evident by the rising or lifting of the water in the neck of the flask <note>original: "mattrass," a long-necked glass vessel.</note> or glass. 

We do not say that the entire reason for condensation and expansion <term>rarefaction</term> comes from the Spirit in the Sun alone; that same Spirit is just as present in this earthly <note>original: "Elementary"</note> region as in the heavenly <note>original: "æthereall"</note> one. He holds the power and life of the winds under his rule, by which—in both winter and summer—he raises or lowers the waters in the glass. Consequently, he causes the thickening <term>condensation</term> and thinning <term>rarefaction</term> of the air, both inside the instrument and outside it. By that means, he causes a daily <note>original: "diuturnall"</note> change in the general waters below the moon <note>original: "Sublunary"</note>, or the universal element of air, shifting it through a four-fold nature from one condition to another. This change or alteration of the lower watery nature from one form into another is commonly called "Elements," as will be explained later. But first, we will discuss the structure of the heavens and show how they were formed through condensation and expansion, performed by this one Eternal Spirit of God <note>original: "Ruach Elohim"</note>.

---

### CHAPTER IV.

->How this Eternal Spirit or Spirit of God <note>original: "Ruach Elohim"</note> framed the heavens and shaped or made the stars by his act of condensation and expansion.<-

<margin>2 Peter 3:5</margin>
It is the Apostle Peter’s assertion that *the heavens and the earth were made of the waters and by the waters, by the Word of God.* So we see that the Word is the agent both in the thickening <term>condensation</term> of invisible waters into visible waters, and then of those visible waters into a visible earth. Thus, the world was generally divided into thicker and thinner regions by that divine Spirit, the Spirit of God <note>original: "Ruach Elohim"</note>, which moved upon the waters. 

This is well argued by Hermes in these words: <margin>Pimander 3.</margin> *When things were distinguished and balanced, which were carried by a fiery Spirit, the heaven shone out in seven circles.* <note>original Latin: "Distinctis libratisque rebus, qua igneo Spiritu vehebantur, emicuit cœlum, septem in circulos"</note> Here he signifies that it was a fiery Spirit; a little earlier, he calls it the *Holy Splendor* <note>original Latin: "Splendorem Sanctum"</note>, which sustained and bore up every circle or sphere of the heavens in its proper place. 

Regarding this, the Wise Man says: <margin>Wisdom 11:20.</margin> *You have disposed or tempered all things in measure, number, and weight.* <note>original Latin: "Omnia mensura, numeroque, & pondere, disposuisti seu temperasti"</note> That is to say, in a distinct measure and proportion, in heaviness and lightness, and in a proper and fitting number—namely, into seven distinct spheres and an infinity of thickened <note>original: "condensed"</note> bodies. For although all the heavens are composed of air and fire—and therefore it is called *Ether, as if it were fiery air* <note>original Latin: "Æther quasi igneus aer"</note>—yet by the rule of <margin>Hebrews 11:3.</margin> Saint Paul (who teaches us that *things which are seen were not made of things which do appear*), we are instructed that both the visible bodies in heaven and all visible lights were first made of invisible waters and invisible formal light. This light has its root in God, the bright eternal Unity of all created numbers. 

Therefore, just as Aristotle says that *the stars are the denser parts of their orb* <note>original Latin: "Stella are densiores partes sui orbis"</note>, I say that while the substance of the heavens is invisible because of its thinness <term>rarity</term>, the stars are similarly visible because of their density. For it was condensation that caused visibility, and expansion <term>rarefaction</term> that causes invisibility. Yet, despite this, it is not concluded—as Aristotle did—that the stars are simply the denser parts of their spheres. Rather, they are lights that were included in the spirit of the dark shadow of the abyss. This spirit, in separating light from darkness, soared upward by virtue of the light within it, and so, according to the proportion of that eternal formal fire...

It moves neither lower nor higher than its formal vigor allows, and it remains there until the force of the corruptible and wasting fire is spent; then it falls down again. But the Light of the star carries and raises up the spiritual body according to the proportion of the mounting Light, which soars as high as its power and the weight of the body will permit. Thus, it hangs perpetually at a certain distance from the center because the fire is of an eternal and incorruptible nature, and will not fade as that artificial fire of the firework does. 

Now, all the illuminating powers and animating forces or flames that are imparted to the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> waters were bestowed on them by that bright universal Spirit or emanation, which was sent forth by God to be carried on the waters, and which (as Scripture asserts) is brighter than the Sun or stars. So, there is none of all those Lights which are separated or divided in essence from that glorious and glittering Spirit, whose beams were dispersed over all the waters in the abyss, giving them life and being. For this reason—because each Light had a different proportion of essential brightness and degree of physical density <term>corpulence</term>—it is that one celestial body varies in its manner of virtue, motion, and influence from another. 

However, because the extracted purest essence <term>quintessence</term> (or the purer material essence of the entire Chaos) was united with the purity of Light that issued from the creating Spirit into an angelic distinction <note>original: "alterity"</note>, both of those natures, in the form of one mass, soared up out of the dark abyss into the center of the heavens. There they claimed the Royal Throne of the Sun <note>original: "Phæbean Throne," referring to Phoebus Apollo</note>, and that spherical mass is to this hour termed the Sun of Heaven. As the created fountain of Light, it ignites and essentially enlightens all the rest of the stars in the heavens above, as well as the elements and created beings below. So, after the universal contracted Light was formed on the fourth day of Creation, it was ordained to be that primary organ of life and growth <term>vegetation</term> in the starry world, sending and showering down its influences and fiery breaths <term>spiracles</term> of life, preservation, growth, and multiplication upon the earthly <term>sublunary</term> world.

Thus, in a few words, you have the reason for that thickening <term>condensation</term> and thinning <term>rarefaction</term> by which both the invisible heavenly substance and visible celestial bodies were made. And it seems not to disagree with the opinions of the learned theologians, Basil and Damascene <note>St. Basil the Great and St. John of Damascus, prominent early Christian thinkers</note>, regarding the causes of the divine Spirit's action in thickening and thinning before the appearance of the Sun in the heavens. For they maintain that the day's expansion, or clear heaven, was occasioned by an emission of Light ordained by the divine will or act of this Omnipotent Spirit. But they think that the night's contraction, and the opaque or dense bodies in the heavens, are effected by a contraction of Light, which was also caused by the sacred Spirit's will <term>volunty</term>. 

Thus, we see from the confession of certain primary Fathers of the Church what the cause was of the cold, contracting Night and the hot, expanding Day, before the Spirit was gathered into the dwelling place or purest essence <term>quintessence</term> of the Sun—which was extracted by the chemical <term>spagerick</term> or separative action of the divine Spirit out of the huge, deformed waters of the abyss. And therefore, this must also be the reason for thickening and thinning unto this day. For when the Spirit in the Sun is far from us, it is as if it is contracting its beams toward itself or absenting itself from our hemisphere. In that case, the cold waters incline toward the nature of their mother, Chaos; because of this, the night and darkness are long, and the light and day are but short and faint in heat. So also in that season, the common earthly <term>sublunary</term> element is subject to thickening <term>condensation</term> and density <term>incrassation</term>. Therefore, it is constrained or contracted into the consistency of frost, snow, hail, ice, and cold showers, etc. 

Again, when the Sun is near to us, it dilates itself, and by its heat and presence, the cold waters become hot, and the days are lengthened and strengthened in heat. Then the common earthly element is ready for expansion <term>dilatation</term> and refinement <term>subtiliation</term>, being easy to be inflamed and set on fire with lightning, flashes <term>coruscations</term>, and such things. But I leave the history of the thickening and refining of the heavenly <term>æthereal</term> Spirit to descend to similar acts or conditions in the earthly element.

#### *How the lower waters, or universal sublunary element, were distinguished, ordered, and shaped into various distinct spheres, which are called particular Elements, by the aforementioned all-working Spirit, or divine Word.*

**S**ince it has already been most certainly proved that the universal substance of the world's machine was made of only one thing—namely, a matter produced out of the potential depths <term>original: "bowells"</term> of the dark chaos or abyss by the alchemical power <note>original: "spagerick vertue"</note> of the divine Word—which matter Moses termed "Waters" and Hermes called "the moist nature," from which (as both Moses and St. Peter testify) the heavens and the earth were made of old; it must follow that the universal sublunary element was derived from this universal mass of waters. This element is commonly called by the name of *Air*, just as all that moist substance in the celestial orbit is called *Ether*. Now, this general element is altered and changed from one shape into another by the breath of the divine Spirit, the *Ruach Elohim* <note>Hebrew: "Spirit of God"</note>. For that which we see as visible water was first made of air, which is an invisible water; likewise, visible water is made into earth through condensation.

<margin>
Hebrews 11:3.
</margin>
And this is proved, first, by the words of St. Paul, who says: *By faith we understand that the world has always been acted upon by the Word, so that those things which are seen were made from things which could not be seen.* <note>original Latin: *Per fidem agnovimus quod semper ita actum sit cum mundo per Verbum, ut ex iis quæ videri non poterant fierent ea quæ possunt videri.*</note>

<margin>
Wisdom 11:18.
</margin>
And again, Solomon says *that the world was made of a matter that was not seen.* But besides these proofs, we are taught by chemical experience that earth is nothing else but coagulated water; nor is visible water anything else but invisible air reduced to visibility by condensation; nor is fire anything else but rarefied air. In conclusion, all the sublunary waters were in the beginning nothing but an invisible, moist, or watery spirit, which we call by the common name "Air." Consequently, the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> sublunary element was in its origin nothing but air, given that heaven was made before the seas or the earth, as Moses teaches us. 

Therefore, by faith we must believe—according to St. Paul's doctrine—that all visible things, including the seas and the earth, were first made or produced out of things that are not visible; that is to say, things aerial or heavenly. For it is one universal air that fills the vast cavity or vault of the world. Because of its lightness, thinness, or invisibility, it is called "Heaven"; conversely, the earth and seas are so named because of their weight, density, and visibility. Since it is evident that the universal sublunary air is the main material ground and substance of what the world calls "elements," and that it is altered and changed from one state to another by the Word or divine Spirit (*Ruach Elohim*)—that is, by eternal wisdom—let us consider how this powerful Spirit effects such shape-shifting <note>original: "Protean"</note> transmutations within that same uniform, invisible, thin water or air. These changes create a clear rotation from one nature into another, which are therefore termed distinct elements.

<margin>
Ezekiel 37:9.

We must first consider that this was that life-giving Spirit which the Prophet called from the four winds, saying: *Come, Spirit, from the four winds and breathe upon these slain, that they may live again.* <note>original Latin: *Veni, Spiritus, a quatuor ventis & insuffla interfectos istos ut reviviscant.*</note> Therefore, this one Spirit, the *Ruach Elohim*, was the royal commander of the four winds. Consequently, he could contract the air by his windy instruments and dilate it again at his pleasure. It was he, and no other, who animates the four winds and directs the Angels—who are his subordinate governors over them—to alter and change the invisible air into visible shapes whenever and however he chooses.

By wisdom he gives weight to the air, weighs the waters in a measure, binds the thick clouds so they do not split, establishes laws for the rain, and makes a path for the lightning of the thunders.* <note>original Latin: *Aer subito cogetur in nubes & ventus transiens fugavit eos. Thus, out of the invisible air, we clearly see three degrees of visible substance produced by condensation: namely, a vaporous air; a thick, visible water (which is rain); and a dense, heavy earth, which is the stone called a **thunderstone** <note>original: "Lapis ceraunius"; these were often fossilized objects or ancient stone tools believed to have fallen from the sky during storms</note>. For by this true Philosophy, we find it to be an **Angelic Breath** <note>original: "Spiracle"</note>, or essential blast of wind infused by the Spirit of God in various ways into the airy or spiritual vessel. This alters and changes the moist <note>original: "humid"</note> passive nature from one condition into another according to his will.

For example, the Easterly element brings forth "children" like itself, such as the fiery and light meteors: namely flashes <note>original: "Coruscations"</note>, lightnings, comets, and such like, according to the nature of the "seed-like" <note>original: "Seminary"</note> influences that descend from heaven at that moment. The Southernly wind brings vapours, clouds, lightning, and thunder. The Westernly brings cold rains and, as it were, snowy dissolutions. The Northernly brings frost, snow, ice, and hail.

I answer that if they listen to St. Peter's doctrine, he teaches that the **Earth was made out of waters**; therefore, the waters existed before the Earth. Again, the heavens were made before the Earth, as Moses shows. Therefore, the Earth appears to be the **dregs** <note>original: "Faeces"</note> or the grosser part of the lower waters, and the visible water the grosser part of the Air.
