<margin>Hebrews 11.</margin>
As mentioned before, that visible things first came from invisible things? The change, therefore, of all things visible or invisible is effected by the condensing or contracting faculty and property of the all-acting Spirit. The reducing of them again from a visible state to an invisible one is caused by the rarefying or dilating act of the same Spirit—identical in essence but differing in property. Therefore, just as air was changed into water, and water into earth, by degrees of cold, so also is earth changed insensibly into water, and water into air, by several degrees of heat. If this were not the case, how is it possible that so much water falling from the clouds should not increasingly augment the seas and diminish the air? Or why should so much earthly coal and whole mountains of wood that are burnt not make the earth smaller in consistency, if there were not an hourly supply and transformation <note>original: "transmutation"</note> of air into water, and from water into earth? Though this divine nature effects this secretly and insensibly, it is proved true by the effect. For when the wood and coal are consumed, we find that their earthly bulk or bodily mass is almost entirely resolved by fire and heat into watery smoke and misty air. 

But the philosophical axiom is that everything is resolved back into its first matter or principle. Therefore, it is apparent that both the water and airy smoke—which make up the earthly bulk of a great oak or a mountain of pit-coal—were originally made of the invisible air. Again, if this were not so, the sulfur <note>original: "brimstone"</note>, stones, and dust—which the authority of the Bible and common experience teach us descend from heaven—would increase the earth more and more, given that they fall in one place or another daily. But leaving these speculative proofs, I will descend to such visual <note>original: "ocular"</note> demonstrations as I have learned from my experimental glass.

### The Demonstration.

We find that from the lower region of the calendar or weather-glass <note>An early type of thermoscope or thermometer that used the expansion and contraction of air to move a column of water.</note> to the summit or top of the head, there is nothing but a portion of the common invisible element, namely, the air within it. But we shall find even in this little model of air strange mutations or alterations effected by the power of the four winds which blow in the open element. For when the hot Easterly wind blows, it expands <note>original: "dilateth"</note> and extends itself all along the neck of the glass and beats down the water to the lowest degree because of its expansion, so that it approaches the nature of fire. For fire is said to be nothing else but air extremely expanded, though indeed it is the abundant presence of the bright "form" <note>In this context, "form" refers to the organizing divine principle or light that gives matter its properties.</note> which expands it so. 

But if the South wind blows, then the air will not be so extremely expanded, but it will take on the middle nature of air, and therefore it will draw up the water by certain degrees. But if it happens that the Westerly wind has sole dominion in the sublunary element <note>The region below the moon, meaning the Earth and its atmosphere.</note>, then the air in the glass will grow thicker, and for that reason, it draws or attracts the water higher. For cold has a great power in that air, and its nature is to condense and thicken.

Lastly, if the cold Northern winds govern or dispose of this universal sublunary element, then the enclosed air will be contracted or compressed into a very narrow <note>original: "strait"</note> space. This is proven by the fact that the colder the wind is, the higher the water will be elevated in the glass. Therefore, it is made manifest that the more the air is contracted, the more it is thickened, and consequently, it must be made heavy <note>original: "ponderous"</note>, considering the proportion of the space in which it is. For all the air that weighed a certain amount in half a yard of space weighs at least that much in two inches of space after contraction.

Thus you see that in truth there is radically but one universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> sublunary element, though it is shaped and altered in four ways by the angelic spirit that blows from the four corners of the heavens. This led the ancients to imagine in their fantasies four distinct elements of equal birth and being from the beginning. But you see clearly by what has been said that this position of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who taught that there were four distinct elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> and other sects is false, even though it has gained a universal name and dominion in this world among both the learned and the ignorant. The latter ground their sayings on the doctrine of the "learned" of this world, who are corrupted and seduced from the truth by pagan teachings <note>original: "Ethnick discipline"</note>. I will now express to you in the last part of this book how all generation and corruption in this world occurs; and that the lowest depth, or the end point to which <note>original: "terminus ad quem"</note> the motion of corruption tends, is only to the simple element of nature. Then a new generation begins from that principle, being altered in four ways...

### CHAP. VI.

->*The true Mystery of Generation and Corruption (also a touch of Regeneration or Resurrection) is, according to the doctrine of Holy Scripture, expressed herein.*<-

As we have plainly, though in few words, described a dark and hidden <note>original: "privat-"</note> principle—namely, that which seemed to exist without form before all beginnings, and which therefore brings death and deprives things of life, existing as if beyond our capacity to understand because the active, life-giving light does not shine forth but is hidden in the center—so also have we revealed another spiritual principle, which is Light, now shining out of Darkness. This is the only thing that informs, gives life to, and animates all things. I told you that all was but one essential Unity: for the three Divine Persons were but one and the same in essence. Therefore, that Light was like Darkness to Him, and consequently, He was the beginning of all beginnings; that is to say, He was the principle of both deprivation <note>original: "Privation"; the loss or absence of a quality</note> and corruption, as well as of creation <note>original: "Position"</note> and generation. One of these is the act leading toward life—namely, the uncreated Light—and the other is the passive element of life or death, which is the waters. For as much as they were derived out of Darkness, they participate in the experiences <note>original: "passion"</note> of both the negative and the positive principles; for that reason, the actor in both extremes is God, who is Unity. By withdrawing His life-giving Spirit from the creature, He causes death and deprivation, and consequently leaves nothing in it but the signs of corruption and ruin. Contrariwise, by keeping His incorruptible Spirit in the creature, it remains without corruption by that presence. Also, after God withdraws His Spirit from the creature, then the creature dies; if He sends His Spirit of life into the creature again, it revives and rises again. This was the reason, in one sense, for the Resurrection of our Savior, who for that cause was termed the firstborn of the resurrection from the dead <note>original: "Primævus resurrectionis à mortuis"</note>. And in another sense, it was the cause that Elijah <note>original: "Elias"</note> raised the widow's child from the dead; that the bones of Elisha <note>original: "Elizeus"</note> caused the murdered Amalekite to rise again; and also that Christ caused Lazarus to revive when he was dead, as shall be shown hereafter. I will therefore explain to you from the Scriptures, first, that God is the only actor in both death and corruption as well as life and generation. (The act of deprivation is as natural to Him as that of creation, if we only consider the watery or passive composition, since it shares in both extremes). And then secondly, I will briefly prove to you the manner in which the same Unity in essence operates 이렇게 contrarily in the watery or bodily subject of all things.

Specifically, by the presence and kind action of the incorruptible Spirit of the Lord, life is continued; and conversely, by its absence, departure, or removal from the creature, the creature dies and decays. For as long as the incorruptible Spirit of the Lord acts and works in the creature, it is impossible for it to die or decay. But when it departs, death and decay must follow.

Also, when the Spirit remains in the body but rests from its action—or, as it were, withdraws its active beams from the circumference toward the center (which the Prophet calls "the hiding of God’s face")—then the creature is troubled, which is to say, it is sick. But if the Spirit is totally taken away, then the creature is forced to expire and die for lack of it. To conclude, if the Spirit returns and shines out again upon the creature, then it revives again—as happened to Lazarus and to the widow’s child whom the Prophet raised.

# Mosaical Philosophy: Book 4

<margin>Job 33:4</margin>
...the real, life-giving Spirit of God, which expressly gives life to man. We have this confirmed by *Job* in another place: *The Spirit of God made me, and the inspiration of the Almighty has given me life* <note>original: "Spiritus Dei fecit me & inspiratio Omnipotentis vivificavit me"</note>. It follows, therefore, that if the presence of this Spirit causes generation, life, and preservation, its absence must necessarily cause corruption, death, and destruction. For when the Spirit of the Lord is removed from the physical mass of a creature, it leaves it deformed—a kind of second chaos, or *an empty and void earth* <note>original: "terra inanis & vacua"</note>—because it is destitute of the Spirit of life that allowed it to act and exist in its specific nature. And because this incorruptible Spirit preserves the physical mass from decay by his own incorruptible power, it follows that when the Spirit departs, or is completely withdrawn into itself without any external action, the mass must immediately die and return to a state of nothingness.

Now, there is a difference between a resurrection from death (or rather a "deadly sleep," for Christ said of *Lazarus* that he was not dead but sleeping) into a temporary life, and a resurrection into an eternal life. Just as nothing hinders death more than the presence of the incorruptible Spirit, so too nothing hinders the perpetuity of living more than a corruptible body—a body subject to death and decay. Therefore, that body must die so that it may put off corruption and be clothed in incorruption. This happens through <margin>1 Cor. 15:36</margin> purification and the separation of the corruptible additions. This process is achieved by loosening the bonds of the alterable elements and freeing the spiritual part of the physical composition from its long captivity so that it may become pure and clean. 

Once this is done, the union of the incorruptible Spirit with the body will make everything spiritual. Thus, according to the <margin>1 Cor. 15:37, 38, 39</margin> *doctrine of St. Paul: That which is sown will not be brought to life unless it dies.* And that which you sow is not the body *that shall be, but God gives it a body as he pleases. Therefore, just as the body is sown in corruption, so it rises in incorruption; as it is sown a natural or elemental body, so it is raised a heavenly and spiritual body.* So, the body must die to shed its corruption—the impure portion of the base elements—so that, being made spiritual, it may remain with the Spirit of life forever. For this reason, Paul <margin>1 Cor. 15:50</margin> affirms that *flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God*, because in their elemental nature they are subject to decay, and therefore cannot inherit the land of incorruption. Rather, it is the pure spirit of the blood and flesh that rises to incorruption (after they have cast off their coarse tabernacle <note>meaning: the physical body as a temporary dwelling</note>), being animated by the incorruptible Spirit of the Lord. This Spirit causes only a temporary life in the natural or compacted elemental mass, but an eternal life in the spiritual and refined body, which is opposite in condition to the natural body, as <margin>1 Cor. 15:44</margin> the Apostle confirms; for through purification, it is changed from an elemental body into a heavenly and spiritual one. 

Do we not see, following the same example, how a grain of wheat is so exalted in power after it has endured decay and been freed from its coarse elemental bonds? It would mount and soar upward toward the heavens if the spirit, once set at liberty, were not held back by the elemental matter that hinders its ascent. Nevertheless, it is so dignified after its decay that its power is increased many times over, as is seen in the abundant multiplication produced by its expanded spirit through the abundance of the incorruptible spirit it receives.

Regarding the other kind of resurrection, which is back to a temporary life, it occurs because the body is not fully corrupted. There is no loosening of the elemental bonds through total dissolution, which would allow the spiritual body to be purified and completely separated from the elemental dregs <note>original: "dreggs"</note> that come from the "lower waters." In these cases, the hidden spiritual body is not yet free to embrace the spirit of life with eternal bonds. Christ performed this kind of resurrection on the widow’s son, who was being carried to his burial, when <margin>Luke 7:14</margin> he said, *Young man, I say to you, Arise; and he who was dead sat up.* He also caused a similar resurrection for the dead daughter of one of the Rulers of the Synagogues, crying out and saying, *Maid, arise; and her spirit came again, and she rose up immediately.* *Lazarus* was also raised to such a temporary life. Again, by the prayer of *Elijah*, the widow's son was raised; for the Text says that <margin>1 Kings 17:22</margin> *at the voice of Elijah, the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived.* From this, we should note two things: first, that these bodies were not wholly corrupted...

# Section 1. Mosaical Philosophy

I mean that the elements of the composition were not separated by dissolution <note>original: "resolution"; the process of breaking a compound down into its basic parts</note>, and therefore, though the Spirit returned into them, it brought their bodies back only to a temporary life. It might be argued that Christ's body was not corrupted, yet he had a resurrection from death unto eternal life. I answer that the Scripture says he would not *suffer his Holy One to see corruption* <margin>Psalm 16:10</margin>, and for that reason, he was resurrected on the third day after he died. His body was without sin and therefore free of corruption. However, I leave this mystical doctrine to the research of the learned Theosophists <note>scholars who study the nature of God and the universe through direct spiritual insight</note>.

Secondly, we must note that it is the presence of the life-giving Spirit of God that causes both generation <note>the creation or birth of a being</note> and resurrection from death. Conversely, it is the absence of that Spirit which induces death and corruption. For the Scriptures say that it was the soul of the child which returned to the child to make it alive again. Another text says, *her spirit came again, and she revived*. Therefore, Job said in the place mentioned above <margin>Job 24:3</margin> <note>While the margin cites Job 24:3, the text describes Job 34:14–15</note>: *If God should withdraw his Spirit or his breath of life from the creature, all flesh would perish*. And David says: *If you take away their breath, they die; if you send forth your Spirit, they revive or are re-created* <margin>Psalm 104:29</margin>.

Now, if we compare our principle of generation and corruption with that of the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note>, we shall find as much confusion in theirs as there is a clear explanation in ours. They define generation as *the change of matter from its original substantial form into another substantial form* <note>original: "mutatio materiæ à forma substantiali pristina in aliam formam substantialem"</note>. They also claim corruption is *the change and loss of a substantial form which was first in the matter, but is now no longer in it* <margin>1. Velcurio, Book 2, Chapter 13, *Commentary on Physics*</margin> <note>original: "mutatio & amissio formæ substantialis quæ prius inerat materiæ, sed nunc non inest eidem"</note>. Thus you see how they name a "substantial form"; but what it is, how it enters the body to cause generation, or in what manner it departs again to cause death and corruption, they do not say. Therefore, we are left with an explanation of *the unknown by the even more unknown* <margin>1. Velcurio, Book 3, Chapter 14, *Commentary on Physics*</margin> <note>original: "ignotum per ignotius"</note>.

In truth, it is the Spirit of God that gives form and life to all things. Its presence causes both generation (which Aristotle observed) and resurrection (which he never knew or could discern by his worldly philosophy). Likewise, its absence causes corruption, deprivation, and death. In this change or passage of a creature from one state to another, we find a specific pattern: just as the world and all things in it were made out of one dark and deformed potential principle by the shining forth of actual Light—which gave form to and created all things out of nothing—so too, by the absence of that all-forming Light, each thing becomes dark, dead, and destitute of its essential form. This lasts until a new Light manifests itself in a way that transforms the watery substance <note>the underlying "matter" of the body</note> from the shape it had at first.

So, the body or carcass of a dead man is in the state of a deformed chaos because it has lost its accustomed human substantial form or action. It is no different than if the Lord took away his Spirit from the world: all things would return again to nothingness, or to a deformed chaos and dark abyss, as it was at the beginning. But when the effective action of a new form breaks forth out of the dead carcass, causing the entire mass to become verminous or full of worms, then we may say that the "corruption of the one is the generation of the other." This principle always holds true as long as the elementary material is still present. Thus, "privation" <note>the state of being without a form</note> is the middle point between them both—a kind of vacuum or "nothingness" between two forms. I will demonstrate the mystery of generation and corruption in this manner.

Now that I have shown you the progression or ranks of the world's creation and its simple members—which consist of four ranks, a state in which the world must endure until it is refined with fire—I will move from these simple members of the world’s existence to the order of degrees in composition. These degrees have their beginning and foundation in the elements, moving from the first rank of generation or composition to its completion. Just as there must be a middle ground or "imperfect mixture" between the start of a mixture and its perfection, so there must be an intermediate composition between a simple element and a perfect body. This intermediate state is of a "meteorological" nature <note>referring to intermediate or transitional states, like vapors or clouds, rather than the study of weather</note>. For example, in the generation of a man, the beginning (which is founded on the universal watery element and takes its place in the first rank) is sperm. It is a watery or fluid substance, only slightly altered; and just as the whole structure of the world and the seeds of all things were in the water...

...implicitly <note>original: "complicitly"; meaning folded together or contained within</note> contained, and yet nothing appeared externally but water. These will appear explicitly by degrees, namely in the sixth rank: for the substance will be altered from a fluid <note>original: "humour"</note> to a solid, with a certain distinction of the three principal members <note>likely the heart, liver, and brain</note>. In the seventh rank, it takes an embryonic shape. In the eighth rank—which completes a "cube" from the material root of 2, or the "square" of 4 (which is characterized in the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> element by the impressions of the four winds)—it becomes a perfect creature.

In like manner, we see in the great world that the simple element, namely the general air, appears externally as plain simplicity and an invisible nothing. Yet, it implicitly contains a cloud, water or rain, fire or lightning, and a heavy stone, along with salt and such like; these appear explicitly by degrees through the power of the four winds. Thus, a vapor occupies the first rank, the cloud the sixth, the lightning and cloud the seventh, and the earthly stone represents an exact rotation of all four wind-driven forms into one mixture <note>original: "mixtion"</note>, which represents the eighth place in composition or generation. 

But when a man comes to corruption <note>the process of death and decay</note>, then his parts proceed in a backward resolution <note>the breaking down of a compound into its parts</note>: namely from 8 to 7, from 7 to 6, and from 6 to 5, until he returns to the point of the simple spermatic element from which he began. There, he begins a new generation in another form, for the all-acting nature is never idle. Likewise, the stone is resolved into water, the water into a vaporous cloud, and the cloud into the air from which it came. This is the simple universal element, which allows for no further or deeper resolution through corruption.

Now, the only operator in both of these works is the Spirit of God. In generation, it shines forth from the center of the universal element (or the internal part of the sperm) toward perfection and continues its action until a perfect man is produced. <margin>Job 10:10-12</margin> Job confirms this, saying: *Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh and knit me together with bones and sinews; you granted me life and favor, and your providence has preserved my spirit.* <note>original Latin: *Nonne sicut Lac fudisti me? & sicut caseum coagulasti me? cute & carne texisti me, ossibus & nervis induisti me: cum vita benignitatem exercuisti erga me. Et visitatio tua conservavit spiritum meum.*</note> 

Conversely, when the Spirit of God withdraws his beams from the circumference of generation and composition back toward the center of simplicity, he ceases to "visit" the spirit of the creature. Consequently, it must fade and return through decay to the principle from which it came. From there, if the same Spirit is pleased to shine forth again, a new generation begins where the corruption or resolution ended.

### CHAPTER VII.

*That God (contrary to* Aristotle's *assertion and the opinions of various other pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophers) does not act out of necessity for the creation and preservation of his creatures, but by his own will and kind <note>original: "benign"</note> inclination.*

<margin>Johannes Velcurio, Book 1, Chapter 5, *Commentary on Physics*</margin>
We properly define as "Necessary" that which cannot be any other way. Conversely, we consider things to be "voluntary" or "fortuitous" <note>happening by chance</note> if they could have happened differently. A great dispute has arisen among the pagan philosophers regarding whether God acts in this world voluntarily, or by necessity—as if by compulsion. Most of them are flatly of the opinion that God acts in this world out of necessity, both in the creation <note>original: "generation"</note> and preservation <note>original: "conservation"</note> of things, as well as their decay. They believe he does not act by any voluntary choice. From this, it would follow that he was forced to do what he does from all eternity by some other nature—one that was either co-eternal with him or existed before him. Or, they suggest he was driven or pushed against his will to do this or that by some creature he had made. 

I will briefly explain to you how erroneous and far-removed from the truth all of this is. First of all, I ask you: what is older <note>original: "of greater antiquity"</note> than God, since he existed before anything else? In geometry, what comes before a point, or is smaller in measure? Or in arithmetic, which number is as ancient as unity <note>the number one</note>? Therefore, it must follow that God is free and voluntary in his actions. He existed by himself and for himself, without regard for any other principle—whether preceding him or co-eternal with him—from the very beginning. Therefore, he was sufficient in and of himself to work and act by his own power from all eternity.

The primary reasons for the aforementioned pagan opinion are two-fold: first, because God acts through his own essence and not through any acquired power <note>original: "vertue"</note>; and second, because the effects seen in the world seem to be necessary. From this, they conclude that these effects cannot come from any contingent <note>subject to chance</note>, fortuitous, or voluntary action of another. 

Regarding the first point, it seems to me they are arguing against themselves. Since he acts by his own essence or substance, it is evident that he moves of his own accord, and consequently not by any external compulsion or internal necessity. Furthermore, within the vastness <note>original: "latitude"</note> of Unity, there can be no compulsion or forced action <note>original: "coaction"</note>, because Unity cannot be acted upon <note>original: "suffer"</note>. Again, it is impossible for him to be urged to work by any external or foreign <note>original: "alien"</note> cause. Remaining primarily fixed and steadfast in and of himself, he works as the original fountain of all things by his own power, emitting his

To the second point, I say that necessary effects do not in any way imply any necessity in the first efficient cause [God], because secondary causes (which *Plato* and other wise men called Handmaids or Slaves) act at the command and prompting of Him, who is the unity of all multitude, and therefore "all in all," according to a necessary order. This also happened beyond the expectation or understanding of the astrologers and naturalists of this world; for at the instant of that eclipse or "passion" of the Sun, the Moon was neither in the head nor the tail of the Dragon <term>Head or tail of the Dragon: Astronomical terms (Caput or Cauda Draconis) referring to the lunar nodes, the points where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic; an eclipse usually requires the Moon to be near these points.</term>, as *Firmicus*, that great expert in astronomy, witnesses. Therefore, it was accomplished against the common course of nature. All these events could never have happened if God acted out of necessity in this world. It follows, therefore, plainly, that God operates in this world of His own free will, not out of necessity, to effect the ordinary or annual course of things according to the laws and necessities of nature; all of which He also effects voluntarily and of His own free will—namely, for their creation and preservation as well as their final decay <note>original: "corruption"</note>.

But come here and listen, O you vain philosophers, who would have God—who is the actor and ordainer of all things—be bound by the laws of necessity. What honor and glory can any man justly attribute to God for His wisdom, justice, and mercy <note>original: "clemency"</note> if He were constrained by necessity not only to create all things after this or that manner, but also to nourish and sustain them, and afterward to bring them to decay? What thanks, or service, or adoration should we owe Him if what He did for us was out of necessity? Why, O *Aristotle*, is it according to your assertion that we should offer sacrifice to the roots of nature? Or what would it avail us mortal men to pray and pour out our supplications to God (a duty which nevertheless *Plato*, *Porphyry*, *Iamblichus*, and *Proclus* teach us to be most necessary) if He could not be won over or appeased by praying, since He works only by necessity? Or why did *Socrates* and *Pythagoras* (who, by the testimony of the Oracle, were esteemed the wisest persons of their time) customarily pour out their prayers to God, if God were only constrained to act and operate whatever He did in the world?

<margin>Psalm 30:8</margin>

Or why does the Prophet proclaim, *That God alone was to be called upon and prayed to* <note>original: "Quod Deus sit solus inclamandus & deprecandus"</note>, if there were any necessity in God to act in the generation and conservation of things? Indeed, it is clearly demonstrated by what has already been said that God, by means of prayer, is customarily inclined toward mercy and pity, and that it is within His free will to deal either in severity or mercy with the world and its creatures. Consequently, He is not urged by necessity to operate or bring forth effects, as certain vain pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophers have claimed. Among these, I must name a remarkable personage and a follower of *Aristotle’s* doctrine, namely *Galen*, that prince of the pagan physicians, who speaks atheistically in these words: *Moses thinks that God can do all things, even if He wanted to make a horse or an ox out of ashes. Now, since it would be better for the hair in the eyebrows to always be equal in size and number, I affirm that it is not He who would have it so—for if He had, they would have been made that way immediately—but that He could not do it. And I say that even if He wanted them that way a thousand times over, they would never become so if they had been produced out of soft skin.* <note>Fludd is quoting Galen (c. 129–216 AD), an influential Greek physician and philosopher, to illustrate a "pagan" view that limits God's power to the constraints of physical matter.</note> Look how atheistically he speaks, and how he tries to restrain the omnipotence of God and limit His actions with the heavy shackle of necessity—and indeed, with a supposed impotence in His power!

<margin>Daniel 4</margin>

But there are certain other philosophers who behave more modestly regarding this doubt. For *Avicenna* <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina, c. 980–1037) was a Persian polymath and one of the most significant thinkers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> affirms that these actions are neither governed by necessity nor are they violent, but consist in a middle ground between the two; and based on this, he concludes that it lies within the will of the Agent. In this resolution, he seems not to vary much from the Scriptures, which say: *God has punished us for our iniquities; He will save us for His mercy’s sake.* <note>original: "Deus castigavit nos propter iniquitates nostras, ipse salvabit nos propter misericordiam suam."</note> By this, this "chosen vessel" <note>A biblical term for a person used by God, usually referring to St. Paul, though here Fludd applies the logic of the quote to the nature of God's will.</note> suggests that there is a free will in God to punish or to show mercy. 

This is expressed in plain words in this manner: *God acts according to His will, as much with the powers of heaven as with the inhabitants of the earth.* <note>original: "Deus juxta voluntatem suam facit, tam in cœli virtutibus, quam in habitatoribus terræ."</note> In these words, the Prophet evidently shows that every operation in this world is brought about by the Will, and in or by the Word or Spirit of the Almighty. Therefore, it is not by necessity, as *Aristotle*, *Galen*, and many other pagan philosophers have claimed—claims which detract from God and tarnish His omnipotence. 

However, it is clearly evident that there is an undeniable necessity in the organic causes and in the effects that flow from God’s acts within them. For this reason, the prophet *Baruch* says: *The Sun, Moon, stars, lightning, winds, clouds, etc., obey God in everything.* <note>original: "Deo obediunt per omnia, Sol, Luna, Sydera, Fulgur, Ventus, Nubes, &c."</note> *That is, they are prompted by His Word and necessarily moved to carry out His pleasure.* It does not follow, therefore, that He who commands must be forced to act in that authoritative manner, since He does so as a "first mover" who has no other actor before Him or co-eternal with Him. Consequently, He operates out of a free will that is fundamentally grounded in Himself. Regarding this, the Apostle asks: *Who is able to resist the will of God?* <note>original: "Voluntati Dei quis resistat?"</note> And the Prophet: *My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be accomplished.* <note>original: "Consilium meum stabit, & omnis voluntas mea fiet."</note> And *Job*: *Whatever God has willed, that He performs.* <note>original: "Deus quodcunque voluit hoc facit."</note> Therefore, He does not act involuntarily or out of necessity, but voluntarily and according to His free will.

We conclude, therefore, that while that which is "necessary" <note>original: "Necessarium"</note> is that which cannot happen otherwise but must be so, that which is "contingent" may happen or be brought about in a different way—such as something that happens by chance or by will. Now, the fact that God's acts in this world are voluntary, and therefore cannot be bound by the chains of necessity, is proved by this: they can happen differently than they usually do according to the laws or rules of nature. Examples of this include when it was God's will for the Sun to stand still, or to move backward, or for it to be eclipsed when the Moon was in none of the points of the "animal intersection"—that is, neither in the "head" nor the "tail" of the Dragon, etc. <note>The "head and tail of the Dragon" are historical terms for the lunar nodes, the points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path. Eclipses normally only happen at these points; Fludd argues that "impossible" eclipses prove God's free will over nature.</note>

# Mosaical Philosophy. Book 5.

## The fifth Book of this present Section.

### The Argument of this Book.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter "A" featuring scrolling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>
After the author had expressed the original nature of the *two essential properties—namely, Heat and Cold—and had proved their main effects to be Rarefaction and Condensation, by which the Heavens and Elements were framed:* He now proceeds in this book to the mystery of *meteorological impressions* <note>In the 17th century, "impressions" referred to natural phenomena or effects produced in the atmosphere, such as rain, wind, or lightning.</note>, *which are the first degree of composition. He shows that their structure is the act of the Divine Spirit, carried out in the universal element of the world's lower region. Consequently, they do not proceed from such accidental and external grounds or beginnings as the Peripatetics* <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> *falsely surmise.* For this reason, he has compared the *meteorological* doctrine of *Aristotle* with that of the *Holy Scripture*. And finally, by subjecting the *Pagan philosophy* regarding these *airy impressions* to the *Lydian trial* <note>original: "Lidian tryall." A "Lydian trial" or touchstone was a traditional method for testing the purity of gold.</note>, or *touchstone of Truth*, he finds them to be false, counterfeit metal—indeed, mere dross compared to the *golden Truth*.

## CHAP. I.

->*In this chapter, you shall find a brief repetition of the preceding discourse. Also, an exposition of the word* Meteoron *or* Meteor. *And lastly, the method which the author intends to follow in this book is explained.*<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter "I" within a square border, depicting a pastoral scene with trees, a building or tower, and rolling hills.</image-desc>
IN my preceding discourse, I briefly pointed out first the principles of things—namely, the root of everything that was: the *Dark* or potential unity, from which sprang forth the *Light* or actual unity. I told you that both were but one thing in essence, because *Light* was one with darkness to the eternal unity, though to our weak capacities they are opposite in property. Then I indicated that out of the first obscure unity, by His other manifest property, waters appeared—arguing thereby that of or from this unity, by this unity, and in this unity, are all things.

After that, I showed how waters were the material or passive principle of all things, just as the illuminating and formal Spirit was the actual and informing beginning of every being. Both of these issued (as I said before) out of one Root, which for that cause is rightly said to be "all in all." Then I explained to you how *Cold* was an essential companion to privative rest, and the strong offspring and champion of darkness. Conversely, *Heat* was the immediate issue and companion of essential action or motion, and the inseparable champion or assistant of *Light*.

Then I told you how *Humidity* (moisture) and *Siccity* <note>original: "Siccity"; dryness.</note> had their origin from the mutual presence or absence of the two active virtues or essential properties mentioned before, *Cold* and *Heat*. Lastly, I declared to you the reason and manner of *Condensation* and *Rarefaction*, and that the main matter or subject of these was the waters, but the universal Actor was and is the *Word* or *Spirit of God*. He acts first in His *Angelic organs*, through the *stars* and especially the *Sun* in *Heaven* above, and the winds beneath, upon the general sublunary waters or elements according to His will <note>original: "volunty"</note>. He alters them in a four-fold manner through the formal properties of the *four winds*, either by *condensation* or *refinement* <note>original: "subtiliation"; the process of making a substance thinner or less dense.</note> into various shapes and dispositions.

Now, in this book, I will reveal to you in a true and infallible manner (for it shall agree in all points with the contents of Holy History) how the blessed *Word* or sacred *Spirit of the Lord* produces and brings forth all *meteorological* bodies in our universal sublunary element through *Condensation* and *Rarefaction*. But before I enter into this discourse, it is proper for me to tell you what the ancients mean by this word *Meteor*. Those apparitions...

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Book 5 of Fludd's *Mosaical Philosophy*. Having previously introduced the concept of "impressions" (atmospheric phenomena), Fludd now shifts to a direct critique of Greek philosophy, specifically Aristotle, in preparation for his discussion on the winds.</meta>

Sect. 1. Mosaical Philosophy.

These things which are seen in the air are called *Meteors* <note>original: *Meteora*</note> by the Greeks, not because of their natural essence, but because of their high position. Others call them more naturally "Impressions," because they are shaped and imprinted above in the universal element called Air.

But regarding their essential makeup, they are properly called *imperfectly mixed or composed bodies* <note>original: *Corpora imperfectè mixta aut compoſita*</note>. This is said either because of their sudden creation—appearing unexpectedly and with short warning—or because their composition does not seem to involve a change of substance or quality. Or perhaps they are called this because they are not as precisely composed as living bodies, which are perfectly mixed. Finally, these impressions are so named because they have not reached a perfect form, nor does there seem to be much change in their parts, since the components of the altered element are mixed together. 

However, it appears that such names are assigned to these kinds of impressions based on the whims or ideas of this or that philosopher. In truth, they are *great works of God* <note>original: *magnalia Dei*</note>—a mystical body, I say, framed and fashioned by the finger of God out of the depths of the universal element below the moon <note>The "sublunary" region was the space between Earth and the Moon, where all change and weather occurred.</note>, to carry out His will upon the earth, whether for judgment or mercy, as will be explained more fully later. In this sense, they may rightly be called the signs or marks of God’s kindness and mercy, or His vengeance and severity upon the earth. 

My purpose in this meteorological account is to guide you toward the path of true wisdom, so you may better understand and decode such a great mystery as the meteorological act of the Spirit of God. By this means, I hope to lead you out of the mire and puddle of pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophy, in which we Christians—to our everlasting shame—remain stuck and wallow like brutish pigs. To achieve this, I will compare the absurdities of the false Aristotelian <note>original: "Peripateticall"</note> philosophy with the infallible truth of the Holy Scriptures. By weighing the contradictions between the two in the balance of justice, every Christian may open their intellectual eyes, follow what is good, and forsake the bad—embracing the truth and fleeing from what is deceptive <note>original: "prestigious"</note> and false. Thus, they may finally see clearly the main difference between the wisdom and philosophy of this world (which the Spirit of God has declared to be mere foolishness) and the wisdom of God, which is the real and essential truth. 

In these few words, you can see the method of my book. I do not intend to be overly tedious, but to briefly complete this meteorological wisdom. Because of its worth, it deserves to be recorded in a much larger volume and polished with a more elegant style and refined speech.

# The Fifth Book of This Present Section.

### The Argument of this Book.

After the Author had expressed the original nature of the two essential properties, namely Heat and Cold, and had proved their main effects to be Rarefaction <note>The process of becoming less dense or more "subtle."</note> and Condensation, by which the Heavens and Elements were framed: He now proceeds in this Book to the mystery of meteorological impressions <note>Atmospheric phenomena like rain, wind, and clouds.</note>. These are the first degree of "Composition" (the mixing of elements). He shows that their construction is the act of the Divine Spirit, carried out in the universal element of the world's lower region. Consequently, they do not proceed from the accidental and external grounds or beginnings that the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Aristotle, known for walking while they lectured.</note> falsely suspect. For this reason, he has compared the meteorological doctrine of Aristotle with that of the Holy Scripture. Finally, by bringing the Pagan philosophy regarding these airy impressions to the Lydian trial <term>Lydian trial</term> <note>A test using a touchstone to determine the purity of gold; a metaphor for a definitive test of truth.</note>, or touchstone of Truth, he finds them to be false, illegitimate metal—indeed, mere dross compared to the golden Truth.

---

## CHAP. I.

->*Herein you shall find, in few words, a repetition of the previous discourse: also an exposition on the word "Meteoron" or "Meteor." And lastly, the method which the Author intends to observe in this Book is expressed.*<-

In my previous discourse, I briefly pointed out the Principles of things: namely, the Root of everything that was, which is the Dark or potential unity, from which sprang forth the Light or actual unity. I told you that both of them were but one thing in essence; for Light was to the eternal unity the same as darkness, though to our weak capacities they have opposite properties. Then I signified that out of the first obscure unity, through His other manifest property, waters appeared. This argues that of or from this unity, by this unity, and in this unity, all things exist. 

After that, I showed how waters were the material or passive Principle of all things, just as the illuminating and formal Spirit was the actual and informing beginning of every being. Both of these issued (as I said before) out of one Root, which for that cause is rightly said to be "all in all." 

Then I expressed to you how Cold was an essential companion to "privative rest" <note>Rest caused by the absence of motion.</note> and the powerful offspring and champion of darkness. Conversely, Heat was the immediate child and companion of essential action or motion, and the inseparable champion or assistant of Light. Then I told you how Humidity and Dryness <note>original: *Siccity*</note> had their origin from the mutual presence or absence of the two active virtues or essential properties mentioned before, Cold and Heat. 

Lastly, I declared to you the reason and manner of Condensation and Rarefaction. I explained that the main matter or subject of these processes was the waters, but the universal Actor was and is the Word or Spirit of God. He acts first in His angelic organs, then through the stars (especially the Sun in Heaven above) and the winds beneath, upon the general sublunary <note>The region below the moon, consisting of the Earth and its atmosphere.</note> waters or elements according to His will. He alters them in a four-fold manner through the formal properties of the four winds, either by condensation or refinement <note>original: *Subtiliation*</note> into various shapes and dispositions. 

Now, in this Book, I will reveal to you in a true and infallible manner—since it shall agree in all points with the contents of the Holy History—how the blessed Word or sacred Spirit of the Lord produces and brings forth all meteorological bodies in our universal sublunary element through condensation and rarefaction. But before I enter into this discourse, it is proper for me to tell you what the Ancients mean by this word *Meteor* <note>original: *Meteoron*, from the Greek for "high" or "suspended."</note>. Those things which are seen in the air are called *Meteors* <note>original: *Meteora*</note> by the Greeks, not because of their natural essence, but because of the highness of their position. Others term them more naturally "Impressions," because they are shaped and imprinted above in the universal <note>original: catholick</note> element called Air.

But regarding their essential makeup, they are properly called "bodies that are imperfectly mixed or compounded" <note>original: *Corpora imperfectè mixta aut composita*</note>. This is either because of their unexpected generation—since they are procreated and appear suddenly and with short warning—or because their composition does not seem to follow a change of substance or alteration of quality. It might also be because they are not as precisely composed as other animated bodies that are perfectly mixed. Finally, these impressions are so named because they have not attained any perfect form, nor does there seem to be any great alteration of parts in this kind of composition, seeing that the parts of the element so altered are confused with one another. 

However, it appears that such names are assigned to this kind of impression according to the fancy or whim of this or that philosopher, when in truth they are the great works of God <note>original: *magnalia Dei*</note>. They are, I say, a mystical body framed and fashioned by the finger of God out of the depths of the universal sublunary <note>The region below the moon, subject to change and decay.</note> element to carry out His will upon the earth, either for judgment or mercy, as shall be explained more fully hereafter. So, in this sense, they may rightly be termed the characters or signs of God’s kindness and mercy, or His vengeance and severity upon the earth. 

My purpose, therefore, in this meteorological account is to direct you into the path of true wisdom, so that you may better analyze and decipher such a great mystery as the meteorological act of the Spirit of God. By this means, I hope to lead you out of the mire and puddle of Pagan <note>original: Ethnick</note> philosophy, in which we Christians—to our immortal shame—stick fast and willingly wallow like brutish swine. To better achieve this, I will compare the absurdities of the false Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>Referring to the philosophy of Aristotle and his followers.</note> philosophy with the infallible truth of the Holy Text. Thus, every Christian, weighing in the balance of justice the contradictions expressed between the two, may open his intellectual eyes and sincerely follow what is good and forsake the bad. He may betake himself to the truth and fly from that which is deceptive <note>original: prestigious</note> and false. By this means, he may at last discern with open eyes the main difference between the wisdom and philosophy of this world (which the Spirit of God has pronounced to be mere foolishness) and that of God, which is the real and essential truth. 

Thus, in few words, you may discern the manner and order of my method in this book. I do not intend to be overly tedious, but to briefly finish this meteorological wisdom, which—due to its own worth—deserves to be recorded in the everlasting monument of a much larger volume and to be polished or burnished with the luster of a more elegant style and refined manner of speech.

...will express what the pagan Peripatetics <note>Followers of the philosophy of Aristotle</note>, and their Christian followers, have determined and do determine concerning them.

The Peripatetic philosophers are of the opinion that the wind is a hot and dry exhalation—being difficult to ignite—which arises out of the earth and soars up into the middle region of the air. From there, it is immediately repelled downward because of the coldness of that region. As it attempts to move upward again—partly because of its lightness and partly because of other rising exhalations it meets during its forced and compelled descent—it moves sideways in the lower region of the air. It ventilates and stirs this air so that, for want of motion or stirring, the air does not rot. This is the sum of their opinion concerning the creation of the winds. I will therefore focus on this Peripatetic or *Aristotelian* definition, or rather description, of the winds.

First, I do so because those false Christian philosophers, as if they were incited by a kind of unbridled madness, do not hesitate to defend and uphold his opinion with their best efforts. They do this in their public schools and private studies, as well as in their writings, and with such stubborn certainty as if it had been divinely revealed to the world or pronounced by the sacred Oracle of Truth itself.

Secondly, I focus on it because the place where this imaginary exhalation is said to be generated, and from where it is derived, is considered by them to be the earth. The destination to which it desires to ascend is (according to their doctrine) the middle region of the air. Because of the cold temperament of that region, the exhalation is not permitted to enter or penetrate it. Instead, the middle space is where it moves naturally upward and—by compulsion or against nature—downward. Lastly, by the jostling or struggling together of other rising exhalations and the forced descending fumes, it moves "laterally"—that is to say, toward the right or left hand—in the lower region of the air.

Thirdly, I focus on it because they seem to claim, as it appears by this definition, that the agent, mover, or efficient cause of this exhalation (both downward and sideways) is double or twofold. Namely, one cause is the cold of the middle region of the air, which forces and presses downward toward the earth that barely imaginable vapor. The other cause is the troop of other rising exhalations, or subtle smokes, which successively rise out of the earth. In their motion upward, they meet the vapor that is forced to descend; they strive and, as it were, wrestle with it, and consequently create a noise in the air, which is called the Wind.

And this is the Peripatetic philosopher's "windy fiction," which in the conclusion, after a proper examination, will prove to be but a bubble or a vain puff of wind—that is to say, merely words without any substance. Now the final end or cause why their "nature" has ordained these windy motions in the air is (as their definition testifies) so that by this manner of ventilation, the air may be preserved, cleared, and purged from all rot and corrupt disposition. But whoever will give credit to this pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> definition—especially if he is a true lover of wisdom—I counsel him first to examine every particular part of it. Having made a diligent inquiry, let him see and discern whether they agree with the laws of true reason and wisdom.

In the first rank and order, therefore, let us mark or observe whether in the first part of his description there is any probability of truth to be found. By it, we are told and taught that the material substance of the wind is a hot and dry exhalation arising and surging out of the earth. But by Holy Scripture (which all true Christians ought to believe before all things), we are taught that the wind has its origin or beginning from the Spirit or breath of *JEHOVAH*: "By the blast <margin>Exodus 15:8.</margin> of your nostrils" (says *Moses*) "the waters were gathered together; you blew with your wind, and the sea covered them" <note>original Latin: *A flatu narium tuorum coacervatæ sunt aquæ, flavisti vento tuo & operuit eos mare*</note>. And *Job* says, "God brings forth the ice with his breath; when <margin>Job 37:9. 28:25.</margin> God blows, the frost and ice are created" <note>original Latin: *Glaciem edit Deus ventu suo, flante Deo concrescit gelu*</note>. "God gives weight to the winds" <note>original Latin: *Deus facit pondus ventis*</note>. And the Prophet *David* says, "Who makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flaming fire" <note>original Latin: *Qui facit angelos ventos, & ministros suos ignem urentem*</note>. And hereupon, such learned personages and Doctors as have profoundly seen and dived into the mysteries of true nature do declare that the external part of the Angels is air (or the subtle, moist nature of the world) and that their internal or formal portion is a hidden divine fire. And for this cause, *St. Denis* <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a high-ranking theological authority in the Renaissance</note> calls the Angels...

The body which is subject to corruption does weigh down and depress the soul; and we scarcely conjecture or guess at those things which are upon the earth. But to proceed to the doubt, which is: whether according to Aristotle's intention, the original matter of the wind is from the earth, and its first motion is from the earth into heaven? A man far more learned and wise in the mysteries of nature than Aristotle ever was answers in this manner:

Man does not know the way or path of the winds; man does not know the work of God, namely, by what means he effects these things. But Aristotle was a man—indeed, a pagan man—and therefore could judge even less rightly of such abstruse things as these. Therefore JEHOVAH, seeming to deride the boldness of such a worldling, and as if in reprimand of him, speaks in these words:

<margin>Job 38:24</margin>
> Do you know where the way is in which the exhalation is divided, which spreads the wind upon the earth? <note>original: "Noſtine ubinam ſit via, in qua dividitur exhalatio qua ſpargit ventum ſuper terram?"</note>

He argues here that it is impossible for a worldly man's capacity to conceive or understand these things unless he is taught and instructed by the Spirit of wisdom, who teaches all things; this Spirit is bestowed by God on whomever he pleases. And yet Aristotle seems impudently to answer God and say, "I know it well; for the way of this exhalation is from the earth upward, into the middle region of the air." There, he claims, it is partly driven downward again by an <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>The Aristotelian concept of a quality being intensified or repelled by its opposite—in this case, heat being driven down by the cold of the middle atmosphere.</note> caused by cold, and partly by other exhalations which are successively ascending; thus the exhalation is compelled to move sideways upon the face of the earth, etc. But I will show the impossibility of this reasoning by what follows immediately hereafter.

To the second and third part of this clause, I say that the <term>medium</term> <note>The environment or space through which something moves.</note> by which the winds are carried or moved is far more vast and large than what Aristotle assigns to it; for the wind does not blow and act only in the lower region, but also in the middle, and even in the upper region of the air. If, therefore, the wind blows in the middle region of the air, then the vigor of Aristotle's definition will be taken away. This is because the effectiveness of his definition chiefly consists in this: namely, that such a hot and dry exhalation as is the cause of the wind is not permitted to penetrate the middle region of the air, but is reverberated, precipitated, and beaten down again by the virtue of the middle region's cold, which resists the heat of the rising exhalation. 

Now, if there is any wind in the middle region of the air, this cause of the wind will be dismissed; for then the exhalation will not be repelled downwards into the lower region (where it should meet other ascending exhalations to make a noise and be dispersed sideways on the earth). Instead, the exhalation which causes a wind in the middle region is not driven down by the cold, but is observed to blow and to move the clouds and thunders in the middle of that sphere. Indeed, it is made manifest by daily experience that the upper or higher clouds (which are white and yellow, and therefore more light and subtle because of their fiery brightness) as well as the lower clouds (which are grosser and darker) are driven and pushed by the winds from any quarter of the world to the opposite one. Unless the winds were also present in that upper region, the clouds could never move as if on the wings of the winds in that manner. 

Do we not also observe that the south wind blows from the southern horizon, and another from the northern horizon, so that both winds have dominion in both horizons at the very same time? From this it often happens that great and dark clouds, moving from opposite quarters—driven by four of those contrary angelic spirits—meet at a point in the horizon and cause one mass or huge sea of clouds. This serves as a tabernacle for the great spirit of wonders who works or causes these things. By this, any wise man may easily perceive that worldly wisdom or Peripatetic philosophy <term>the philosophy of Aristotle and his followers</term> is plain foolishness. It falsely tries to persuade the world that such essential acts as the angelic winds (whose inward essence is the bright Spirit of the Lord) are caused accidentally and are stirred up by external force.

According to the doctrine of true wisdom, it is evident that winds are endowed with essential internal agents. Therefore, they move where and when they please, according to the previously mentioned words of St. John: "The Spirit [or wind] blows where it wills" <note>original: "Spiritus spirat ubi vult"</note>. Since it is apparent that the wind has an "essential and inward act, form, and principle" <note>original: "actum, formam, & principium internum"</note>, it moves <gloss>whichever way the inward mover pleases, and therefore the Text says, "It blows where it wills"</gloss> and consequently, it is endowed with a volition or will. 

By this, any man may see how far from the truth the Peripatetic reasoning is on this point. They admit no essential or internal form to the winds but make them something merely accidental. For example, they claim the stars' heat draws up smoke from the earth; this smoke, soaring high, is pushed down again by the coldness of that region, and then forced to move sideways by other ascending fumes. I ask those of you who are wise and impartial: teach me which of all these external accidents in the creation of the winds can be considered that internal or essential principle which can cause a will or voluntary motion in the winds, or can produce any angelic act in the air? For the Text says, "The Spirit blows where it wills." 

If no such essential will or internal agent can be found or even imagined in Aristotle’s fiction of the wind, then let the breath of those who teach Christians such falsehoods be considered as empty as his doctrine is deceptive <note>original: "prestigious," which in this era meant deceptive or like a magic trick</note> in itself. Was it not the unlikelihood of the Aristotelian assertion that made some of his wisest followers doubt and plainly turn away from their master's vain doctrine regarding the winds? Among them was John Fregius, a man well-versed in the philosophy of Aristotle. After he mentioned the causes of meteors <term>in this era, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including wind, rain, and snow</term>, he immediately broke away from his master’s view on winds and wrote these words: 

"Although the whole dispute regarding the winds, as well as the rest of the meteors, is full of the wonderful works of God—for which no firm or sufficient causes in nature can be provided—it is still useful to look into this mystery as far as human reason is able to penetrate. Sacred Scripture says that God produces the winds out of his treasury, whereupon we hear their blasts, but know not from where they come or where they go." <note>original: "Quanquam tota disputatio de ventis, sicut de aliis Meteoris plena sit admirabilium operum Dei, quorum nullæ firmæ & sufficientes in naturâ causæ proferri possunt, tamen prodest videre quousque humana ratio progredi possit. Sacra quidem literæ dicunt Deum ventos producere de thesauris suis unde ipsius flatus audimus, sed unde veniant aut quò vadant nescimus."</note>

...expelled out of the clouds, and yet for some reason he will not admit that a hot and dry exhalation can penetrate into the middle region because of its coldness. But so that we may dive a little deeper into the abyss of his absurdities, he confesses that the cause of all fiery meteors and comets is a hot and dry exhalation that is terrestrial, dense <term>original: "crasse," meaning thick or coarse</term>, fat, and oily, and therefore prone to being ignited or set on fire. Now, he assigns the place where comets are generated to be the higher region of the air; yet he denies passage to the exhalations that cause the winds into the middle region, which is not flammable, but thin and light. 

Can any person be so ignorant of natural effects as not to judge and imagine that cold will more suddenly resist and withstand that which is flammable and of an actual fiery nature (such as the exhalations that cause comets) than that which is neither actually flammable nor fiery of itself (namely the fumes said to be the origin of the winds)? Again, it appears by his description of comets that their material substance is heavier, more terrestrial, dense, thick, or compacted than that of the winds. Therefore, it must naturally be less able to ascend and penetrate, as all heavy things tend downward by a natural inclination. This is in contrast to the substance of the winds, which is more light, subtle, and thin, and consequently more able to climb upward. Therefore, it would be impossible for the thicker fumes that cause comets to ascend and penetrate into the upper region—due to both their flammable heat and their compact, heavy nature—and yet have the fumes of the winds be barred from passing higher, since their heat is not actually flammable but light and penetrative because of their subtlety.

But I come now to the examination of the third part. Although I have already spoken somewhat concerning it, it is appropriate that I express my mind a little more fully here, because it is most relevant to our exposure of this "worldly wisdom's" folly and error. In this part, he describes a double action of the wind, both of which he calls "accidents." He speaks as if they do not move from an internal and essential principle, but rather by external accidents—namely by the heat of the Sun or stars, by the cold of the middle region of the air, and the jostling or encounter of other ascending fumes. By this, he concludes that the wind moves the air sideways, and consequently it happens by chance and through external means. 

What a glittering and golden lie this is, much like one of those fabulous fictions of the ancient poets! It is a thing, I say, that makes a fair showing, but is, in truth, without substance. For by this assertion, he makes the winds nothing more than something that happens by accident <note>original Latin: "quid per accidens"</note>. On the contrary, the mouth of Truth flatly contradicts such a falsehood, affirming that the wind proceeds primarily from the Divine Spirit, or breath of God. Indeed, it is termed by Truth an Angel, which is expanded and sent forth everywhere to carry out the will of Him who gives it life. 

*Who makes his angels winds* <note>original Latin: "Qui facit Angelos ventos"</note>, <margin>Psalm 104:4</margin> says David. That is, God animates them essentially with His breath and sends them forth as His messengers to do His will. <margin>Baruch 5:60</margin> Therefore, the same Prophet says in another place: *The angels of God carry out His word* <note>original Latin: "Angeli Dei efficiunt verbum ejus"</note>. <margin>Psalm 103</margin> And the Prophet Baruch says: *The wind carries out the command of God* <note>original Latin: "Ventus facit mandatum Dei"</note>. <margin>In the Canticle (Song of the Three Children)</margin> And in another place: *The stormy or tempestuous wind carries out the Word of God* <note>original Latin: "Ventus procellosus efficiens verbum Dei"</note>. And the three children in the fiery furnace said: *O you winds, bless the Lord and exalt Him above all things forever* <note>original Latin: "O venti benedicite Domino & exaltate eum super omnia in perpetuum"</note>.

The "Prince of our Philosophers" <note>Aristotle</note> will not blush (forsooth) to say that the wind is something merely accidental, and that it has its motion only from external principles and not from that central and internal agent which is the actor and operator of, and in, all things. Consequently, he argues it could not blow or breathe where it wishes, nor could it hear the voice of the Lord when it was commanded to come from the four winds. According to his own fancy, he says that this "figment" of his is extracted out of the earth, while the Scriptures say that it is the most lively and agile creature of God, which he brings out of the heavens (which are his treasure-house). In this, both the Prophets, **Jeremiah** and **David**, agree. But in this part of his definition, he concludes that the lateral motion of the wind is caused through that resistance and impediment made by such exhalations as they ascend. 

Oh, what a poor argument from such a mighty philosopher! It is as if such a wind-driven motion <note>original: "ventall"</note>—moving from the north to the south, and so forth—could be so certain and direct in its course while being guided by such an uncertain agent as the accidental striving and contention between ascending and descending fumes!

<margin>Ezekiel 37.</margin>
I beseech you, tell me (my clever <term>original: "quaint," meaning overly-refined or pedantic</term> **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note>), what kind of exhalation rose out of the earth to shoulder, shove, and resist one another in that emission of Spirit which happened when the Prophet said, "Come from the four winds, O spirit" <note>original Latin: "A quatuor ventis adveni, Spiritus"</note>? It seems to me that I see the Christian pages or disciples of **Aristotle** become completely mute, lacking tongues to answer. And if they should say that it was a miraculous wind and not a natural one, I answer that I know of no more efficient causes in nature, or out of nature, but only one. 

Therefore, it is said regarding the production of **Meteors**—namely, in the common course of this world’s nature—that God blows from the north. God produces frost, snow, and ice by his breath. God thunders from heaven. God melts the thick clouds into rain. God sends lightning from his throne and coals of fire out of his mouth. God makes the dark clouds his hiding place. God comes from the forest <note>likely "fourth" or "forth" in OCR; context suggests "forth"</note> in thunder. The voice of the Lord makes the cedars of Mount **Lebanon** stoop and causes the deer to miscarry their young. God is a consuming fire. Who can stand or resist the cold of God? And so forth, in many more places in both the New and Old Testament. 

To conclude, God operates all in all, and he gives life to all, etc. But our **Peripatetic** philosophers come with their school-tricks and idle distinctions, saying, "It is true indeed that he is the principal efficient cause <note>original: "causa efficiens principalis"</note>, but there are many secondary and subordinate causes in nature which act of themselves." I say, plain dealing is a jewel; and truth, being one simple essence, hates double-dealing. Let us imitate her in plainness and simplicity of understanding. We cannot attain this unless we abstract our minds from the subtle multiplicity of worldly philosophy and vain fallacy (which **St. Paul** bids us beware of). For in a multitude of causes lurks an infinity of errors, but in unity consists that unique verity which is true wisdom. Why then should we distract men's thoughts from the simple sense of Scripture by a multiplicity of distinctions, which seem to twist it like a nose of wax a hundred different ways?

Therefore, he alone works in and through them according to his will, both immediately and absolutely; and this is what the Apostle intends when he says, "God works all things in all people" <note>original: *Deus operatur omnia in omnibus*</note>. 

But to return to my purpose: how deaf and dull would this invocation by the wise **Solomon** have been if the essence and life of the winds were nothing other than what **Aristotle** described? I come now to the last part of the <term>Peripatetic</term> definition, which concerns the <term>final end</term> <note>The ultimate purpose or reason for a thing’s existence in Aristotelian philosophy</note> or reason for the production of the winds. Along with **Galen** and **Hippocrates**, we observe that southerly winds are contagious and plague-ridden, because they make the air thick and cause it to become putrid and rotten through their harmful heat and <term>dampening moisture</term> <note>original: "lax humidity," referring to humidity that "loosens" the air or the humors of the body</note>. Indeed, all winds in general, as well as the other <term>meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just space rocks</note> of heaven, are ordained by the Creator as much for a whip and scourge as to assist, preserve, and save his creatures. We are assured of this by many places in Scripture, and **Job** has taught us this in express terms. Therefore, **Aristotle** erred in his judgment concerning the <term>final cause</term> of the winds, just as he did in all the rest.

<margin>Zechariah 6:1</margin>
We may justly conclude from this that the definition provided by our pagan <term>Peripatetic</term>, whom we Christians adore and follow with such devotion and reverence, is altogether false and invalid. This is because the winds are creatures of a nature more essentially eminent and divine than either **Aristotle** or any of his faction ever understood. They are not things without <term>internal lights</term> <note>Spiritual or divine essences residing within physical phenomena</note> and essences, nor do they consist only of external and <term>accidental motions</term> <note>original: "adventitious motions"</note>. That is to say, they are not made of fumes or <term>exhalations</term> <note>Vapors or gases thought to rise from the earth to form weather</note> arising by accident or chance from the earth. Instead, as **Zechariah** teaches us, they are created and animated by an <term>angelic spirit</term>. They stand before the Lord of all the earth and are hidden in the power or treasury of their Lord, from which he calls them at his pleasure to accomplish his will upon the earth and the seas—either "for vengeance or punishment" <note>original: *ad vindictam seu punitionem*</note> or "to show mercy and kindness to his creatures" <note>original: *ad misericordiam & benignitatem creaturis præbendam*</note>.

### Section 1. Mosaic Philosophy.

The wind is an airy spirit, of a moderate consistency, inspired and animated by the breath or inspiration of JEHOVAH, which he draws forth from his treasury to execute his will and pleasure, either by way of a curse and vengeance, or of blessing and mercy <note>original: "misericord"</note>.

<margin>Exodus 15:8; Job; Exodus; Ecclesiastes 9; Psalm 104.</margin>
Every part of this definition is proven from appropriate places in the Holy Scriptures. First, that its external form is air, of a moderate consistency, is made manifest by the fact that the words for "air," "wind," and "spirit" are expressed in many places of Scripture by one and the same Hebrew word, namely, *Ruach* <term>Ruach</term> <note>A Hebrew word meaning breath, spirit, or wind</note>. Again, that its internal or moving soul and central action is the divine Spirit or inspiration is proven and confirmed by the places cited before: "By the breath of your nostrils," says Moses, "the waters were gathered in a heap; you blew with your wind, and the sea covered them" <note>original: *A flatu narium tuarum coacervata sunt aquæ, flavisti vento tuo, & operuit eos mare*</note>. And again, "The mighty God brings forth ice with his breath," etc. <note>original: *Glaciem Deus fortis edit flatu suo*</note>, as if they had said, God inspired the air with his Spirit. 

So it appears there is no difference between an angelic creature and the air when it is so divinely inspired; for the air is said to be the external or manifest form of an Angel (both good and bad) animated by God to carry out his will—either to punish, or to extend and show forth his kind mercy or clemency. Just so, the wind's internal and hidden <note>original: "occult"</note> portion is the immediate breath of God. Therefore, as I said before, they are termed *Algamatha* <note>A term used by Pseudo-Dionysius (St. Denis) to describe angels as "clear mirrors" that reflect divine light</note> by St. Denis—that is to say, clear mirrors or looking-glasses that receive the light of God. Is it not expressed in plain words by David, "that he made his angels winds"? <note>original: *Quod angelos suos fecerit ventos*</note> In this context, "his angels" refers to the emissions from his throne, and when they are incorporated with the air, they are termed angelic natures. 

Again, Jehovah said of the Angel that went before the Israelites to lead them in the wilderness: "Do not provoke him, for he will not bear your errors, because my name is in him" <note>original: *Nolite exacerbare eum, nam non feret defectiones vestras, quoniam nomen meum est in eo*</note>; that is to say, "the bright impression of my Word." For the Son of Sirach said that wisdom went before them in a pillar of cloud, and was a light to them in the night and a shadow or cloud in the day to keep them from the extreme heat. For this reason, the same Angel is called in many places of that book sometimes "Jehovah," in regard to his inward and uncreated essential act, and sometimes "Angel," in regard to his "otherness" <term>alterity</term> <note>The state of being "other" or a composite creature, rather than the "identity" or simple unity of God</note>, or composition of two, as he was a creature. Therefore, just as God is "identity"—namely, an absolute, simple, pure, and uncreated essence—so an Angel is termed "Otherness" <note>original: *Alteritas*</note> by the wiser Rabbis. This is because he is composed of the uniform inspiration of God and the humid or airy nature of the world—that is, of a created spirit or a created air. This led the Psalmist to say what was cited above: "Who makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flaming fire" <note>original: *Qui facit angelos ventos, & ministros suos ignem urentem*</note>. In this saying, he seems to include both the hidden and the manifest nature.

<margin>Psalm 135; Jeremiah 51.</margin>
Regarding the next clause of this definition—which is that God draws or calls his angelic winds out of his treasury to carry out his will—we have it confirmed by the pens of the prophets David and Jeremiah: "He brings the winds out of his treasuries," they say <note>original: *Depromit ventos è thesauris suis*</note>.

<margin>Baruch 3:60; Psalm 148:8; Psalm 103; Psalm 104; Job 38:35; Job 38:8.</margin>
Lastly, concerning the use of the winds, or the final cause for why they were created or sent forth, the Scriptures inform us extensively. Baruch says, "The wind performs the commandment of God" <note>original: *Ventus facit mandatum Dei*</note>. And the Psalmist says, "The spirit of the storms carries out his word" <note>original: *Spiritus procellarum facit verbum ejus*</note>. And again: "The angels of the Lord, who are very strong in power, carry out his word and pleasure" <note>original: *Angeli Dei validissimi robore efficientes verbum & placitum suum*</note>. And again, "He makes the angels lightnings <note>original: "coruscations"</note> his ministers."
