### Sect. 1. Mosaical Philosophy.

### *The demonstration or proof of how the annual winds are moved by the life-giving spirit within the Sun.*

I have already told you that the whole effect of divine action in the moist nature of this lower world consists of freezing <term>congelation</term> and thinning <term>rarefaction</term>. The first was caused by the negative and northern action of God’s Spirit, which operates through cold; the other by his positive operation, which is guided by heat. Now, just as these two have their period of dominance or decline based on the presence or absence of the Sun, so also is the universal air more cold, dense, opaque, and sluggish or dull when the Sun is farthest away; and again, it is more hot, subtle, bright, transparent, agile, and active when the Sun is nearest. 

Observe, therefore, the properties of the air enclosed in the glass vessel of the calendar-instrument <note>an early form of thermometer or weather-glass used to observe atmospheric changes</note>, and remember that it is but one and the same Spirit in essence that works both negatively and positively. For it was one and the same Spirit which was called by the Prophet from the north and south, for the Text says, *“Come, Spirit, from the four winds,” etc.* <note>original Latin: "Veni spiritus à quatuor ventis, &c." referencing Ezekiel 37:9</note> Therefore, this Spirit is what governs the universal earthly <term>sublunary</term> air, both negatively and positively. And although this Spirit is most plentiful in the Sun, it is nevertheless everywhere, and is able at all times and in every place to express itself in both properties. I come now to the main point.

In the first chapter of the first book of this present section, I have most clearly demonstrated to you that the air enclosed in the weather-glass <note>a device used to measure the expansion and contraction of air due to temperature</note> has, in every respect, a relationship to the air, or universal element of the great world. There it is also proved that the airy, moist nature exactly fills every place of the vaulted world where the earth or water are not, lest any vacuum should be found in its cavity—no differently than the expanded air in the head and neck of the weather-glass fills its cavity. 

Therefore, just as the air enclosed in the glass works by expansion at the presence of the Sun (namely, in the summer season, when the external air is heated), so also, and in the exact same manner, will the air of this Northern Hemisphere be expanded when the Sun is present. Indeed, the nearer the Sun is, and the more perpendicular its beams are, the greater will the general air's thinning <term>rarefaction</term> be, and consequently the rarefaction of that specific air which is in the glass. 

On the other side, when the Sun is absent from the northern <term>Boreal</term> hemisphere—namely, when it moves beyond the Equator <term>Equinoctial</term>—then the common air in that hemisphere will grow cold and be contracted and condensed. Consequently, the specific air in the glass will be contracted in the same proportion. This may easily be measured or understood by the degrees the water rises in the glass, just as the expansion may be calculated by the water's descent. 

Once this is well understood—that the cause of this expansion is the presence of this divine act in the "sunny tabernacle," and that the reason for the condensation is the absence or remoteness of that act (or operating and emanating Spirit), and consequently the presence of the divine power which is darkness—for (as we said) the absence of heat is the presence of cold, which is the essential worker in the divine power. Again, the presence of heat is the absence of cold. So also the absence of positive light creates negative darkness, and the absence of negative darkness grants the presence of positive light.

We may easily, therefore, conclude the reason for the annual winds and perceive what their external cause is, and how that air is animated by the life-giving Spirit which is sent out from the Sun. Consider, therefore, that when the Sun is present with us, the summer is created by its presence; the air is warmed <term>calefacted</term> by the bright beams of its Spirit, and through warming it is thinned, and by reason of the thinning of its parts, it requires a larger place for its existence. 

As an example: We put two pounds of vitriol <note>sulfuric acid or a related sulfate mineral</note> into a retort <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note> and fasten its neck to a huge receiver, sealing the joints tightly so that the spirits do not escape in any way. We force the spirit out from the retort into the receiver, and we find it proven by experience that when part of the vitriol is expanded into spirits, those spirits—finding the large receiver insufficient to contain them—violently break the receiver into an infinite number of pieces. By this, it is made plain that a thing which is condensed will occupy only a small space; but when it is expanded, it will require a very large container for its existence. All this is argued plainly by our experimental instrument; for when the Sun is present, the enclosed air is immediately expanded more or less, according to the vigor...

Their general descriptions should include every specific type that falls under them. I will begin briefly with Aristotle’s opinion and then compare it with the testimony of Holy Scripture. In this way, its essence may be tested in the fire of truth to see if it can withstand the trials of truth’s touchstone.

<margin>Aristotle’s definition of a cloud.</margin>
His opinion, and that of his Christian followers, is that a cloud is produced from a vapor raised from the earth and water into the middle region of the air by the attractive power of the Sun or stars. There, it is contracted and, as it were, congealed into the consistency of a visible cloud by the extreme coldness of that place. Afterward, this cloud is moved here and there through the middle region of the air, partly by the heat of the Sun and partly by the force of the winds. Look! This is the substance of the Aristotelian <term>Peripateticall</term> definition of a cloud.

To better understand the truth of this matter and discover whether Aristotle is a true or false prophet in this description, let us consider what the Bible <note>original: "Book or Bible of verity"</note> teaches us about the generation of a cloud. We will see how the parts of this definition agree with its actual meaning. To do this more clearly and with a more exact method, we intend to compare their views and meanings here. In this way, any person—even those with only a basic education <note>original: "meanly literated"</note>—may easily judge the case as it truly stands.

In the preceding definition, he identifies the heat or action of the Sun as the efficient and procreating cause. He says that by its attractive power, the vapor—which is the matter or substance of the cloud—is drawn out of the earth and water and raised <term>sublimed</term> into the middle region of the air. He also asserts that it is moved here and there, partly by the motion of the Sun and partly by the winds. Furthermore, he suspects that the cause of the vapor’s contraction or thickening into a cloud is the coldness of the middle region of the air. # Mosaical Philosophy. Book 3.

[Aristotle] assigns no internal cause of motion to the cloud, viewing it as something dead and without an active spirit.

For this reason, several doubts present themselves for every wise man's consideration. These must be thoroughly resolved and determined before he can rightly judge the truth of this definition. Namely: first, whether the heat of the sun draws and attracts vapors out of the earth and waters into the middle region of the air to compose and shape a cloudy meteor <note>In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or snow, not just falling stars.</note>. Second, whether the coldness of the middle region of the air causes the condensation, or thickening, of a thin vaporous substance into the consistency of a well-compacted cloud. Third, whether clouds are only moved by external active forces <term>efficient Agents</term>—namely by the winds and sun—because they lack an internal active principle or central driver <term>centrall Agent</term>, or if they are instead moved and animated by an internal spirit. I intend to answer each of these three questions or doubts in the order they were proposed.

Regarding the first objection, I say: It is a most false and erroneous belief of the followers of Aristotle <term>Peripateticks</term> that the sun, stars, or fire draw any vapors or exhalations toward them. Experience proves that they actually expel and scatter <term>dissipate</term> things that have been thinned <term>rarified</term> by them, rather than drawing and luring them in. Nor is it true, as most men falsely dream and imagine, that the sun draws fumes upward, or that fire sucks the vaporous substance of thinned <term>attenuated</term> water into itself. Instead, their job is to thin and refine <term>subtiliate</term> the waters and to turn the moister part of the earth into vapor. It is then naturally characteristic of those light substances, by their own inclination, to ascend and mount upward without any other external force. 

We have plainly demonstrated all of this with our experimental instrument <note>The author refers to a thermoscope or "weather glass."</note>. For if you place your hand on the glass bulb <term>bolts head</term> (the round glass at the top), the air will expand <term>dilate</term> itself and immediately fly away from the heating <term>rarifying</term> force that expands it; therefore, that force is even less likely to suck or draw it toward itself. By this, it is evident that while it seemed to worldly "wise men" that because a vapor or fume rises, that motion from the earth must come from the attractive power of the summer heat, it is now proven to be completely false and erroneous. The nature of heat and light is entirely opposite to attraction. They expel by expansion and they scatter and enlarge, which is contrary to the nature of attraction—gathering together and thickening—which are the properties of cold, as shown by our experimental machine <term>Machin</term>.

# Mosaical Philosophy. Book 5

...no further. But I will tell you of an experiment of my own, by which I was led to the truth concerning the generation of mists and clouds. When in my travels I journeyed from Venice to Augusta (or Augsburg) in Germany, as I traveled between the high mountains and rocks of the Alps, on a certain day when the heavens were perfectly clear and without any cloud to be seen on the horizon—the sun also being exceedingly bright (as it usually is in those times)—I saw a certain fog or mist arise little by little on the top of a steep mountain where the sunbeams were beating strongly. It thickened more and more until it grew from a slight vapor into a mist, and from a foggy mist at last into a thick cloud. All this while, the air was clear everywhere else, except only on that side of the hill which we were watching, from the top to the bottom.

It made me marvel a little, and therefore alighting from our coach, I took some grass and flung it into the air to see which way the wind blew. I found it to be blowing directly against that prominent hill, which rose toward the heavens above its neighbors. From this, I immediately gathered that the degrees of progression—from a vapor to a mist, from a mist to a fog, and so on to the consistency of a cloud—were caused by the compression of the common air. The air was driven before the wind little by little against the lofty rock or mountain; because the mountain hindered its passage or flight, the air following behind was added to the air in front. By this adding and compressing of parts of the air into other parts, a perfect cloud was made, shaped only to that part of the mountain. Immediately, when it became heavy and ready to reflect the sun's light, it resolved itself into rain for a space of four miles on this side of the rock, while all the rest of the air remained clear and without any cloud.

By this I immediately understood that clouds were not created in the manner described by the **Peripatetics** <note>original: "Peripateticks"; referring to the followers of Aristotle, whose scientific theories dominated universities at the time.</note>—that is, by vapors rising out of the earth and waters—but by the **thickening** <note>original: "inspissation or incrassation"</note> of the thin and invisible air into a thick, dense, and visible cloud. This agrees with the previously mentioned passage from Job: *Suddenly the air shall be condensed into clouds, and the passing wind shall drive them away.* <note>original: "Subitò aer condensabitur in nubes & transiens ventus fugabit eas."</note>

But then I was a little troubled when I remembered that mountains and high rocks cannot always be the cause of clouds by resisting and stopping the fleeing air, since we find that clouds appear everywhere—even in plain deserts and open seas where there are no hills. After I had considered this for a little while and weighed this objection, I quickly conceived an infallible answer to resolve this doubt. I considered that there is no wind that blows in the heavens with dominance that does not have some opposite or transverse wind blowing with it, even if it is not noticed because the mightier wind obscures the action of the weaker—just as a candle is scarcely noticed in the open sun.

I will prove by common experience that two or more winds blow at the same time. Being often on the seas, I have observed that when the force of the predominant wind has dropped slightly in fits and pushed the ship's sail only weakly, an opposite wind has immediately revealed itself and moved the sail the contrary way, until the other wind rose again and filled the sail toward our intended destination. 

But we also have Scriptures to testify that opposite winds often blow at the same instant. First, the self-same Spirit was called from the quarters of the four winds by Ezekiel and Daniel:

Daniel 7
Zechariah 6:1
</margin>

By their opposing blasts, clouds, whirlwinds, tempests, lightning, and thunders are commonly produced. All of this the profound poet **Homer** seems to include in a few verses, translated here into Latin:

By **"Brothers,"** Boreas (the North Wind) understands the Southern blast and the other cardinal winds. When Boreas meets them in the air, their contentious struggling and wrestling produce thunder, whirlwinds, and similar tempestuous storms. Therefore, we should not doubt that two or more winds blow at the same time—either from opposite directions or crosswise—in the open air. Because of this, the invisible air in between is thickened by compression. It is condensed from the state of ordinary air into a barely visible vaporous substance, then into a more visible misty density, and finally into a most apparent and visible cloud. 

Nevertheless, that cloud is pushed and driven forward by whichever wind in the heaven has the greatest power and influence. This power confirms in every point what was spoken by **Job** and cited before: <margin>Job 37:21.</margin> *Suddenly the air will be thickened into clouds, and the wind passing through will drive them away.* <note>original: "Subito aer condensabitur in nubes & ventus transiens fugabit eas"</note> From this, it is easy to gather that a cloud is framed from the air in this fashion: <margin>Psalm 104:3.</margin> The air fills the entire vaulted heaven, and therefore the sublunary world is violently forced to move before the breath of <margin>Psalm 147:15.</margin> one wind. When it is encountered in its flight by a wind opposite to the first—even if it has a weaker force—the second wind resists the chased air in its motion. <margin>Nahum 1:3.</margin> By that resistance, as air is joined to air, it thickens by degrees. It is just as I told you regarding the <margin>Job 37:11.</margin> steep mountain or rock: by denying passage to the air that was fleeing the pursuing wind, the mountain caused the air's condensation.

This therefore being rightly considered, it is apparent that the <term>Peripatetic</term><note>Aristotelian</note> assertion is unjust and erroneous. They claim that a vapor raised out of the earth and water up to the middle region of the air is transformed into the form and substance of a cloud by the coldness of that place. This is also (as already proved) most improbable because the southerly winds are the chief parents of clouds and abundant rain. Seeing as they are hot—due to the temperature of the places from which they are sent—their warmth would likely counteract (as already said) the coldness of the region through which they march or pass. Therefore, they would either cancel the effect of that cold property or else so weaken and dull its power that if it produced any clouds at all, they would be thinner and smaller than those produced by any of the cold winds. Likewise, the East Wind (**Eurus**) would have the same effect because of his great heat. 

And yet, we find all of this to be quite the opposite by experience. The southerly winds <term>incrassate</term><note>thicken</note> and produce clouds that are generally more moist and thick than any of the others are accustomed to do. Indeed, the south wind so condenses the air by his presence that (as **Isidore** affirms) it makes objects appear...

### Section 1. Mosaical Philosophy.

-> *Great noise was raised in the Elysian hall,* <-
-> *When gods with gods did enter cruel wars:* <-
-> *Phoebus Apollo there with Neptune jars,* <-
-> *Pallas of Athens foul with Mars does fall.* <-

In this passage, the author uses the "gods" to represent opposing angelic spirits that emerge from the winds. When these winds meet in the open "aerial sea," they fight and struggle tempestuously with one another, matching the meaning of the previously mentioned text from Daniel. By Neptune, he means the ruler of the occidental <note>original: "occidentall"; western</note> winds, which are cold, moist, and watery; by Phoebus, he intends the oriental <note>original: "orientall"; eastern</note> ruler, whose blasts are hot, dry, and fiery; and by Mars, he signifies thunder and lightning. The poet Ovid also notably expresses the combat that occurs among the winds in these verses, speaking in the person of Boreas, the North Wind:

> *I also, when I have found my brothers in the open sky (for that is my field), I struggle with such a great effort that the middle air resounds with our collisions, and fires, forced out from the hollow clouds, leap forth.* <note>original: "Idem ego quum fratres cœlo sum nactus aperto / Nam mihi campus is est, tanto molimine luctor / Ut medius nostris concussibus insonet Æther / Exiliantque cavis elisi nubibus ignes."</note>

> *When I meet my brothers in the air,*
> *(Which is my field) I wrestle with such anger,*
> *That the middle heavens echo at our encounter,*
> *And hollow clouds vent forth flashing fire.*

<margin>Job 37:21.</margin>
By "brothers," Boreas (the North Wind) refers to the Southern blast and the other cardinal <note>The four primary directions: North, South, East, and West.</note> winds. When Boreas meets these in the air, their contentious struggling and wrestling produce thunder, whirlwinds, and similar tempestuous storms. Therefore, we should have no doubt that two or more winds often blow at the same time—either from opposite directions or crossing each other—in the open air. This causes the invisible air between them to be thickened or condensed by compression. It changes from an ordinary state of air into a barely visible vaporous substance, then into a more visible misty "corpulency" <note>A solid or thick body.</note>, and finally into a fully apparent and visible cloud. Nevertheless, that cloud is pushed and driven forward by whichever wind in the heavens has the greatest power or dominance. This power confirms in every point what was spoken by Job and cited before: *The air will suddenly be thickened into clouds, and the wind passing through will drive them away.* <note>original: "Subito aer condensabitur in nubes & ventus transiens fugabit eas"</note>

From this, it is easy to understand that a cloud is framed from the air in this way: the air fills the entire vaulted heaven, and therefore the sublunary <note>The region below the moon; the Earth's atmosphere.</note> world is violently forced to move before the breath of one wind. When it is encountered in its flight by a wind coming from the opposite direction—even if that second wind is weaker—it resists the air being chased. Through that resistance, air is joined to air and thickens by degrees. It is just as I told you regarding the steep mountain or rock: by denying passage to the air that was fleeing the pursuing wind, the mountain caused the air to condense.

When this is rightly considered, it becomes apparent that the Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> assertion is unjust and erroneous. They claim that a vapor raised out of the earth and water up to the middle region of the air is transformed into the substance of a cloud by the coldness of that place. As has already been proven, this is highly improbable. The southerly winds are the primary source of clouds and abundant rain; yet, because of the climate of the places they come from, these winds are hot. Their warmth would likely neutralize <note>original: "qualifie"</note> the coldness of the region through which they pass. Therefore, the heat would either cancel out the effect of the cold or weaken its power so much that if any clouds were produced, they would be thinner and smaller than those created by cold winds. The East Wind (*Eurus*) would also have the same effect because of its great heat. 

Yet, we find through experience that the opposite is true: the southerly winds thicken the air and produce clouds that are generally more moist and thick than any others. Indeed, the south wind condenses the air so much by its presence that (as Isidorus <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar.</note> affirms) it makes objects appear...

<summary>The author argues that clouds are formed by the physical compression of air when opposing winds collide, rather than by rising vapors cooling in the upper atmosphere. He uses classical mythology and biblical texts to illustrate the "war" of the winds as a mechanical cause of weather.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the definition and description of clouds, emphasizing that they are not mere physical accidents but are consciously formed by the Spirit of Wisdom out of the air (the divine treasury) to carry out God's will on earth.</meta>

# Mosaical Philosophy. Book 5.

A cloud is the revealing and making manifest of the invisible mundane spirit <term>mundane spirit: the *Spiritus Mundi*, or cosmic spirit that animates the world</term>, which is hidden in the treasury of God—namely, the heavens—by the central operation of divine wisdom and its windy ministers. Being incited thereunto by the will of God, it is formed into a vaporous mass or cloudy substance, which the said spirit of wisdom sets up as its secret place or vehicle to move in, and for the effecting of its will as well in heaven above as in the earth and waters beneath.

->Or, in this way:<-
A cloud is the transformation of the invisible air into a visible, thick, and gloomy consistency, which is effected by the will of God through the meeting of opposite or transverse winds for the accomplishment of his secret will and pleasure.

->Or else, this way:<-
A cloud is a certain visible, condensed heap of air, which the Spirit of Wisdom—being spread everywhere—does make and compose as if out of nothing. That is to say, it is made of an invisible airy substance which it extracts out of its mystical treasury to do and effect the will of God, both in heaven and on earth.

In these definitions, or rather descriptions, the material substance <term>material cause: the physical matter from which something is made</term> seems to be a coagulated mist or condensed mass of air. The formal cause <term>formal cause: the essential shape or nature that makes a thing what it is</term> is expressed in the shape and form of the cloud. The efficient cause <term>efficient cause: the primary source of change or rest; the agent that creates the thing</term>, or central agent, is the essential act of the divine wisdom, who employs and rouses its windy ministers to work externally by way of compression. We also have the storehouse or treasury out of which the substance of the winds is produced: namely, the heavens or air, which is termed *God’s treasure chest* <note>original: "Arca Dei thesauraria"</note>. To conclude, the final cause <term>final cause: the ultimate purpose or end for which a thing exists</term> is manifested in this: that the cloud is ordained to bring forth the effects of God’s mercy and kindness, as well as his severity and anger.

<margin>Job 28:25.</margin>
Now, in defense of the first part of these descriptions, we find it written: *By his wisdom, God proportions the weight of the air, and hangs the waters or clouds in measure; he assigns laws to the rain, and makes a way for the lightnings of the thunder.* <note>original: "Deus sapientiâ suâ aptat pondus aeri & appendit aquas in mensura, facit pluviæ statuta & viam fulgetro tonitruum, &c."</note> That is to say, according to the will and ordination of the divine Spirit, the air or substance of heaven is changed from a lighter or thinner state or weight into a heavier or thicker one. The degrees of this change <note>original: "mutation"</note> are expressed in the following words: first it was air, then clouds, then rain, or common water <note>original: "vulgar water"</note>. Also, the Text seems to make the lightnings the internal or formal light of the cloud, which is not revealed except by the breaking or rupture of the compound and the removal <note>original: "ablation"</note> of darkness. Again, it is said by *Job* (as is already related), <margin>Ecclus. 43.</margin> *The air will be thickened into clouds, and the passing wind will drive them away.* <note>original: "Aer condensabitur in nubes, & ventus transiens fugabit eas"</note> And regarding the clouds of snow: *The gathering together of the spirit scatters the snow upon the earth.* <note>original: "Congregatio spiritus aspergit nivem"</note>

Regarding the efficient cause, it appears to be God, or eternal Wisdom; and therefore in the previous text it is said, *God by his wisdom hangs or balances the waters or clouds in measure.* <note>original: "Deus sapientia sua aptat pondus aeri, & appendit aquas vel nubes in mensura"</note> And again, <margin>Psalm 147:8.</margin> *God covers the heavens with thick clouds.* <note>original: "Nubibus densis obtegit Deus cælos"</note> But all this has been sufficiently expressed before. As for the final cause set down in the aforementioned definitions, it is confirmed by the Scriptures in this fashion: <margin>Job 37:11.</margin> *For the sake of watering the earth, God tires the thick cloud, and he disperses everywhere the light of his cloud; whatever he commands them to do upon the earth, whether it be for a scourge or else in favor and kindness, he makes them ready to accomplish it.* <note>original: "Pro irrigatione fatigat Deus densam nubem, & dispergit lucem nubis suæ, quodcunque præcipit illis faciendum in terra sive ad flagellum, sive ad faciendam beneficentiam efficiet ut præstò sit."</note> <margin>Baruch 6:60.</margin> And *Baruch* says, *When God commands the clouds to pass over the whole earth, they perform what is commanded them.* So we see that these creatures are drawn out of their secret dwellings to do the will of him who created them.

## CHAPTER 7.

### How by our experimental instrument, the reason for the composition of clouds is visibly demonstrated. Also in this chapter, snow is defined both falsely and truly.

Now I think it most fit to demonstrate to you how clouds are produced by the opposing blasts of two winds of a contrary nature: namely, a Southerly wind in dominance and power, and a Northerly spirit which also blows, but imperceptibly. I told you in the chapter where I demonstrated—by using our experimental instrument—the reason for the Southerly winds that occur in winter, that just as the air included in the *weather-glass* <term>weather-glass: an early scientific instrument, similar to a thermoscope, used to observe the expansion and contraction of air in response to temperature</term> expanded by the mere touch of a warm hand, and in that expansion fled from the hand of the toucher toward the cold region of the water (which was clearly proved because the water immediately moved downward), so also the thick winter air in the Southern Hemisphere expanded at the approach of the sun toward the regions beyond the Equator. This happened by the power of that ever-acting and refining <note>original: "subtiliating"</note> spirit which placed its tabernacle in the sun. 

Thus, the expanded Southern air traveled quickly away to seek a larger space; but upon entering the Northern Hemisphere (which, due to the sun’s absence, had become brumal <term>brumal: relating to winter</term>), the stable air of that region was now contracted by the Northern cold. Because of the cold’s dominance, the North wind blows to a greater or lesser degree, even if imperceptibly. When it meets the warm Southern spirit, it condenses that spirit along with the rest into clouds. This is the reason why almost always (specifically where no Northern blasts are felt), Southerly winds bring an abundance of clouds and rain. The hot Southern power of the divine agent further refines and thins the winter air it finds there until it has purified it through rarefaction <term>rarefaction: the process of making a substance less dense; the opposite of condensation</term> and reduced it to the nature of true summer air. Consequently, the surplus parts of the air after expansion were chased away (as was said) into the Northern region. There, the air is condensed again, partly by the restrictive act of divine power and partly by the density <note>original: "spissitude"</note> of the Northern air, which denies it free passage and forces it into the form of clouds. For the cold, thick air of the Northern Hemisphere, stirred and animated by the Northern blast or character, resists the hot, vaporous air, and so it condenses little by little.

To conclude, I could here set down the Aristotelian definitions of snow, frost, hail, ice, and other similar meteors, and then strongly challenge and contradict them by offering other true descriptions of them, proved by the testimony of Holy Scripture. For example, *Aristotle* seems to claim that snow is a cloud congealed by great cold, which is changed into a snowy substance before it can be perfectly dissolved into water by a vaporous state. In this definition, we should in no case believe him, because he is ignorant of the composition of a cloud, as has already been proved. Furthermore, he wanders from the meaning of the Scriptures; according to the mind of the Scriptures, we have defined snow in this way:

> Snow is a meteor which God draws out of his hidden treasury in the form of wool to carry out his will upon the earth, either by way of punishment or mercy.

->Or in this way:<-

> Snow is a creature produced out of the air, or the heavenly treasury of God, by the cold breath or blast of the divine spirit in the form of wool, to perform his will on the earth.

In this view, the fountain of its original substance is identified as the air, or the matter of the heavens. Therefore, the Text says, <margin>Ecclus. 43.</margin> "The gathering together or condensation of the spirit sprinkles the snow upon the earth" <note>original: *Congregatio spiritus aspergit nivem*</note>. And *Job* asks, <margin>Job 38.</margin> "Have you entered into the treasuries of the snow?" <note>original: *Pervenisti ne in thesauros nivis?*</note>. Also, its form and its cause are expressed thus: <margin>Psal. 147:16.</margin> "God by his word sends out the snow like wool; who is able to resist his cold?" <note>original: *Deus verbo suo nives emittit sicut lanam, coram frigore ejus quis consistat?*</note>. So we see that God, through his Word—which operates in its restrictive property through cold—is the essential, efficient, and all-powerful actor in the production of snow.

### CHAPTER 8.

#### What **Aristotle's** opinion is regarding the generation of fountains and rivers, and whether his opinion matches the truth of true wisdom.

Since it is therefore apparent that **Aristotle's** doctrine is erroneous and deceitful regarding the generation and essence of the winds and clouds, we purpose in the third place to bring his judgment and opinion concerning the beginning and origin of fountains and rivers to the touchstone of truth. This way, we may see whether it will endure the trial and not shrink (as the proverb says) "in the wetting" <note>original: "shrink in the wetting" – a phrase referring to poor-quality cloth that shrinks when exposed to water, meaning it fails when put to the test</note>.

The Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's philosophy, named for his habit of walking while teaching</term>, both Christians and Gentiles, are as much deceived in their meteorological foundations concerning the generation of fountains and rivers as in the rest of which we have spoken before. Therefore, their Master, Aristotle (all things being well weighed in the balance of justice), ought to be considered by all true Christians as a seducer and deceiver of the world; consequently, his doctrine regarding this point ought rightly to be repudiated and rejected.

Aristotle and his Peripatetic sect or faction are of the opinion that, since the belly or bowels of the earth are full of cavities and hollow passages, vapors must necessarily ascend from the center or bottom of it to avoid a vacuum <note>original: "vacuity"</note>. As these vapors ascend, they cling to the sides of the hollow vaults and narrower passages or veins of the earth and resolve into water. This water, dripping down in drops, engenders fountains and rivers.

In this opinion of theirs, they conclude that the matter of fountains is nothing but a vapor arising from the bottom of the earth, which is resolved, liquefied, or condensed into water through the combination of cold and heat within the earth. This is no different, according to them, than how clouds, rain, snow, and hail arise and are generated in the air from a vapor that is first condensed and then liquefied.

But if we duly examine every part of their description, we will see that they require both a double matter and a formal agent in the generation of fountains. For they imagine that the remote matter is a vapor, and then the near and immediate matter is drops of water caused by the thickening <note>original: "concretion"</note> or condensation of that vapor. They also create two efficient causes: cold and heat. For, they say, it is the job of cold to condense and congeal the trapped vapor into water, and it is the heat and cold together that make the water fluid and movable. Let it therefore be lawful for me (*judicious Reader*) to answer these Peripatetic philosophers with an over-worn axiom of their own, and consequently to fight them with their own weapons. Their axiom is, *It is done in vain by many things which can be done by fewer* <note>original: "Frustra fit per plura quod fieri potest per pauciora"</note>. Now, if that original work of producing fountains can be performed most conveniently by one and the same subject of water, without first altering it into vapor by refining it <note>original: "subtiliation"</note> and afterward condensing that subtle vapor back into water, then I have no doubt you will conclude with me that this Peripatetic definition is vain, imaginary, and sophistical by their own rules.

But I will make it apparent hereafter, by a visible demonstration, that it is possible through a natural course alone for water—without any change to its consistency—to be drawn or sucked up out of the vast seas through the secret veins and narrow passages or conduits of the earth to the top or summit <note>original: "summity"</note> of the mountains. This happens after it has left its salt nature behind by soaking through the sands and porous <note>original: "pory"</note> substance of the earth. When this is clearly shown to every person's senses, the vanity of Aristotle's invention will soon be discovered by wise men. Besides all this, the weakness of his reasoning or invention—which would pretend that these vapors cling to the sides of caverns or hollow places and must there (forsooth) be converted into drops of water which then issue forth into rivers—will be obvious and manifest if we consider that these drops so made are more likely to circulate and...

### CHAP. IX.

->*In which Solomon's assertion regarding fountains and rivers is maintained, partly by a visual demonstration and partly by true philosophical reasons founded upon it.*<-

I informed you, learned reader, in my previous discourse, that God’s Spirit operates annually in the common element of the sublunary <term>sublunary: the region of the universe below the moon, specifically the Earth and its atmosphere</term> world by a double virtue. One is expanding <note>original: "dilative"</note>, which is carried out in his positive and manifest property—namely, in his light, active, and warm disposition. He has made the sun the principal treasury and storehouse of this virtue, because his bright, emanating Spirit of Wisdom chose that pure vessel for his tabernacle. The other virtue is contracting <note>original: "contractive"</note>, which is carried out in his hidden and secret condition—namely, in his dark, fixing, and cooling disposition. Its principal treasury is located around the poles, for since its effects are contrary to the first virtue, it is seated in the farthest quarters or points of the world from the sun.

Thus, the life-giving Spirit seated in the sun operates only by expansion in the common sublunary element, banishing the northern cold and undoing its actions by way of thinning the air <note>original: "rarefaction"</note>. In the same way, when the sun is absent, the spirits of the polar property take possession of that portion of the element and undo all the subtle actions of the spiritual and active solar virtue by way of freezing <note>original: "congelation"</note>. 

For example: in the winter time among the nations of the Southern world (that is to say, beyond the equator <note>original: "the line"</note>), while the sun is in the Northern Hemisphere causing our summer season, the Antarctic pole's cold property carries out its effects. It thickens the air, raises the fountains or springs, multiplies the waters, and produces snow, frost, ice, and hail; it kills the herbs, fruits, and plants. When the sun next visits those quarters—which occurs during our northern winter—it will undo those effects by the virtue of that expanding and life-giving Spirit from the Father of Light. It will convert the thick air to thin, push the fountains back down toward the bowels of the earth (which were raised in the winter), and dissolve the snow, frost,

To conclude, there is nothing that the polar cold prevails over in one hemisphere that the solar heat does not operate upon in the opposite way, and in the same proportion, in the other region of the world. If this were not so, the world would have to endure an increase or a decrease in its substance—that is, it would sometimes be larger and sometimes smaller. But, as Solomon asserted, just as the seas are never any larger despite all the rivers flowing into them, so also, though fountains rise in one part of the world and sink in another, the world remains the same. And although the air—through thinning <note>original: "attenuation"</note> caused by the active spirit of the Lord—moves from the warm or summer hemisphere to the cold and winter hemisphere, the world is no larger or smaller in its existence because of it. 

Therefore, whatever winter specifically operates in one hemisphere of the world, the summer hemisphere must necessarily act in the same proportion in the opposite one. For if great rains are produced in the winter beyond the Equator <note>original: "the Line"</note>, we must necessarily have great drought in the summer on this side of the Equator. When it is hottest for us, it will be coldest for them; if it proves temperate for us, it will be so for them; just as when the sun is at the Equinox <note>original: "Æquinoctiall"</note>, it makes days and nights equally long and the season temperate for both hemispheres. 

These things being maturely considered first, I proceed to my practical conclusion. My natural observation regarding this is that the air trapped inside the Weather-glass <term>An early scientific instrument, a precursor to the thermometer and barometer, which used the expansion and contraction of air to move a column of water.</term> is made wintry <note>original: "Hybernall"</note>, or takes on the nature of winter, by the dominion of cold. As soon as the head of the glass feels the external cold, the air contained within will immediately shrink and contract itself into a small space, and consequently, the air is made more dense and thick. That this is so is proven by the rising or "attraction" of the water; for there is such a natural tie between the air and the water that if the air contracts itself into a narrower place, the water will immediately move up with it and toward it, because the water is touching <note>original: "contiguous"</note> the air. 

By this, therefore, it is apparent that the contracting and attracting virtue of the northern spirit—or rather, the divine power <note>original: "puissance"</note> which is manifested in cold—first attracts, contracts, and condenses the expanded air. Then, the air contracted by this northern spirit draws or attracts the water from below upward, and it does so without altering that water in any way from what it was below; in conclusion, it is the exact same water. 

Look here! By this demonstration, it is proven feasible and possible that water may be sucked and drawn from the caverns of the earth (which is fostered and maintained by the sea) even to the tops of high mountains. This happens by natural means or operations, without any necessity of changing the form of the water into vapor, as *Aristotle* vainly surmises. Indeed, Aristotle's theory contradicts his own axiom: *It is done in vain by many things which can be effected by fewer* <note>original: "Frustra fit per plura quod fieri potest per pauciora"</note>. 

On the contrary, we see and observe in the Weather-glass that if the expansive <note>original: "dilative"</note> power of the sun or hot winds heats the head of the Weather-glass, or inflames the outward air, then the air within the glass will also expand <note>original: "dilate"</note> itself. By its expansion, it will strike down or push away the water that the air (when contracted by cold) had sucked or drawn up. Once again, the visible sinking of the water points to and proves the invisible expansion of the air.

Thus, the expanding, thinned air passes from the south and is condensed into clouds in the north. We conclude, therefore, that when the hot spirit of the Sun in the height of summer greatly thins <note>original: "rarifie"</note> the air in our northern hemisphere, that air seeks a place for its expanded spirits. This is no different than how external cold contracts the air in a weather-glass <note>An early thermometer where air expansion or contraction moves a column of water.</note> and, through that contraction, attracts or draws up the water inside.

So, here we have two ways that fountains are raised and lowered. Just as the warming action <note>original: "calefying act"</note> of the spirits strikes them down across the northern hemisphere in the summer, the cooling action of the spirits raises them up in the southern hemisphere, where winter holds power. Thus, there are two forces pushing it down in the northern parts: the present northern Sun (the divine positive act) and the absent southern cold (the divine privative act <note>In Fludd's philosophy, "privative" refers to the absence of the Sun's light and heat, which manifests as cold.</note>).

Furthermore, when the Sun moves from the northern regions to the southern after passing the barrier of the Equator, the exact same effects will occur, but in the opposite regions. Then, the cold of the north will help raise the fountains in the north and push them down in the south; meanwhile, the southern heat will depress them in the south and consequently help raise them up in the north. This is demonstrated as follows:

Therefore, I conclude that when the general <note>original: "catholick"</note> northern air of the hemisphere **EFG** is cold, it sucks in or contracts the air within the vein of the earth **A**. This contracted air then lifts the water out of the wide sea **D**, as is clearly demonstrated by the *weather-glass* <note>An early type of thermometer where air expansion or contraction moves a liquid column.</note>. For when the cold external air has contracted the air in the head and neck of the glass through chilling <note>original: "congelation"</note> (this head and neck I compare to the vein in the earth, as the vein is enclosed and has no other outlet), then the water is drawn up by the contraction of the air out of the vast reservoir of water in the pot or basin, which I compare to the sea. 

On the other hand, in the summer or southern hemisphere **EHG**, where the Sun is present, the general air is thinned or rarified. This expanding air around the fountain and in the cavity of the vein beats down and lowers the water in the southern mouth of the earth's vein **B**, toward **C**. Consequently, in the summer, springs are often found either completely dried up or at least significantly lowered. 

Therefore, I say that because the waters are pushed down in the summer-like South by the thinning of the air, and drawn up in the winter-like North by the cold, the water is more easily raised in the cold North. Furthermore, the rising of the waters in the North—which were lowered the previous summer—is caused by the contraction of the empty air that occupied the space in the vein of the earth during the summer. Just as we see in the *weather-glass*, through the expansion of the air in the South, the water is easily hidden there within the earth. So it appears that the water is partly driven and pressed down in the South by heat (making it easier to draw up in the North), and partly lifted in the North by the winter cold. It is as if a cord were threaded through a hole in a large piece of timber, going down at one end and coming up at the other, like this:

If the cord is strongly pulled up from the North **A**, and simultaneously pushed or pressed down from the South **B**, it will sink more easily at the South **B** and rise at the North **A**.

The exact same thing happens, but in reverse order, when the Sun (and therefore summer) is in the northern hemisphere **EFG**; for then the springs will be lowered there and raised in the southern parts. The sea, soaking into the depths of the earth **D**, acts as the common medium or cistern for both extremes; it receives the water pressed down and distributes that excess upward to the surging, growing winter fountains.

Since this is the case—as proven by the coldness of springs in the summer—then by that same logic, this reinforced cold in the summer should also trap, preserve, and strengthen the internal heat at the center of the earth that supposedly causes those vapors. Consider the conclusion: if that were true—namely, that the central heat were greater in the summer—then vapors would be even more abundant in the summer, for the greater the fire, the more smoke it produces. And again, by reason of the great cold in the caverns...

I know it will be objected that we can see with our own eyes that standing ponds and similar wet places are dried up by the summer heat. How can that happen, unless the Sun attracts the moisture and consumes it by converting it into vapors? I answer this: first, the Sun does not "draw" the water but only rarifies <note>original: "rarify"; to make something less dense or more thin</note> it, and then the rarified substance tends to rise upward. However, if the Sun were to use up all the moisture of lakes and ponds in that way—specifically by converting it into air—an absurdity would follow. If the Sun reduced all those waters into vapors, it would thicken the air. On the contrary, our weather-glass <note>An early type of thermometer where air expansion or contraction moves a liquid column</note> teaches us, by the sample of air contained within it, that heat thins and rarifies the air rather than thickening it.

Furthermore, a greater error would strike at the heart of *Aristotle’s* doctrine concerning the creation of clouds. Since his opinion is that a cloud is generated from vapors pulled out of the earth and water by the attractive force of the Sun and stars, it would follow that we should have more clouds and more rain in the summer than in the winter. But this is as false as his other claims. Instead, I say that the air is rarer and thinner in the summer because of the presence of the "divine act" in the Sun, which thins the air through its constant action. This is why we have fewer clouds in the summer. As I proved before, clouds are created by the compression of air. The air is then renewed in a circular cycle when those meteors <note>original: "Meteors"; in this period, the term referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, snow, or clouds</note> are resolved back into their original, invisible state, which was simply air.

I admit that some part of the water is made thin <note>original: "subtiliated"</note> and, through expansion <note>original: "dilatation"</note>, is pushed into the winter hemisphere. However, the greatest part sinks down through the tiny, invisible pores of the dry and thirsty earth. The earth drinks it up and keeps it in its "bowels" until it is sucked back out by the contraction of the air that fills its pores and cracks—a contraction caused by the cold of the following winter. We find that even a single large barrel <note>original: "Hogshead"</note> of water will last a long time before the hot Sun evaporates it. Moreover, it is certain that whatever the Sun thins during the day so that it rises as vapor, usually falls back to earth at night as foggy mist and dew. Thus, it is moved from a concentrated place, expanded, and sprinkled as mist and dew over the wide fields. This is evident because we always observe that summer mists and dews are most frequent around lakes and rivers. To conclude this book and this entire section, I will examine the opinion of our "princely Peripatetic" <note>original: "Peripatetick"; a follower of Aristotle</note> regarding lightning and thunder, so that we may also judge the validity of his physical doctrines in that area.

Good God, what a jumble <note>original: "Gallimofry"</note> he makes! What a confusion of external actions or efficient causes does he invent, when there is really only one internal or essential cause that moves however it pleases and operates in all things. Are these superficial, incidental, and external formal causes the primary movers and life-givers of the bright lightnings? The second story is this: during the time of the great plague <note>original: "great sicknesse time"</note>, I returned from Wales and stayed for a while with my noble friend, the Lord Bishop of Worcester, at Hartlebury Castle. While there, I was informed of a strange accident that had been caused by lightning and thunder about five weeks before my arrival, some three or four miles from the castle. I felt compelled to go see the place, and in the company of my worthy friends Mr. Finch and Sir Thomas Thornborough, I inspected the site. It was under a tall, wide-spreading elm tree on a small hill. 

The inhabitants living nearby related that the sons of two wealthy farmers <term>yeomen</term> were passing by with a load of hay drawn by four oxen and two horses, driven by one of their fathers' servants. As the thunderstorm overtook them, the driver went up the hill and placed the load and the animals under the elm tree. The driver crouched under the load of hay for shelter, and the two youths sat upon a bench or turf seat built around the tree. Finally, there came a terrifying bolt of thunder. The workman crouching under the cart said, "Good Lord, what a crack that was!" At these words, the boys laughed out loud and mocked him, repeating, "A crack!" 

But immediately, a noise was heard in the upper branches of the tree, and a solid mass of fire came down directly between the boys. It struck the hair of one of them into the tree and set the other so intensely on fire that the man under the cart and others were forced to run down the hill to fetch water to extinguish the flames. When the fire was out, the boy's skin was as hard as roasted pork. Thus, they paid dearly for their mockery and contempt of God's judgments; indeed, they ought to have prayed to God to preserve them from the agents <note>original: "ministers"</note> of His wrath. ### CHAPTER XII.

->*How lightning and thunder ought rightly to be described by the true Philosopher, following the spirit of Holy Scripture.*<-

Since it has been made manifest in the preceding chapter that Aristotle has utterly erred in his ideas regarding the material, essential, and formal causes of lightnings, let me gather—as nearly as my weak capacity will allow—what the true nature and original essential cause of lightnings should be, according to the harmonious agreement of the Holy Scriptures.

**1.** Lightning is a certain fiery air or spirit, animated by the brightness of JEHOVAH and drawn out of His treasury (which is the heavens or the universal air) to do and execute His will, for the benefit or the harm of His creatures.

**Or else in this manner:**

**2.** Lightning is a shining brightness proceeding out of the clouds (which are the pavilion of JEHOVAH) and is sent from the throne of God down even to the earth, covering the surface of the seas.

But if we wish to describe lightning with all its accompanying effects, and consequently express the whole essence of thunder (which is of a mixed nature), we may do so as follows, based on the testimony of the Holy Bible:

**3.** Lightning is a fire burning from the face or presence of JEHOVAH, at the sight or touch of whose brightness the clouds pass away; and the Almighty thunders and utters His voice from heaven, sending forth His arrows for the destruction of the wicked.

**Or thus:**

**4.** Lightning is a fire proceeding from JEHOVAH, sent out of His dark tabernacle from above; at the sight of it, the waters or clouds flee in terror, and the abyss is troubled. In this turmoil, the voice of His thunder moves in a circle, and fiery or kindled coals are sent forth like arrows from a well-bent bow to carry out His will, whether for blessing or for vengeance, both in heaven and on earth.

**Or in this fashion:**

**5.** Lightning or coruscation <note>original: "coruscation"; a flash of light</note> is a clear and pure light in the clouds above, which the passing wind purifies, etc.

By the first of these descriptions, the clear material cause of lightning is shown to be a fiery air; the place from which it is drawn is the treasure-house of God, or the heavens. Also, the formal cause <note>the essence or design</note> is expressed by lightning being described as a fiery spirit or air. I have stated the efficient cause <note>the agent that brings it into being</note>, according to the testimony of truth, to be the will or word of God, upon which depends that spirit of wisdom by which God operates all things. Lastly, the final cause <note>the ultimate purpose</note> is also noted, because it is said that lightning was created to do the will of Him who ordained it, whether for the pain or pleasure of mortal men. All of this is evidently confirmed by the passages of Scripture mentioned before.

The second definition is confirmed by the Book of Revelation, which says, <margin>Revelation 4. *Lightnings* <note>original: "Fulgura"</note></margin> Lightnings proce— <meta>catchword: proceed</meta>

The **efficient cause** seems to be the lightnings from God, or rather the fiery presence of God, giving life to the lightnings and directing them toward a specific target. So it appears that lightnings are, in a sense, the instruments of God’s wrath; just as a sword is the instrument of the man who strikes. When we speak of a strike, we say it was the man who hit, not the sword. They claim that these exhalations, being trapped in a cloud and ignited—partly by the collision or knocking together of other clouds, and partly by the coldness of the place—cause thunder through the eruption of their flames. 

I would have every wise Christian observe carefully, by what has already been said, whether the mystery of a tempest and whirlwind consists of a thing of so small importance and poor value as Aristotle would make us believe; or if it does not arise out of a far more profound and unsearchable abyss. For lightnings are reported by Truth itself to be the fiery lights of God that issue or proceed from his throne, and thunders are justly termed the voice, word, and eloquence of Jehovah. 

For this reason, Jehovah, rebuking the boldness of these kinds of worldly philosophers—who presume so far as to judge his unsearchable actions, or to dive into the depth of his mysteries regarding the essential causes of these weather phenomena <note>original: "meteors"</note> without the warrant and assistance of God’s Spirit—falsely makes the world believe that his hidden and secret acts are carried out according to their vain imaginations. These imaginations vanish in the end and become as nothing, because they are grounded on nothing else but foolish and self-conceited fantasies and vanities. God seems to speak these words to them:

### CHAP. XIII.

->*A conclusion of this work, including an admonition to all good Christians to beware of pagan philosophy and to cling fast to that which is taught to us by the Scriptures, for the reasons set down here.*<-

Let it now be permitted for me, in the conclusion of this section—O you Europeans, who seem to spend your days so seriously and zealously in the Christian religion—to turn the sharp edge of my pen and the rougher file of my speech toward you. You, being far too much seduced by the false doctrine of **Aristotle**, think and imagine that weather phenomena <term>meteors</term>, but especially lightning and thunder, are common natural things of little or no importance at all, being produced only by nature because of a "hot distemper of the air." 

I would request you, as a true Christian ought to request his brothers, to observe well and attend with diligence to this admonition which I will bestow upon you as a farewell. I beseech you not to scorn or reject my previous assertion, which has told you and sufficiently proved that lightnings and thunders—indeed, all other weather phenomena—are the immediate works of God’s hand. By this endeavor of mine, you may not only bring comfort and consolation to your souls when you hear the terrible voice of the Lord, making you call to mind your past sins and iniquities and pray to him heartily to pardon you (and not to hold your offenses against you in his anger); but <margin>Job 37.</margin> also you may give the honor and glory to him, who, thundering from above, works marvelously.

I would have you know, therefore, that the "worldly wise men" of this our Christian world—who are, as it were, servants or followers of the pagan <term>Ethnick</term> Philosophers—have hitherto erred in their imaginations blindly, or like madmen. This is because, having been instructed in the blind wisdom of this world by their pagan tutors and doctors, they will not be brought to believe that God works all things in heaven and in earth immediately by his Word alone. Instead, they believe he works "mediately"—namely, by other necessary natural or supernatural means as essential, efficient causes. 

Yet the holy Text instructs us in plain terms that it is one and the self-same essence which acts and operates all in all by his Word, using each creature only as his organ or instrument in which and by which he moves and works his will. I ask you: Is not their tenet or assertion altogether opposite and contradictory to the divine authority, which says, <margin>1 Cor. 8. 5.</margin> *Though there be those who are called gods, whether in heaven or in earth (as there are many gods and many lords), yet for us there is but one God, that Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him. But every man has not that knowledge, etc.*? From these words we may gather that although we worldlings attribute this or that work to angels, or stars, or winds, or a created "nature" (according to the doctrine of pagan wisdom), yet such true...

# Mosaical Philosophy. Book 5.

Christian Philosophers, such as St. Paul, acknowledged only one God, from whom all actions in this world proceed; and one Word, through which alone—and not by any creature in the world—every thing is immediately produced in this world. Although all of this seems like truth and certainty to real Christians, this kind of doctrine issuing from heavenly wisdom is rejected and derided by the philosophers and wise men of this world. And why? Truly, because (as the Scripture teaches us) not every man has this knowledge. The reason is that they respect the wisdom of this world—which is earthly and animalistic <note>original: "animal," referring here to the lower, unspiritual part of the human soul</note> and, as St. Paul says, mere foolishness before God—more than the wisdom from above, namely, from the Father of Light. *And so they vanished in their imaginations.* <note>original Latin: "Et sic evanuerunt in imaginationibus suis." A reference to Romans 1:21.</note> I heartily wish, therefore—you who are raised with and made familiar with the holy Bible, nourished spiritually, and guided by the law of our Lord Jesus Christ—that you would seriously conceive and perpetually reflect upon the fact that God created the first substance of things (namely, the moist and fluid waters) by His Word. They remain in the Word and by the Word in that same moist or wet state as they were even until this very day.

<margin>2 Peter 3.</margin>
Also, He framed the heaven and the earth out of this universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> water by His Word (as St. Peter says). Again, He produced the light in heaven by His said Word—the Sun, the Moon, the Stars, the day, the night, and all other creatures—and ordained them to serve as various instruments <note>original: "Organs"</note> by which He might variously act or operate His will, as much in heaven above as in the earth and waters beneath. All of these move and work in and by the Word. And, in conclusion, God by His Word exactly and solely "operates all in all," as the Apostle says. This being so, I would gladly know: where is this "physical nature" of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, who believed nature operated by its own inherent laws rather than direct divine intervention.</note>, to which they assign an essential form of action of itself and by itself? Truly, it is most apparent that there is no such universal actor as the Peripatetics imagine. Instead, there is only one Word of God; one universal Christ, who fills all things; one eternal <term>Sapience</term> <note>Divine Wisdom</note> which replenishes the world; one incorruptible Wisdom which is in all things, that alone works and effects immediately all in all. And therefore, it is apparent that without it, nothing can exist and act.

### Section 1. Mosaical Philosophy.

<margin>Wisdom 13.</margin>
In their mouths and writings, the lying and false spirit of *Aristotle* has taken too deep a root or possession, and claimed for itself the primary and superior place. Although this my admonition may seem wild, ridiculous, and of little or no value to those who are wedded to their own will and blinded <note>original: "hood-winked"</note> by *Aristotle’s* subtle teachings, yet I would have them know that it is a matter of great importance and high consequence, because it concerns and touches the honor of God. 

For by this doctrine, true *Christians* may fundamentally know and understand the real and essential causes of tempests and other natural operations that belong to them. They may thereby perceive that these things do not happen by mere chance <note>original: "case fortuit"</note>, nor do they operate by any power of their own—as the imaginative pagans <note>original: "phantastick Ethnickes"</note> have devised or invented in their writings. Instead, they are brought forth <note>original: "traduced"</note> out of the holy storehouses <note>original: "Treasuries"</note> by Divine Providence and are sent down here below by the operation of the Word and the execution of His angelic ministers. This is done either to afflict and punish the wicked for their offenses, or to remind them of their sins so that, through fear, they may be driven to repent. 

So it is that when they, to their terror, hear the voice of the Lord in thunder from above and behold the fiery flashes of His wrath and indignation, or see the dreadful floods <note>original: "inundations"</note> caused by an abundance of snow or rain, they might be led to repentance. They might be humbled and encouraged to call upon their Creator for help, praying to Him heartily to turn away all dangers from them, to calm His tempests, and to pacify the fury of His fiery or watery ministers. They may ask Him to grant them milder and more favorable weather, with gentle and fertile rains, and to bless and save the fruit of their lands, preserving their cattle which feed upon them, as well as their houses and other such necessary possessions <note>original: "additaments"</note> from the violence of His tempestuous angels or spiritual instruments. 

On the other hand, whoever neglects this doctrine (which is founded on true wisdom) and wallows like a sow in the mire, committing himself to the rules of that worldly wisdom which is but mere foolishness before God, will consequently imagine all these meteorological marvels to proceed by chance and accident, without the action of any internal divine principle. For that reason, he will neglect them, viewing them only as "natural" things. Therefore, he will neither fear them as he truly ought to do, nor acknowledge Him who is their true author and the immediate actor in them. Such a man is justly numbered among those whom the Wise Man <note>Refers to Solomon</note> targets in this speech: *“All men (says Solomon) are vain by nature, in whom there is ignorance of God, and who cannot understand Him through those things that are made, nor recognize the craftsman by considering his works.”*

# The Epilogue to this Section.

Thus (*Judicious and Christian Reader*) you have understood the main difference between the wisdom of the world—which the Apostle affirms is but mere foolishness before God—and that which descends from above and issues from the *Father of Light*, which is the *essential and true Spirit of Wisdom <note>original: "Sapience"</note> or Discipline*. 

Consequently, you may easily discern how *Pagan Philosophy* <note>original: "Ethnick Philosophy"</note>, which is grounded upon *worldly wisdom*, is but a *useless fallacy* or a *deceptive illusion* <note>original: "prestigious Figment"</note> because it relies only on the *traditions of men* and the *elements of this world*. Therefore, only the philosophy of the *Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles*, which is founded upon the *Universal Christ* <note>original: "Catholick Christ"</note> or the *Eternal Spirit of God*—in whom is the *fullness of Divinity*—is the only *true, real, and essential* philosophy. Therefore, I may boldly conclude and speak to you, along with other *Christians*, in the language of *Moses*, saying:

<margin>Deuteronomy 30:19</margin> I call Heaven and Earth to witness today against you <note>original Latin: "Contestor hodie contra vos Coelum & Terram, me vitam & mortem, bonum & malum, benedictionem & maledictionem praeposuifse tibi. Quare elige vitam, ut tu cum semine tuo vivas."</note>, that I have set before you life and death, good and evil, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life, so that you and your descendants <note>original: "seed"</note> may live, *and increase in the knowledge and understanding of God, since in true Wisdom consists all true Philosophy, certain Science, and complete Discipline.*

## *The Second Section of this*
# TREATISE.
## The First Book.
### The Argument of the First Book.

After the author had understood through diligent inquiry that all **sympathy** and **antipathy** sprang immediately from certain different passions of the **soul**, or the life-giving **spirit**—one being <term>concupiscible</term> <note>original: "Concupiscible"; relating to strong desire or attraction</note> and the other <term>irascible</term> <note>original: "Irascible"; relating to anger, rejection, or repulsion</note>—and yet perceived these effects to exist in **vegetable** and **mineral** creatures as well as **animals**, he was struck by a special desire to find their fundamental cause or beginning. When he had well pondered and considered that eternal **unity** (which is the head and root of all things) in its simple and absolute nature, he could discern no such diversity in its essence, seeing that it exists forever as only one and the same **identity**.

<margin>Psalm 139:12</margin>
For, according to Holy Writ, "As His darkness is, so also is His light" <note>original Latin: "Sicut tenebræ ejus, ita & lux ejus"</note>. Therefore, he concluded that a twofold airy effect or principle, completely opposite to one another in condition and disposition, must necessarily spring and arise from these two distinct properties within that one entire essence: namely, <term>nolunty</term> <note>original: "Nolunty"; the divine act of "not-willing" or withdrawal</note> and <term>volunty</term> <note>original: "Volunty"; the divine act of willing or desire</note>. The first was expressed by **darkness**, and the other by **light**. 

For when this **mental eternity** and **infinite light**—in whom in truth there is no **darkness**—does not will, it reserves itself within itself. That is, it reflects its beams back into itself and so gives form to nothing by its presence, but leaves the universal **abyss** or **chaos** (which is said in this state to dwell and exist in the divine power) dark, deformed, quite void, and destitute of its life-giving act or resplendent brightness. This negative action is the perfect character of His **nolunty**, the general effects of which are **darkness** and <term>privation</term> <note>original: "privation"; the state of being deprived of light or existence</note>. 

But when this hidden unity sends out the kind and healing brightness of its essence—which is the expression of His **volunty** or will—into the deformed **chaos**, then deformity, **darkness**, and **privation** are forced to give way to their opposite rivals: **conformity**, **light**, and **position** <note>original: "Position"; here meaning "affirmation" or the act of bringing something into existence</note>, which are the affirmative acts of life and essential existence. 

By this object of his contemplation, he gathered that the act of **volunty** and that of **nolunty** were within one essential **unity**, which was all goodness. Consequently, **nolunty** within it is nothing other than its **volunty**; since it is one and all, so also is its **volunty** but one **identity** within it, and yet all and over all with it.

<margin>Daniel 4</margin>
For by this, it acts or works its pleasure, both negatively and positively, as much in the heavenly virtues as in the inhabitants of the earth. And therefore darkness and light are all one in this **archetypal unity**, because...

# *Mosaic Philosophy.* Book I

<margin>2 Peter 3.</margin>
...all within it is good, because it is only and absolutely good in itself. Regarding the **contrary effects**—namely, the deformed and <term>privative</term> <note>original: "privative"; having the nature of a lack or absence (like darkness is an absence of light)</note> darkness of the **raw chaos**, or **undigested abyss**, and the shaping act or **positive emanation of light**—they indeed appear as opposites to created beings. They seem to produce an infinity of contradictions in the world, which mortals judge to be either "good" or "evil" based on how they are affected by them. 

Nevertheless, it seems most apparent to the **Author** that these two contrary outflows, or extensions, proceeding in truth from one **eternal essence**, were the principles of all things. The dark Chaos provided and produced from her womb the **waters**, which were the only matter from which the world—and consequently the heavens and earth—was made. Meanwhile, the **life-giving emanation or irradiation of the eternal light** bestowed upon it form, shape, power, and motion. 

When the **Author** had discovered all of this and seriously pondered it, his reason clearly informed him that the world was composed and framed from opposing materials. For how is it possible that opposite and discordant parents should not bring forth children whose conditions differ from their kind? And yet, such was the will of the **Creator** that these two dissonant notes should—in the beginning and the shaping of an Image like himself—be united into one Unison or unity by the unbreakable bond of his never-dying Spirit of love and concord. 

In this way, the matter (which is the substance of the dark waters) might serve as a female to the formal and masculine irradiation or illuminating spirit that issued from him. Thus, out of that duality or "confusion of unities," he made a <term>typical Trinity in Unity</term> <note>original: "typicall Trinity in Unity"; a symbolic representation of the Holy Trinity found within the structure of the natural world</note>, patterned after the likeness of the <term>Archetype</term> <note>original: "Archetype"; the original divine model or pattern in the mind of God</note>. 

Because the Archetype is purely spiritual and was the eternal life and formal being of the world (existing itself without any beginning), the world—being its image—must also have a <term>universal life or soul</term> <note>original: "catholick life or soul"; "catholick" here means universal or all-encompassing</note>. Through this soul, the world may act and live according to the pattern from which both the form of its essence and the matter of its existence flowed. For that reason, the world must be endowed with the opposite properties of "willing" and "not-willing," or **Volunty** and **Nolunty**, and consequently, of lovely attraction or hateful expulsion.

Based on this, the author observed that both the internal and external model of the world must necessarily be subject to contrary passions and alterations. These proceed from similar properties: 

1.  The world is sometimes inclined toward the disposition of darkness, following by a natural instinct the condition and inclination of matter or water (the offspring of the dark **Abyss** or **Chaos** over which divine power has dominion). In this state, it takes on the character of the Unity’s **Nolunty** (the divine "not-willing"). 
2.  At other times, it affects and imitates the action and property of light, which flows from the eternal and all-acting fountain of Unity. This is the virtuous effect of the sacred **Volunty** (the divine "willing").

It seemed to the **Author** that because the entire world was composed of these two contrary properties—formal light and the moist, dark matter—it must follow that its universal soul (the general life-giving spirit) must be subject to opposite passions and alterations. Consequently, every particular essence or form derived from that universal soul—no differently than beams from the Sun—must also be vulnerable to these opposites. 

From this source springs that original love or hatred known to exist between good Angels and evil Spirits. From here issue all those constant mutations and alterations that happen in the ethereal and <term>sublunary</term> <note>original: "sublunary"; literally "under the moon," referring to the changing Earthly realm as opposed to the unchanging heavens</note> heavens, specifically because of the conflicting variety of the stars' influence. From here proceed those oppositions and contrary effects breathed out by the winds. From here are derived the discord and concord of the **Elements**, along with the diverse natures found in meteorological phenomena. Finally, from here flow the many different affections, the opposition of dispositions, the passions of spirits, and, in a word, the **sympathy** and **antipathy** observed between all creatures—whether they are simple or compound, animal, vegetable, or mineral.

<summary>This page argues that the world is composed of two opposing principles—divine light and chaotic darkness—which are unified by God's Spirit to create a "universal soul." This duality explains the origins of all cosmic and earthly tensions, including sympathy, antipathy, and the behavior of elements and living things.</summary>
