Section 2: Mosaic Philosophy.

Therefore, the author concludes on these grounds that it is only just and reasonable to agree with the opinions of those two notable and famous philosophers, Heraclitus and Empedocles, regarding this point. The first has presented it as an infallible maxim <margin>Ecclesiasticus 42:25.</margin> that **all things are made and composed of strife and friendship** <note>original: "Quod omnia fiant per litem & amicitiam"</note>—that is to say, of hatred and love. The second has proclaimed it as an oracle of truth: **"That the soul is composed of four elements, and of peace or concord, and contention or discord"** <note>original: "Quod ex quatuor elementis, & ex amicitia & lite composita fit anima"</note>. By this, he signifies that contrary disposition between the watery spirit and the bright mental beam regarding their origin. For by "strife," he argues for both spiritual and physical contention, regarding that contrary power and ability existing between formal light and dark matter. This applies both to the body during the act of corruption when the soul would depart from it, and to the excitable or angry passions of the soul, in which the spirit labors and suffers unnaturally. In these opinions, the aforementioned philosophers do not seem to differ from the Son of Sirach <note>The author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus.</note>, who speaks thus: **"All things are of a double nature, one of them contrary to the other, and yet there is nothing made which is defective"** <note>original: "Gemina sunt omnia, quorum alterum est contrarium alteri, nec quicquam factum est quod mancum fit"</note>.

It cannot be enclosed or contained by any part, nor divided into distinct portions, nor defined by any substantial <term>quiddity</term> <note>original: "quiddity"; the inherent nature or essence of someone or something.</note> or entity. 

Based on this, wise men have judiciously concluded that Unity is the most ancient and fundamental principle of all others. It encompasses within itself all substances, quantities, and qualities, just as the geometrical <term>prick</term> <note>original: "prick"; a point or dot.</note> or point, when considered in its naked simplicity, is observed to be indivisible and scarcely perceptible. Indeed, it is almost impossible to define; and yet, the point is clearly known to be the infallible beginning not only of every geometrical line, but also of all other continuous mathematical dimensions. It contains all magnitudes and is not contained by any.

Since these two principles of all dimensions precede and excel all others in order, rank, and antiquity, expert mathematicians invented them as a symbolic imitation or image of the most internal, central, and hidden point of Divinity—the most divine and brightest Unity. This Unity remained in that very state in which it stood before the creation of the world: namely, when it kept itself within itself and remained hidden from all potential creatures. It later chose, by revealing itself or releasing its life-giving light, to enact and make itself manifest as a dwelling place in its simple and absolute nature of unity, without having any regard or consideration for the things it would create. ...should not be regarded as God: for since up to this point it had not produced any creature by which it might be worshiped or recognized as God; neither could it rightly be styled or called a Father. For it did not appear to have thought of any Son or issue, whether archetypal <note>The original model or ideal form.</note> and ideal, or typical and worldly. Neither could it be considered the *highest good* <note>original: "Summum bonum"</note>, given that the shapeless matter or dark Chaos—or rather *hyle* <note>original: "Hyle"; a Greek term for primordial matter</note>—did not as yet taste of his bright and all-animating blessing, which was concealed and hidden in its potential darkness and obscurity, and was therefore void of all form. 

Neither could it be called beautiful, because it did not yet impart its beauty for the decoration or animation of any creature; nor could it rightly be said to be eternity, because in this state of being hidden within itself, it seemed to human understanding not to exist at all. Consequently, it appeared to have no relationship or connection with eternity, aeviternity <note>A state of existence that has a beginning but no end, often associated with angels or the soul.</note>, or time. Moreover, it could not claim for itself the name of "principle" or "beginning," because it had no relation yet to anything that sprang or issued from a beginning. 

In conclusion, the nature of this simple, singular <note>original: "Monadicall"</note> existence was so hidden and obscure to mortal understanding before anything was created, and in its order and antiquity so unknown—indeed, so inscrutable and incomprehensible in its essence—that it could not in any way be defined as substance, quantity, or quality. Rather, it was conceived to be a certain transcendent entity or existence, reserved only in itself and consisting of itself. It had no principal root or beginning from which to spring and exist, but existed only from and of itself. In its Divine Power <note>original: "Puissance"</note>, as in a place without end or limits, all things which are now explicitly visible were then implicitly contained, although in regard to our human capacity, they were considered to be nothing. 

And for this cause, those who were well-versed in the laws of true wisdom have recorded in their everlasting registers that this mystical infinity—when it was thus wrapped in the gloomy tangle <note>original: "clew," meaning a ball of thread or a labyrinthine path</note> or profound abyss of darkness, and remained as it were vacant or resting in itself without any action or (as they say) having regard for nothing—was therefore termed in Hebrew *Ayin* <note>The Hebrew word for "Nothing" or "Naught."</note>: <margin>Reuchlin, Book 3, *On the Art of the Kabbalah*.</margin> that is to say, *Nothing*, *Infinite* <note>original: "Non finis", literally "No end"</note>, and *Non-Being* <note>original: "Non Ens"</note>. In plain English, it is "Nothing at all" in our imagination, because the slenderness and poverty of man’s capacity and intellect in regard to Divine things is such that we are accustomed to judge that something does not exist at all if it does not appear manifest to our sight. 

For this reason, therefore, the wisest persons in the abstruse and hidden Kabbalah <note>A Jewish mystical tradition.</note> have termed this original Unity in its secret state the *Dark Aleph* <note>original: "Aleph tenebrosum"</note>. The Hebrew letter Aleph is used among the Jews and Kabbalistic Rabbis as the figure for "one" in arithmetic, and consequently, it is taken hieroglyphically for God, as He is understood to be that absolute Monad or Unity <note>The number one as a philosophical principle of wholeness.</note> which was only in itself, and did abide and rest in itself, without any act of flowing forth <note>original: "emanation"</note>. He later used this act when He was pleased to work through Creation. Therefore, the wise philosopher Hermes—not disagreeing in this from the Holy Scripture—<margin>Poimandres, Books 1 and 3.</margin> says, *"Unity, before the world's beginning, shone only to itself and in itself, and not to anything else."* <note>original: "Monas ante mundi exordium sibi ipsi & non aliis reluxit"</note> 

And in another place: *"There was an infinite shadow in the abyss; moreover, water and a thin intellectual spirit were in the Chaos through divine power."* <note>original: "Erat umbra infinita in abysso, aqua insuper, & Spiritus tenuis intellectualis per divinam potentiam in Chaos inerant"</note> And <margin>1 John 1.</margin> Moses, to confirm this saying of that wise philosopher, says: *"Darkness was upon the face of the abyss."* <note>original: "Tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi"; Genesis 1:2.</note> 

By this, wise men may discern and contemplate, though from afar, what the Divine Power <note>original: "Potentia"</note> was before any creature clearly appeared out of darkness. They may also easily gather what the true principle and foundation of Darkness is: namely, the enclosing or retaining of the actual beams or light of immortal life and being within this bright, fundamental Unity, in which there is no darkness. Thus, the original darkness can be considered nothing else but the absence of the radical Unity’s bright flowing forth, which is the fountain of all action. Neither can that Divine, life-giving <note>original: "vivifying"</note> and creating Light be present when the will of that simple and absolute essence in Unity is not minded to send forth the treasure of its shaping <note>original: "informing"; in a philosophical sense, to give form to matter.</note> <margin>Genesis 1.</margin> beams toward deformity. And hereupon it follows of necessity that darkness was upon the face of the abyss, and that the earth was void and without form, before the Divine Essence shone forth; and that darkness was made the dwelling place of rest and repose, because where the Divine act or sacred emanation is absent, all things are only potential, and consequently without actual truth, being as it were stark dead,

Thus have I expressed and made manifest, according to the small strength of my understanding, the state and being of this radical and eternal Unity before anything was created by it, along with the effects that it produced in the potential and deformed Mass—the material subject of all things. This matter was implicitly <note>original: "complicitly"; meaning "folded in" or contained within</note> or hiddenly detained and comprehended in that Omnipotent and incomprehensible point of Divine perfection. In that uncreated condition, it remained as Nothing, *as far as we are concerned* <note>original: "quoad nos"</note>; for it was without form, and it is form alone that gives a thing a name and essence. Therefore, in the state of its non-actual being, wise men have termed it "Divine Power" <note>original: "Potentiam Divinam"</note> or the Divine

...a mere point into a circle or circumference, verifying that saying of the wise Philosopher: *God is the center of everything, whose circumference is nowhere to be found;* that is, in all and beyond all. To confirm all this, we may boldly and without offense infer this much: namely, that everything that is begotten, <term>originated</term> <note>original: "principiated"</note>, created, produced, or separated, does radically proceed from one that is unbegotten, infinite, not made or created, nor separated, but only one Unity, individual in his essence. For it is an easy matter to consider that every inferior thing does issue from a superior; every corporal thing from a spiritual; every visible thing from an invisible; every temporal thing—namely, that which has both a beginning and an end—from a thing that is <term>aevial</term> <note>original: "æviall"; meaning something that has a beginning but no end, like an angel or a soul</note>; and every aevial thing from an eternal thing, to wit, that which has neither beginning nor end. Therefore, that eternal point or brightest Unity which has no beginning, and consequently no end, is the fountain from which all aevial and temporal things essentially proceed, no differently than how *all numbers flow from Unity* and are comprehended in Unity. For however far a number extends itself, it always has an unity to begin it and an unity to conclude it, and in truth, it has nothing besides an unity to create and compose it within. 

But for your better instruction, you may observe by a diligent insight into <term>algebraic numbers</term> <note>original: "cossicall numbers"; from the Italian "cosa," the early name for algebra</note> how the Divine and Centrally formal Unity does comprehend all creatures—as well before they were made as since their creation—within itself. For we must note that there is nothing in the world that is not either a root, or a square, or a cube, or some other such figure which is framed and composed of these. The root represents the beginning of all algebraic proportions or magnitudes; the Square deciphers the simple and spiritual originated figure, which is created or made by the multiplication of the root; the cube is composed through the augmenting of that square or originated shape in its root. So we may discern that the whole cubic body, and consequently the square, is contained in the root, and in conclusion, is nothing else than the root multiplied in itself or from itself. 

But so that my demonstration may approach a little nearer to our purpose, let us, I pray you, with diligence consider the nature and property of this Divine <term>Monad</term> <note>original: "Monady"; the number one as a symbol of God</note> or Unity as it exists in its simple and sincere state. We shall find that—without any exit from its own punctual or central depth—it implicitly comprehends within itself the three previously mentioned algebraic dimensions, and consequently all other things which it has now by Creation explicitly made evident in this physical <note>original: "typicall"</note> world. This is proved easily by this Arithmetical demonstration: For if we multiply an unity as a root by itself, it will produce only itself—namely, an unity for a square—which being again multiplied by itself, will bring forth a cube, which is exactly the same as the root or square; to wit, a simple unity. By this it is evident that although we have here three various branches which seem to differ in their formal progression—I mean a Root, a Square, and a Cube—yet in the essential truth and reality, there is but this one Unity or Identity, in which all things remain potentially and in a most hidden <note>original: "abstruse"</note> manner. And for this reason the Wise Man says: <note>original: "Deo omnia sunt cognita antequam crearentur"</note>

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 23:20</margin>
*All things were known unto God before they were created.*

<margin>John 10:30, 14:10-11</margin>

But lest some critical person should object to these passages in Scripture and elsewhere cited by me regarding this very point, and claim (as some have already done) that my opinions are completely at odds with those of the ancient Fathers and <term>Schoolmen</term> <note>original: "School-men"; medieval theologians and philosophers</note>, I will briefly express some of their thoughts on this subject. 

St. Augustine's opinion is: *That the ideas of things are eternal and unchangeable forms in the divine mind* <note>original: "Quod ideæ sunt formæ æternæ & incommutabiles in mente divina"</note>. And Duns Scotus holds them to be: *Certain objective things known by the divine intellect* <note>original: "Res objectivæ, cognitæ ab intellectu divino"</note>. But there is nothing in God except that which is God, because the Godhead is one and the same Spirit. Therefore, it follows that the Ideas in God—although they are many (for man was made according to one pattern, and a horse according to another, etc.)—are all nonetheless one in God. St. Augustine seems to prove and confirm this elsewhere in these words: *The supreme and highest intellect is a certain art of the omnipotent and wise God, full of all the unchangeable reasons of living things; and all are one in it, just as it is one from the one with whom it is one* <note>original: "Primus & summus intellectus est ars quædam omnipotentis atque sapientis Dei, plena omnium rationum viventium incommutabilium; & omnes unum in ea, sicut ipsa unum de uno cum quo unum."</note>. 

And in another place he says: *You are my God, and the Lord of all that you have created; with you the causes of all stable things remain, and the origins of all changeable things stay unchangeable with you, and the reasons of all rational, irrational, and temporary things always live* <note>original: "Tu es Deus meus, & Dominus omnium quæ creasti; & apud te omnium stabilium sunt causæ, & omnium mutabilium, apud te, immutabiles manent origines, & omnium rationabilium & irrationabilium atque temporalium semper vivunt rationes."</note>. By this, he argues that Unity, in the framing of the Ideal or Archetypal world, sent forth his Word as an essence begotten of itself; and afterward reflected that spirit of wisdom, which issued from them both, back into itself. For the Son of Sirach says: *The fountain of wisdom is the word of God in the highest, and her entrance is the eternal commandments* <note>original: "Pons [Fons] sapientiæ verbum Dei in excelsis, & ingressus illius mandata æterna"</note>. 

In this way, therefore, the Archetypal world was framed in and of one single unity, but in a threefold or triple manner: namely, by the coming forth of one out of one, and by the returning of that emitted unity back into itself through <term>emanation</term> <note>original: "emanation"; the process of flowing or proceeding from a source</note>. Through this, the three divine properties in one infinite essence may easily be understood. We conclude, therefore, that according to this ideal Image in its triple variety, our world was afterwards fashioned and proportioned as a true type and example of the divine Pattern after which it was drawn. For out of Unity in his hidden existence—namely, as it was hid in the dark <term>chaos</term> <note>original: "chaos"; the disorganized matter before creation</note> or potential mass—the bright flame of all formal being shone forth. The spirit of wisdom proceeding from them both joined the formal emanation with the potential matter (which was water). Thus, by the union of these two—the divine emanation of light and the substantial matter of darkness—the heavens and the earth were made of old, and consequently the whole world, as it shall...

This is because the whole <term>typical world</term> <note>original: "typicall world"; the physical world as a symbolic representation of the divine</note> and its parts are shaped after the image or representation of the <term>Archetype</term> <note>original: "Archetype"; the original pattern or model in the mind of God</note>, which is that eternal monad or unity in which all things exist. And **Rabbi Zoar** <note>likely referring to the Zohar, the foundational work of Jewish Kabbalah</note> says, *All things are one in respect of God, but many in regard to us.* **Plato** also states, *Not only are all things in God, but also all things that exist—inasmuch as they are in God and proceed from him—are but one Entity.* Moreover, **Hermes** in his *Smaragdine Table* <note>original: "Smaragdine Table"; the Emerald Tablet, a short, cryptic Hermetic text</note> writes, *As all things were by the mediation of one, so also are all things sprung from this one thing by adaptation.* And **Proclus**, in his *Theological Problems*, says, *As all things are sprung from one only, in like manner do they hasten by a continual course to return unto that unity; the greater the concord with which they meet together, the more they participate in him.* Again, **Plato** says, *All things depart from the high God and strive to return to him again, because in him consists their final repose and the sustenance of their existence.* For this cause, the philosopher **Leucippus** made this essential unity the *summum bonum*, or the sovereign good and happiness. Thus, you see that ancient philosophy does not disagree with the harmony of Holy Scripture on this point. There are some well-versed in this mystical progression who express it in this manner:

By this, we may discern how all things are essentially contained in this eternal and fundamental Unity. Because he is One, he is infinite; and being infinite in his dimension, essence, and power, he must of necessity contain within himself all finite things whatsoever. He is in all and fills all, and yet he is beyond all; he surpasses and encompasses everything and exists only in himself, yet he is not absent from the creatures he has formed by his Word according to his Will. For first, from his Will proceeded his Word, "*Fiat*" <note>Latin: "Let it be done"</note>, and it was done.

This Light also issued from the same original root and most ancient beginning of all things. By doing so, we may, with the best colors of our understanding, depict and describe that excellent essence which redeemed the watery matter out of the captivity of the deadly and misshapen darkness (to use Job's language), and by which all things have their being and beautiful existence.

# Section 2: Mosaical Philosophy

Some stubbornly hold that there were two coeternal principles. They made one of these to be God, whom they termed the "Prince of Light" and the beginner and author of life, health, and all goodness. The other they attributed to the Devil, whom they entitled the "Prince of Darkness" and the original source and principle of opposition, death, sickness, and all evil. They believed the Devil, or Prince of Darkness, was coeternal in existence with God because they thought there can be no goodness that does not have a relationship with its contrary, namely badness. For this reason, they believe—forsooth—that the God of evil and naughtiness must exist coeternally with the God of goodness. By this logic, they would not only exclude the Devil from the list of created beings but also banish Unity from the boundaries of nature, replacing it with the <term>Dyad</term> <note>original: "Diady"; a pair or duality of opposing forces</note> or duality (which in truth is nothing else but a confusion of Unities).

Indeed, this point seemed so sensitive and difficult to analyze and resolve that some of the wiser sort of "poetical philosophers" inclined toward their side, as appears by the mystical and allegorical expressions they enigmatically roll up or wrap within their mythical stories. Among the rest, we find that the poet *Pronapis*, in his *First-World* <note>original: "Proto-cosmus"</note>, asserts that *Demogorgon* (by which is meant the greatest of the Gods) was guarded or encircled by *Eternity* and *Chaos*. 

The story goes that once, while he was in his majesty, he perceived a great tumult and troublesome motion stirred up in the bowels of *Chaos*. To help her in this labor and ease her of her trouble, he put forth his hand and, performing the office of a midwife, suddenly delivered her of the foul and deformed monster *Strife* <note>original: "Litigium"</note>. After this monster had moved great storms and troubles and ambitiously attempted to soar or fly upward, it was immediately cast down into the deep by *Demogorgon*. 

But when he perceived *Chaos* still in labor and miserably oppressed with fervent sighs and dropping sweats, *Demogorgon* would not remove his hand from her during these agonies until she was delivered of *Pan* and his three sisters, who were called the <term>Fates</term> <note>original: "Parcæ"</note> or Destinies. When *Demogorgon* was deeply moved and taken with the beauty and excellent form of *Pan*, he made him the ruler of all his familiar affairs in the world and commanded the three sisters, as his handmaids and ministers, to obey his orders and will. 

It follows that *Chaos*, having been overburdened and oppressed with the weight of so great a heap or mass as she labored with, was now delivered and freed from it. At the persuasion of *Demogorgon*, she placed her son *Pan* upon her throne. This is the parabolic fable of *Demogorgon* and *Chaos*, commonly told by the poets. 

Their allegory implies that the generation and procreation of all things sprang from the highest God or Creator, whom they represent by the name of *Demogorgon*. To him, *Eternity* is joined by an unbreakable link in one essential society because only he is truly to be called "Eternal," who is and ever was the beginning or primary cause of all things. They also imagine that *Chaos* made a third in that endless society; for she is, according to *Ovid’s* account, the common mixed and confused matter or stuff of all things in the world. 

Therefore, the ancients affirmed her to be eternal with God, existing as a crude mass or dark abyss out of which *Demogorgon*, as a universal Father and master-craftsman, did—according to his will—procreate and fashion all things. Therefore, they esteem this universal substance or matter of all things to be the general Mother, on which, and out of which, the universal Father begat and framed everything. For this reason, they concluded that there were two general parents of things from endless antiquity: one was the Father and the other the Mother. 

But they agreed that God was their chief cause, and they wanted *Chaos* to serve only as his passive companion to conceive upon. And although it may appear that the wise and divine *Plato* seems in some way to verify that *Chaos* was God’s companion from all antiquity, he—as well as many others of similar depth—intimates to us that though she is called a companion with God in the Creation, she actually issued from him by a certain eternal generation or production, and that God afterward framed all things out of *Chaos*. 

For this reason, they conclude that it sprang from God and is never divided from him; it also serves God as a female companion for procreation and generation, just as *Eve*, being framed out of *Adam*, was called a companion to *Adam*. This is the opinion of both the heathen philosophers and mystical <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Followers of the Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism often adapted by Christian scholars in the Renaissance</note>. But to proceed in the exposition of this allegory: the hand of *Demogorgon* represents the Divine Power <note>original: "Puissance"</note>. The firstborn of *Chaos*, namely *Strife*, with a foul...

# Mosaical Philosophy. Book 1.

...foul shape, signifies the true Prince of Darkness, the Author of opposition, the Father of discord; and therefore, for his presumptuous attempt against the Prince of Light and the Lord of Life, he was cast down into the abyss. By the second birth of <term>Chaos</term> <note>In this context, the primordial state of matter before creation</note>, namely ***Pan***, they point at the universal nature of the world and the peacefulness and accord of contrary elements. They argue thereby that after that great discord which occurred in the first opening of the womb of Chaos, concord followed in the second place. This concord was as beautiful and acceptable to God in the later birth as deformed discord was foul and hateful in his sight in the first. 

Thus you see how, in the first beginning of the world, all the elements were at strife in the bowels of the Chaos. The three ***Parcae*** <note>original: *Parcæ*; the Three Fates of Roman mythology</note> or Sisters of Destiny—***Clotho***, ***Lachesis***, and ***Atropos***—who were born with ***Pan***, signify the three orders of time: namely, the time present, the time past, and the time to come. ***Clotho*** has the care of the present time, and her office is to twist the thread of life. ***Lachesis*** is the superintendent of the time to come, and looks to the flax or hemp which is not yet spun or twisted. And ***Atropos*** signifies the time past, which is irrevocable, and therefore she finishes and cuts off the thread now spun. 

I infer from this parabolic relation that though the Chaos or dark abyss exists with God before the world's creation, yet the infinite and sole eternal Unity, or radical Essence, created it and produced it out of itself. For that Eternal Unity says: <margin>Isaiah 45:7.</margin> *I am the Lord, and there is no other, who forms light and creates darkness, making peace and creating evil.* <note>original: *Ego Dominus & non est alter, formans lucem, & creans tenebras, faciens pacem, & creans malum*</note> It is as if he had said: "I am the Father of Light, or of the bright Spirit of Wisdom, and I created the dark Chaos out of which I framed the world; and out of her I produced both the concord and discord of the elements in the world"—that is to say, ***Litigium*** <note>Latin: "Strife" or "Dispute"</note> and ***Pan***. 

So we may still discern that there is but one Eternal Unity, which in itself is both male and female and everything that can be imagined. This Unity, of himself and in himself, produces all things, no differently than **Adam** contained within himself **Eve**, who was the Mother of the "little world" (or mankind) after **Adam**. And therefore ***Hermes*** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> says: <margin>Pimander</margin> *God, who is the Mind, being most full of the fertility of both sexes, and being life and light, brought forth another Divine Spirit by his Word.* <note>original: *Mens autem Deus utriusque sexus foecunditate plenissimus, vita & lux cum verbo sic alteram mentem peperit*</note> And the Scriptures seem to suggest as much in this sense: *Shall I, who grant the power of generation to others, be sterile myself?* <note>original: *Qui cæteris generationem tribuo, an sterilis ero?*; a reference to Isaiah 66:9</note>

It is evident, therefore, that out of one and the same radical Unity existing before all antiquity, both the matter and form of all things proceed. These things appear, in terms of their existence or births, to be <term>aevial</term> <note>original: "æviall"; a theological term for something that has a beginning but no end, unlike "eternal" which has neither</note>—that is, having a beginning but no end—though in their essential Root, they are eternal in God, the abstruse <term>Monad</term> <note>original: "Monady"; the ultimate, indivisible One</note> or Unity of all things. 

The dark Chaos and the bright informing Spirit are two principles opposite and contrary to one another in nature and property. From the dark principle proceed discord, evil, cold, freezing, rest, death, privation, and negation or <term>Nolunty</term> <note>The "un-will" or negative aspect of the divine will</note>. But from the other, which is the type of beauty and grace—namely the bright beginning—light, concord, goodness, heat, dissolving, motion, life, and position or <term>Volunty</term> <note>The positive "will" or affirmation of God</note> are poured out into the nature of the world to cause it to exist and live. Even so, both of these are but main branches arising from one and the same essential Unity. Because they cannot pass or exceed the limits of their infinite fountain, they are in Him both light and darkness, and in no way differ in essence from their Root, which <margin>Psalm 139:12.</margin> is all in all. As the Psalmist says: *Darkness is to him as light itself.* <note>original: *Tenebræ sunt ei, sicut ipsa lux*</note> 

For all is one in Him, who is only one and the same <margin>Romans 11:36.</margin> in himself, *in whom, by whom, and therefore from whom are all things.* For his **Volunty** and **Nolunty** are but one in Him who is one simple Identity; and what is his **Volunty** is just as much his affirmation as his negation, which is all but one good in Him who is all goodness. And yet, in regard to the creature, when his negation has the supremacy, he hides the light of his loving countenance and all is dark; he then operates by means of his privation. For where he hides his face, all is deformed and, as it were, void of essence and goodness. Look, here is his **Volunty** in its negative or privative state, which may rightly be termed his **Nolunty**. If his affirmation has dominion, he emits the beauty of his benignity, and the creature's waiting spirit is enlightened by his presence and consequently replenished with goodness. Look, here also is his **Volunty** in its affirmative or positive state, called **Volunty** in the right sense.

### Section 2. Mosaical Philosophy.

...adorn him with understanding. We know that man has but one Divine nature, which gives him intellect: <margin>Job 9</margin> "The spirit is in man (says Job), but the inspiration of the Almighty makes him understand" <note>original: *Spiritus est in homine sed inspiratio omnipotentis facit eum intelligere*</note>. And yet this Unity in essence, which is the Image of God, operates in general by two contrary properties. One of these is inclined to affirm, give, and grant a petition by a friendly flowing out—look here at the act of affirmation <note>original: "position"</note>, marked out in man's spiritual Unity. The other is to deny, take away, or be against the demand of the one who asks by a restrictive removal of the wished-for rewards—look here at the effect of negation deciphered, for the mental beam does not shine out toward the petitioner, but is reserved or contracted within itself.

In these two actions, we may observe only one effect which is praiseworthy in this one simple and absolute unity toward the petitioner. For though I grant a request through the friendly and pitiful flowing out or emission of my mental beam, so that it matches the petitioner's wish; or though I deny his demand, contrary to his desire, so that it appears to be a great evil or mischief to the asker; yet to my own mental spirit, both the affirmation and the negation appear good and are founded upon good reason. Therefore, they are indeed but one thing, though they seem different to the asker. 

In like manner, in the eternal and archetypal mental unity—of which the beam of our understanding is a type or likeness—the act of <term>Volunty</term> <note>Willingness or positive will</note> as well as <term>Nolunty</term> <note>Unwillingness or the act of the will saying "no"</note> is all one, and that is goodness. For He who is all goodness has in Himself no contrariety, although in the creature—which is subject to the effects of either His restrictive or positive will—His private or dark action is esteemed as evil. Conversely, His positive and light emanation, which is full of love and kindness, is received as good and therefore embraced with joy. For does not the holy Text tell us, <margin>Ecclesiastes 11:14</margin> "Good and evil, life and death, are from God?" <note>original: *Bonum & malum, vita & mors, à Deo sunt?*</note> And does it not tell us in another place,

And again, <margin>Job 10:12</margin> <margin>Psalm 4:7</margin> <margin>Psalm 18:29</margin> "Your visitation (says David) preserves my spirit" <note>original: *Visitatio tua preservat spiritum meum*</note>. ...foul shape signifies the true Prince of Darkness, the Author of opposition, and the Father of Discord. ## Section 2. Mosaical Philosophy.

...adorn him with understanding. In the same way, in the eternal and archetypal <note>The original pattern or model from which all things are made.</note> mental unity—of which our own beam of understanding is a type or likeness—the act of <term>Volunty</term> <note>original: "Volunty"; the act of willing or desiring.</note> as well as <term>Nolunty</term> <note>original: "Nolunty"; the act of not willing or refusing.</note> is all one, and that is goodness. Conversely, His positive and light emanation, which is full of love and kindness, is received as good and therefore embraced with joy.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 11:14</margin>
For does not the holy Text tell us, "Good and evil, life and death, are from God"? <note>original: *Bonum & malum, vita & mors, à Deo sunt?*</note> And does it not tell us in another place, <margin>Psalm 104:29-30</margin> "That when God hides His face from the creatures, they are troubled and sick; taking His bright, life-giving Spirit from them, they die; and sending it forth again, they are recreated with goodness, health, and life"? <note>original: *Quod Deo abscondente faciem suam à creaturis conturbantur, recipiente spiritum eorum expirant, emittente spiritum suum recreantur bono*</note> And again, <margin>Job 10:12, Psalm 4:7, Psalm 18:29</margin> "Your visitation," says David, "preserves my spirit." <note>original: *Visitatio tua (saith David) preservat spiritum meum*</note> "Lift up your countenance and send out light upon us, and it will cause us to see light, and it will make our darkness bright and shining." <note>original: *Attolle faciem tuam & emitte lucem supra nos, & efficiet ut videamus lucem, & splendentes efficiat tenebras nostras*</note> And again, <margin>Isaiah 42:16, Job, John 12:35, 1 John 1:6</margin> "I will turn darkness into light for them." <note>original: *Tenebras ponam iis in lucem*</note> "Crafty men shall run into darkness in the daytime, and they shall grope at noon-day as if it were in the night." <note>original: *Tenebras in diem incurrent astuti & quasi in nocte sic palpabunt in meridie*</note> "He is in darkness, and walks in darkness, who hates his brother." <note>original: *In tenebris est, & in tenebris ambulat, qui odit fratrem*</note> And the Prophet says, <margin>Nahum 1:8, Deuteronomy 31:17</margin> "Darkness shall pursue the enemies of God." <note>original: *Tenebra persequentur inimicos Dei*</note> "He hides His face from them, so that many evils and miseries may happen to them." <note>original: *Abscondit faciem suam ab iis ut obtingant iis multa mala & angustia*</note>

And yet all this is only according to His double property of Willingness and Unwillingness—that is, of His granting or positive emanation, and His withholding or negative condition. These are (as I have said) both good in Him, who is nothing but pure goodness in His simple and absolute nature, and therefore they are one in Him, who is sincere unity in Himself. 

Whereupon the wise Philosopher <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Pymander.</note>, agreeing with the Scriptures in this, says, <margin>Pymander 14</margin> "In the divine essence there is nothing but unity and goodness, for from the Creator comes neither evil nor filthiness." <note>original: *Non est in monade divinâ nisi unum & bonum, ab ipso enim factore nihil malum nihilque turpe*</note> And for this reason, when Job saw that God struck him—as it seemed to him, without a cause, since he was a just man and (as the Text says) a man after God's own heart—he was spurred forward, despite all his pains, with a pious zeal toward his Creator. Though he knew that his affliction proceeded from the hiding of his Maker's countenance from him, he broke forth into these terms: <margin>Job 34:10</margin> "And yet, far be it from God to do wickedness, or for the Almighty to commit iniquity." <note>original: *Et tamen absit à Deo impietas, & ab Omnipotente iniquitas*</note> It is most apparent even to the most fleshly <note>original: "flesh-test"; likely meaning carnal or material-minded.</note> Philosopher that God is active in created nature regarding corruption and deprivation just as much as in generation and placement; and yet no good Christian...

<summary>This page explains that God's single, unified essence operates through two modes—willing (affirmation) and nilling (negation)—which creatures perceive as good and evil, respectively. Using numerous biblical and Hermetic citations, the author argues that both properties are fundamentally good within God's absolute unity.</summary>

# Mosaical Philosophy. Book 1.

No one can be ignorant of the fact that either of these opposite properties, so familiar within one pure <note>original: "sincere"</note> essence, is absolutely good because it is completely excellent in its own goodness. This is true even though nothing is more terrible, fearful, abominable, or wicked to a creature than its own death and corruption. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 11:14</margin> If we Christians deny that this property exists in the Ideal Unity—namely, the power to deprive a creature of its life by withdrawing the act of life back into itself—we might justly consider ourselves inferior in judgment to the pagan <note>original: "Infidell"</note> poets and philosophers. These thinkers verify the axiom of the wise man: *Good and evil, life and death, riches and poverty, are all from God.* <note>original: "Bonum & malum, vita & mors, honestas & paupertas, a Deo sunt"</note> By this, he suggests that this one essential divinity operates in opposite ways within the created world through a two-fold differing property.

Their allegorical story is as follows: Proclus, following the ancient theology of Orpheus, Hesiod, Euripides, and Aeschylus—figures who enveloped hidden secrets learned from divine persons and those profound in the mysteries of God within their fabulous tales—deciphers the properties of the supreme and archetypal Son under the shadow of the visible and typical Sun. In this manner, he expresses that one and the same eternal essence performs all actions, both by taking away <note>original: "privatively"</note> and by giving <note>original: "positively"</note>. 

These poets call it by the name **Apollo** during the day because they claim that in his position and benign nature, manifested by the life-giving <note>original: "vivifying"</note> property of the Sun, he composes the creature of seven parts. By the **quaternary number** (4), the Pythagoreans symbolized matter, which is framed of the elements; for it is the square of 2 (an imperfect number) and therefore represents matter. By the **ternary number** (3), which is the number of perfection, they express the form of things. Thus, these two numbers united make up the **septenary number** (7), which includes the perfect completion of the creature. 

Conversely, they entitle it **Dionysius** during the night—that is, in his dark and privative disposition. They say that under this name, he tears and divides that same creature into seven pieces, which he had composed under the title of **Apollo** (his positive property or divine solar nature). So, they seem to argue that the same unity in essence is the author of destruction and corruption as well as the generation and life of the creature. However, they call it by different names according to the variety of its property. 

This is no different than how the Cabalist calls God, in His hidden and privative property, **dark Aleph** <note>original: "Aleph tenebrosum"</note>—namely, when He keeps His beams of life within Himself or withdraws His face from the creature—and **light Aleph** <note>original: "Aleph lucidum"</note> when He shines forth and extends His beams of life upon it. 

By this, we Christians may see that even the Pagans acknowledged what the Scriptures testify, though they did so through allegory. They concluded that it is only in the power of one and the same radical unity to save or destroy, to give life or take it away, to will or to refuse, and, in conclusion, to operate all things in all ways according to its pleasure. 

Thus, we have confirmed that these two members of an opposite condition or disposition spring from one eternal root, and that they operate in this world through completely contrary effects. Consequently, since the mass of waters—from which <margin>2 Peter 3</margin> the heavens and the earth were made of old—came out of the dark chaos and was, as it were, its second birth (which the poets feign to be **Pan**, or universal nature), the wise philosopher can easily see that this passive portion of the world is naturally inclined toward darkness and all its privative conditions. 

If it were not for the formal portion of the world, which proceeded from that bright spirit of wisdom—which <margin>Wisdom of Solomon 7:24–26</margin> Solomon calls *the breath of the power of God, and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty, and the brightness of the everlasting light, and the unspotted mirror of His goodness; that divided the waters into distinct orbs or spheres, and gave a proportional weight to the air, and tied or hung up the waters in the thick clouds by measure, and gave orders to the rain, and made a passage for the lightning of the thunders* <margin>Job 26:7; Job 28:25</margin>—if it were not, I say, for the action of this Spirit, all things would be the same. 

It is this Spirit that said, <margin>Ecclesiasticus 24:3–5</margin> *I came out of the mouth of the Most High, and I alone compassed the circuit of heaven, and walked in the bottom of the deep.* <note>original: "Ab ore altissimi prodij & rotunditatem cælorum circamivi solus in profundo abissi ambulavi"</note> It was the bright wisdom which <margin>Proverbs 8</margin> *the LORD possessed in the beginning of His way, before His works of old; before all time, before the world was made, when there was no depth, before there were any fountains, before the mountains were settled, or the earth was created.*

# Section 2. Mosaical Philosophy.

<margin>John 1.</margin>
*“When he made the heavens it was there; when he established the waters above it was there; when the limits of the sea were framed, lest the waters should pass their bounds; when he gave the earth her foundation, it was there with him, as a helper to compose all things.”* <note>The author is paraphrasing Proverbs 8 regarding Wisdom, though the marginal note refers to the Gospel of John, linking the "Word" with "Wisdom."</note> To conclude, by it all was formally made, and without it was nothing made or preserved. So that if it were not for the present action of this formal spirit, the watery matter of the world would return unto the deformed state of her mother, **Chaos**; for being in this world, it is inclined toward the disposition of her mother, being that it is passive, feminine, and serves in the place of the mother of all things. In another respect, the vivifying and bright emanation of the eternal Unity has become the masculine actor or father of all things, being that it gives life to every thing in this world, as the Apostle teaches us, and as the aforementioned poets seem to suggest to us under the name of **Apollo**, or the father of light.

This therefore being well observed, we may—by the discovery of these two abstruse and mystical principles, I mean Light and Darkness—attain the radical knowledge and origin of true **sympathy** and **antipathy**. It is evident that the first proceeds from that concording and vivifying love which arises from the benign emanation of the Creator, which desires to be joined with its like and seeks to preserve its like by union. The other issues from that discordant, depriving <note>original: "privative"</note>, and hateful affection which darkness and deformity grant to the children of light and life, and to all their beautiful offspring. By this, therefore, it appears that before the separation of these different properties (or effects of one unity)—namely, of light from darkness, which was brought to pass by the divine Word—all things were one and the same without distinction or difference. That unity or "one" was in no way to be numbered among those things which were created, so that light was darkness, and darkness light, and neither of these was discernable. Nothing was really distinguished, but all were one in the first matter of all things, which was in the eternal Unity. So then there was neither light nor darkness, nor day nor night, nor heaven nor earth, nor spirit nor body, nor good nor evil, nor pure nor impure, nor that which can be created nor that which can be destroyed, nor this nor that. And yet, nevertheless, all these—both spiritual and corporal—proceeded from that potential subject which remained folded within <note>original: "complicitely"</note> that infinite Unity, which both was, and is, and ever shall be: all in all, and over or beyond all. 

O admirable wisdom of God in all his works! All things (I say) proceeded from one matter, which nevertheless was none of these things which were made. All things were abstrusely hidden and in secret, but, according to our Savior’s words, nothing was so hidden and obscure that it would not be revealed and made to appear to the sight by the penetrating operation of the admirable word ***Fiat*** <note>Latin: "Let it be done," the command of creation in Genesis.</note>. By its divine spagyric <note>original: "spagericall" — referring to the alchemical process of separating and purifying components.</note> action or virtue, that one thing was divided into two contraries, upon which names well-befitting their natures were imposed. For the one, as I have told you, was called Light, and the other Darkness; the first also was termed Day, and the last Night; and thus was the pure separated from the impure. 

Hence, therefore, it comes that all the world was originally divided into two contrary kingdoms that correspond to these two radical branches of one unity. By this relationship, it is easy to express what in truth is light and darkness, what is day and night, what is goodness and what is badness, what is heaven and what is hell, what is truth and what is falsehood, what is humility and what is pride, what is justice and what is injustice, what is gladness and what is sorrow, what is sweet and what is bitter, what is action and what is passion, what is life and what is death, what is generation and what is corruption, what is pure and what is impure, what is wholesome and what is pernicious, what is a medicine and what is a poison, and, to conclude, what is amiable and what is odious, what is concord and what is discord, and, by consequence, what is sympathy and what is antipathy in an infinity of creatures in this world.

That the whole world and every creature within it is composed of these two contrarieties, or opposite natures, we find justified as much by sacred authority as by the testimony of pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophy. For the son of **Sirach** <note>The author of the biblical book of Ecclesiasticus.</note> says, in the place specified before: <margin>Ecclesiasticus 42:24-25</margin> *“All things are double, one against another, and he has made nothing defective.”* <note>original: "Gemina sunt omnia quorum alterum contrarium est alteri, nec quicquam factum est quod mancum est"</note> And thereupon the philosopher **Heraclitus** concludes that all things in the world are made by strife and concord; and **Empedocles** maintains that the soul is composed of the elements, and of friendship and enmity. To conclude, lest some scrupulous reader...

# Mosaical Philosophy. Book 1.

...lest someone should condemn me for making such a long discourse upon these two contrary principles proceeding from one Root, I thought it most fit to assure every discerning person that the true knowledge of them is of special importance. This is because these two principles are observed to be the real and only foundation of both universal Philosophy and Theology. The root and basis of them both consist in the true understanding of these two opposites. Therefore, if they are not first well-explained and understood, how is it possible for them to be rightly handled either in true Philosophy or understood in those places of Holy Scripture where they are so often mentioned? 

Regarding the explanation of this most profound *Sphinx-like Riddle* <note>original: "Sphyngian Riddle"; a reference to the complex and deadly riddles of the Sphinx in Greek mythology</note> or hidden question—namely, why God in his secret purpose or mental intent did raise up and ordain these two contraries out of the unformed matter (which was ideally sketched within himself), causing all things in the world to be put into a mutual disharmony, or struggle and conflict with one another, so that nothing is found that participates in goodness which does not also have its contrary (that is to say, which does not communicate with badness, insomuch that God himself is not without an adversary)—truly, it is too hidden a mystery <note>original: "occult a Cabal"</note> to be explained by mortal capacity. It may well be esteemed the most profound secret of all the divine mysteries. 

Therefore, a mental perspective is required—one well-purged and purified <note>original: "mundified"</note> from every misty cloud of ignorance and error—to search into the depths of this question. It is impossible to be revealed to anyone except those to whom God immediately bestows his grace and Holy Spirit, which is the searcher of all mysteries. This Spirit is in us; it breathes and blows when and where it chooses. It is called in the Scriptures the Spirit of Truth, the Spirit of Sanctification, the Spirit of Illumination, and the Spirit of Revelation, which is the best interpreter of the Divine Secrets mentioned in Holy Scripture. Truly, it does not become us to inquire of our own accord why God made this or that, or why he did it in a certain fashion. Instead, it behaves the seeker to refer all this to the time when these secrets shall be discovered, which will happen when the **seventh seal** <note>A reference to the Book of Revelation, signifying the final stage of God's plan for the world.</note> is opened. For then that high mystery—which is the final cause of why and for what end God’s Providence reveals itself through these two opposites, and will completely extinguish all enmity out of the world—shall be discovered. 

Nevertheless, regarding the end of this disharmony, the Apostle says that it will be when the Son has delivered the Kingdom to God the Father, and when he has done away with every principality, power, and virtue. He must reign until he has made his enemies his footstool, and the last enemy that shall be destroyed is Death. So, just as two contraries or discords proceeded from one Unity or unison (namely Light and Darkness from one Divine Essence), so also these two discordant branches or confusion of unities will at last be reduced or return again into one harmonious Unity, in which there will be found no disharmony. This will occur when these words of the Book of Revelation are accomplished: 

<margin>Revelation 21</margin>
*Behold, I make all things new: for the old heaven and earth have passed away.* <note>original Latin: "Ecce omnia nova facio: vetera enim transierunt"</note> 

But leaving this side-discussion, we will proceed directly to our argument or inquiry into Sympathy and Antipathy. So that we may penetrate this topic with greater speed and ease, and dive deeper into the study of their actions, it is appropriate that we first describe the manner in which the world lives through the participation of these two—namely, Light and Darkness. I will express to you in few words what the ancient philosophers have determined about the **soul of the world** <note>The *Anima Mundi*, or the concept that the universe itself is a living being with a soul.</note>; and lastly, I will show that their opinions do not err or vary much from the testimony of the Holy Bible.

### Section 2. Mosaical Philosophy.

...some self-conceited and unskilled persons, in so profound a mystery, and one so highly prized and esteemed by others who have (with the sharp, eagle-eyed vision <note>original: "Lyncean eye-sight"; referring to Lynceus, an Argonaut famed for sight so keen he could see through the earth</note> of their understanding) dived and penetrated into the secret depths of Nature, and with due reverence contemplated her central and eternal Agent. Afterward, my intention is to set down the agreement observed between these thinkers and Holy Scripture. 

The Cabalists' belief is that the great Angel whom they term *Metatron* (which by interpretation is *Donum Dei*, or "the gift of God") is that very same universal Spirit which animates the whole world. Based on this, *Rabbi Moses* <note>Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, also known as Maimonides</note> asserts it to be the <term>active intellect</term> <note>original: "Intellectus agens"</note>, or the general intellectual agent from which all particular forms flow. They say that from this universal angelic Spirit, all <margin>Reuchlin, *On the Art of the Cabala*, Book 3.</margin> individual virtues—whether animal, vital, or natural—proceed. These they also call "Angels," of which there are an infinite number beyond our capacity to count. 

The philosopher *Democritus*, as well as *Orpheus* and various *Pythagoreans*, do not differ much from the opinion of these Rabbis, except in the names they use. They imagined that all things are full of gods; therefore, they offered divine honors, prayers, and sacrifices to them within the creatures, and worshiped each of them with a different style of ceremony. But they always maintained such a regard for JEHOVAH, the eternal Unity and Father of all things, that they referred all these "gods" back to one *Jupiter*. Nevertheless, this point being misunderstood by the ignorant was a primary cause of idolatry, as the simple-minded fell into worshiping the creature instead of the Divinity that resided within the creature. For this reason, *Solomon* wrote: <margin>Wisdom of Solomon 13.</margin>

> All men are naturally vain in whom there is ignorance of God. From the good things that are seen, they were unable to understand Him who truly exists; nor, by considering His works, did they acknowledge the Workman. <note>original Latin: "Vani sunt homines omnes naturâ in quibus est ignorantia Dei, & qui ex iis quæ spectantur bonis, eum qui est, intelligere non potuerunt, neque ex operibus consideratis, ipsum opificem agnoverunt"</note>

In other words, all men are naturally foolish if they lack the knowledge of God. They cannot conceive of Him who truly exists by looking at the good creatures they perceive with their senses, nor have they examined and discovered the *Workman* by considering His works. 

In a similar way, the *Platonists* called the general power that produced and preserved all things the <term>soul of the world</term> <note>original: "Animam mundi"</note>. The *Arabic Astrologers* seem to agree with this opinion, for they maintained that every particular thing in the world has its own distinct and peculiar soul derived from this life-giving Spirit. *Mercurius Trismegistus*, *Theophrastus*, *Avicenna*, *Algazel*, and all the *Stoics* and *Peripatetics* <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> also seem to entirely consent or agree with this view. 

Furthermore, *Zoroaster* and *Heraclitus the Ephesian* concluded that the soul of the world is that universal invisible fire, by whose action all things are generated and brought forth from potentiality into actual being. *Virgil*, 그hat excellent Latin poet, calls it that mental Spirit which is infused through every joint and member of the world, by which its whole mass—namely, the heaven and the earth, or spirit and body—is moved in a mysterious way. His words are these:

<margin>*Aeneid*, Book 6.</margin>
> A Spirit within sustains them; and Mind, infused throughout the limbs, moves the entire mass... <note>original Latin: "Spiritus intus alit totamque infusa per artus / Mens agitat molem, &c."</note>

A Spirit (he says) nourishes from within, and being infused through all the joints or members of the world, it moves the whole substance of the same. *Marcus Manilius*, as well as *Boethius* and *Augurel* <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello, an Italian humanist and alchemist</note>, who were later poets, share Virgil’s opinion. For *Manilius* says:

<margin>In *Astronomica*, dedicated to Augustus.</margin>
> The divine power of the soul governs this work, which is built within the body of the vast world. <note>original Latin: "Hoc opus immensi constructum corpore mundi / Vis animæ divina regit."</note>

And *Boethius* writes:

> You connect a central soul of a triple nature, which moves all things. <note>original Latin: "Tu triplicis mediam naturæ, cuncta moventem, / Connectis animam."</note>

And *Augurel* says:

<margin>Book 1, *Chrysopoeia*.</margin>
> Some say that whatever is spread throughout the heavens, the air, the lands, and the wide surface of the marble sea... <note>original Latin: "Nonnulli quicquid diffunditur undique cæli, / Aëraque & terras & lati marmoris æquor"</note>

The author argues that while these groups use different names (like Metatron or the Active Intellect), they are describing the same divine reality.</summary>

# Mosaicall Philosophy. Book. I.

> ->*They say that within all things are moved by a soul, through which they believe*<-
> ->*All things of the world live, and that the world itself leads its life by this.*<-
> ->*But because a soul is entirely free of a body,*<-
> ->*And yet the world and the world's parts consist of body;*<-
> ->*This intermediate spirit is created, which they call neither body*<-
> ->*Nor soul, but that which alone, participating in both,*<-
> ->*Brings these extremes together into one.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Intus agi referunt animâ, quâ vivere mundi / Cuncta putant, ipsumque hàc mundum ducere vitam. / Ast anima quoniam nil non est corporis expers, / Mundus at & mundi partes quoque corpore constant; / Spiritus hic intermedius fit, quem neque corpus / Aut animum dicunt sed eum qui solus utroque / Participans in idem simul haec extrema redacat."</note>

Some say that whatever fills the **Heavens**, the **Air**, the **Earth**, and the wide **Seas** is stirred up by a soul, through the virtue of which all things in the world live; and also that the world itself exists by it. But because there is no soul that is not entirely devoid of a body, and yet the world and every part of it consists of a body, there is an intermediate spirit between this soul and body. This they call neither a soul nor a body, but a middle substance, participating in both, to bring both extremes together into one.

<margin>*The Art of Chemistry*, chapter 4.</margin>
The wiser kind of Alchemists describe the Soul as a certain infinite nature or power in all things, which produces like from like. For this nature generates all things—indeed, it multiplies, nourishes, and sustains them. They also call it the **Ligament**, or the bond of the elements, since by it they are fastened together with the symphonic chords of peaceful harmony, even though by themselves—that is, in regard to their matter—they are discordant. Also, it is termed the true virtue that mingles and proportions everything in this <term>sublunary world</term> <note>original: "sublunary world"; the realm of the four elements below the moon, subject to change and decay</note>, allotting to each specific creature a convenient and well-agreeing form, so that one thing might be distinguished and varied from another. In conclusion, the mystical Rabbis assert that this hidden fire is that Spirit of the Lord, or fiery love, which, when it moved upon the waters, imparted to them a certain harmonious and hidden fiery virtue. Without its lovely assistance and favorable heat, nothing could be generated from them or multiplied within them.

Thus you may discern the many opinions of both Christian and Heathen philosophers concerning this *Anima mundi*, or soul of the world. These views will appear to vary little or not at all from the tenets of Holy Scripture in meaning, but only in words. Neither are these opinions as heinous or abominable as some Christians of our age—who are more superstitiously zealous than truly understanding—would make them out to be, if they would examine the matter wisely and with moderation. For then they would truly perceive that it concurs with the Bible of Truth. To confirm what I now say, my purpose is first to express to every learned and well-minded reader the harmony of the Scriptures regarding this point. Then, I will compare every one of the aforementioned opinions with the meaning and grounds of that harmony, so that every wise man may better guess at the truth of the matter before he rashly begins to judge that deep and profound mystery concerning the Divine action in natural effects.

I told you in my previous discourse that the Eternal Unity, who is the God of gods and the Beginning of beginnings, caused two different principles to issue from Himself by a double property in one essence. One was potential and in no way yet <term>inacted</term> <note>original: "inacted"; brought into actual, manifest existence from a state of possibility</note> by the brightness of His emanation; in that respect, it is termed Darkness, privation, or <term>Nolunty</term> <note>original: "Nolunty"; from the Latin "noluntas," meaning "unwillingness" or the negative aspect of God's will</note>, the opposite of Light and a friend to death and rest. The other was actual, and nothing else but a pure universal form and brightness, which is termed Light, Position, or <term>Volunty</term> <note>original: "Volunty"; from "voluntas," meaning "will" or God's active, creative desire</note>, and is in nature opposite to Darkness and a friend to life and action, or motion. 

And then I indicated to you that by the bright appearance of Eternity, or the Eternal Spirit of Wisdom—which I termed, using the language of the Scriptures, the radiant emanation or "effluxion from the Almighty," which is one with Him in essence—the deformed waters were enacted and made manifest out of this dark Principle or Chaos. That is, they were reduced from *Potentia Divina*, or the **Divine Power** without form in which they remained, into *Actum Divinum*, the **Divine Act**. 

<margin>Genesis 1.</margin>
And because all the moist and passive universal nature, from which both the heavens and the earth were framed, issued from this mass of watery matter—which the Poets call **Pan** <note>original: "Pana"; likely the accusative form of the Greek god Pan, often allegorized as "Universal Nature"</note>, or the second birth of Chaos—we must imagine it to be that spiritual matter of the world which was made fertile and capable of multiplication because of that hidden, active, and formal Light or invisible fire which this increased emanation imparted to it immediately before the creation of the heavens and the earth. ### Section 2. Mosaical Philosophy.

On the holy text, it says: *The Spirit of the Lord moved or was carried upon the waters.* <note>original: "Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas"</note> And as St. Augustine adds to it, *Bestowing upon them a fiery vigor or formal and active virtue.* <note>original: "igneum illis vigorem impertiens"</note> Now, as we see that Man, who is called the "little world" <term>microcosm</term>, is composed of soul and body—where the soul is his heaven or spiritual part (or, as we may say, the superior and higher waters), and the body with its humors (as if it were the lower waters, the earth, and grosser humors)—and each of these two are informed, united, and vivified by the Spirit of life which God inspired into it; even so we may observe that the heaven, or the spiritual humid nature of the "great world" <term>macrocosm</term>, is animated by the eternal emanation or spirit of the supernatural wisdom of God to give life and shape to the world. 

And because it is easy to discern that the macrocosmic heavens are of two sorts—namely, composed of upper spiritual waters, which are called *Ether*, or heavenly; and of the lower spiritual waters, which are called *Air*, or elementary—no differently than in the lesser world (man), where the receptacle of the heavenly spirit is known to be the air, so that physicians distinguish (by reason of this difference) between the vital or ethereal spirits and the natural or elementary body. So we ought to consider that this material, humid spirit of the heavens in both worlds—which is the subtlety of the waters—is in itself dead; but in respect to the super-celestial emanation into them, which informs and vivifies them, they live, move, and are thinner or thicker, according to that more or less formal grace which the all-informing Spirit allots them. For the more the sacred Spirit of life abounds, or really acts, in this or that region of the universal air, the more that sphere is thin, subtle, active, worthy, and noble.

# Mosaical Philosophy: Book 1.

<margin>Psalm 33:6</margin>
...your wisdom. And again, *By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the breath of his mouth all their power.* <note>original: "Verbo Domini firmati sunt cæli & Spiritu oris ejus omnis virtus eorum"</note> These words seem to imply not only the material substance of the world (which is indicated by the word "heavens"), but also the enacting form—that is, the life-giving beginning of all things, which itself has no beginning. This is signified by the "Word" and its offspring, the Spirit, from which the waters first received their being. Then, from these universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> waters, the heavens, the earth, and the elements were made in number, weight, and measure. That is to say, they were brought into existence by a subdivision through the spagyric act <term>the alchemical process of separating and purifying components</term> of the very same Word or Spirit.

<margin>2 Peter 3</margin>
Therefore, Saint Peter says, *The heavens and the earth were of old made of waters and by waters, existing by the word of God.* <note>original: "Cæli erunt priùs & terra de aquis & per aquas consistentes verbo Dei"</note> This is as if to say that after the Spirit of the Lord had issued out of the dark abyss (for it is said, *The Word was in the beginning* <note>original: "Verbum erat in principio"</note>) and had given action and form—and consequently a name—to the waters (for it was said that the *Spirit of the Lord was carried upon the waters*), that same Spirit operated to reveal explicitly and particularly what the Chaos contained within itself at first in a complex and confused way. Therefore, when it had revealed the universal matter of all things, which was water, it gradually analyzed it <note>original: "anatomise it"</note> and opened its secret closets to show forth and make manifest what had lain hidden in it from all eternity. Before this, it was without form or being, and therefore rightly esteemed as "Nothing." First, the substance of the world was made from it in general, as appears by this text:

<margin>Wisdom 11:18</margin>
*The hand of the Almighty made the world out of unformed matter.* <note>original: "Manus omnipotens mundum ex informi materia effecit"</note> And as Saint Jerome interprets it, *Of an unseen or invisible thing.* <note>original: "Ex materia invisa"</note> Then, that watery and moist substance was divided into the heaven and earth by distinguishing the "waters from the waters" by the same Spirit, which is the ministering hand of the Almighty; for the text says:

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 24; Proverbs 9</margin>
*In the holy dwelling place I ministered before him.* <note>original: "In habitatione sancta coram ipso ministravi"</note> And again, *Wisdom was she who composed all things with God.* <note>original: "Sapientia apud ipsum fuit cuncta componens"</note> This was the second day's work. Then the lower waters were divided into elements—namely, earth, water, air, etc.—and that was the third day's separation, as Moses methodically demonstrates. All of this, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and alchemical texts were attributed</note> expresses in this way (as was said before):

<margin>Pymander 1</margin>
*The Word, which was created, issued out of the Voice of Light, and this Word, being present and assisting the moist nature, fostered and preserved it. Then the clear and light fire, proceeding out of the bowels of the moist nature, immediately flew upward and sought the heights. The thin air also, which is the father of the spirit, chose the middle region between the fire and the water for its abode. The earth and water lay so mingled together that the face of the earth was nowhere visible, being overwhelmed by the waters.* <note>original Latin: "Ex luminis voce verbum fatum prodit..."</note> By this, it is evidently proved that this thin spiritual water, or "moist nature," is in itself nothing more than a man's spirit without the life-giving act of life. For just as in the soul of every living creature two things are chiefly required—namely, an "Agent" (the mover) and a "Patient" (the receiver)—where one of these is missing, there can be no created soul. If the world's life were only the essential breath of God, without the medium of the created moist spirit (which is the matter of heaven), then that life would be simple "identity" <note>pure, undifferentiated being</note> and have only one property. Consequently, there would be no variety of action, nor any contraction or expansion—the "systole and diastole" <note>the rhythmic beating or pulsing of life</note>—in things, and therefore no action or passion in the soul. Without a passive nature, there can be no action, and without an active nature, there can be no passion.

Now, matter which proceeds from water is the subject of all "passion" (receiving action), just as here the "Mother Chaos" was the female or passive element to the action of Demogorgon <term>a primordial creator deity or force of nature</term>, or God. Also, "act" or "form," which proceeds from light, is the subject of all action, just as its father, Eternity—the bright emanation of the spirit of wisdom from the fountain of light—was the male or agent. From this, therefore, it is an easy thing to gather, first, what the "Soul of the World" is, and what parts it consists of. We must consider that just as every creature has an interior and an exterior, so we must carefully search for an internal and an external in the Soul, since it is a creature. And again, it is most certain that it is a creature because it is not Identity...

It is that universal or general spirit, divinely animated from the beginning, which afterwards gives life to each particular creature in the world, proceeding from the general to the specific, and from the specific to the individual. 

By this, the mighty question—so often turned over by the Peripatetic <term>followers of Aristotle</term> philosophers, and so poorly resolved by them—may be fully determined and explained. If the wise and impartial reader considers things as they actually are, it is easy to express and distinguish the *divine mind* <note>original: "mentem divinam"</note>, or the *divine emanation*, from the *soul* <note>original: "anima"</note>; and again, the *soul* from the *spirit* <note>original: "spiritus"</note>.

The "spirit" is that inward created spirit of the world, or the subtle substance of the waters, or the humid nature, simply considered in itself, which is animated and illuminated by that archetypal <term>the original model or divine pattern</term> emanation. Finally, the "soul" (or *anima*) is that union which is made between this humid created spirit and the uncreated formal emanation which informs or creates. 

So by this we may discern, first, what the *informing form* <note>original: "forma informans"</note> or *naturing nature* <note>original: "natura naturans"</note> is; then what the *informed form* <note>original: "forma informata"</note> or the *natured nature* <note>original: "natura naturata"</note> is. 

*   The *informing form* or *naturing nature* is **God**, or the divine emanation which created all things. 
*   The *informed form* or *natured nature* is the created light, or the spirit informed or illuminated by the presence of the bright uncreated Spirit.
